def merged_honoring(records: Iterable[IgnoreFileExclusions]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """``honored`` for the records of several scans merged into one record.

    With ``honored_scan_count`` and ``scan_count`` as well when the scans
    disagree. A record that is itself merged counts as the scans it stands for
    (``IgnoreFileExclusions.scan_counts``), so merging merged records keeps their
    counts. ``ash merge`` and a workspace scan's merged results both use this.
    """
    honoring = total = 0
    for record in records:
        record_honoring, record_total = record.scan_counts()
        honoring += record_honoring
        total += record_total
    merged: Dict[str, Any] = {"honored": honoring == total}
    if 0 < honoring < total:
        merged["honored_scan_count"] = honoring
        merged["scan_count"] = total
    return merged

docs.title: ignore_paths_that_skip_scanning(ignore_paths, *, ignore_suppressions)
docs.text:
The ignore paths that keep a file from being converted or scanned at all.

Those the operator supplied. A path a delivered tree's own config supplied (client_supplied) is left to the SARIF step instead, which keeps a finding under it as a marked, suppressed result, so the results show what the client's config hid. Applying it before the scan as well would mean no finding to keep. The cost is that those files are scanned.

None under --ignore-suppressions. An ignore path is a suppression, and the flag lifts every suppression for every scanner: the files under one are converted and scanned, and their findings are reported. Without this the flag's effect would depend on the scanner, since a scanner that reads the whole directory reports those findings anyway and one that is handed only the files left after this filter never sees them. The cost is a slower scan. Keyword-only and required, so every caller states the flag.

Source code in automated_security_helper/models/core.py 
def ignore_paths_that_skip_scanning(
    ignore_paths: "List[IgnorePathWithReason] | None",
    *,
    ignore_suppressions: bool,
) -> "List[IgnorePathWithReason]":
    """The ignore paths that keep a file from being converted or scanned at all.

    Those the operator supplied. A path a delivered tree's own config supplied
    (``client_supplied``) is left to the SARIF step instead, which keeps a finding
    under it as a marked, suppressed result, so the results show what the
    client's config hid. Applying it before the scan as well would mean no
    finding to keep. The cost is that those files are scanned.

    None under ``--ignore-suppressions``. An ignore path is a suppression, and the
    flag lifts every suppression for every scanner: the files under one are
    converted and scanned, and their findings are reported. Without this the
    flag's effect would depend on the scanner, since a scanner that reads the
    whole directory reports those findings anyway and one that is handed only the
    files left after this filter never sees them. The cost is a slower scan.
    Keyword-only and required, so every caller states the flag.
    """
    if ignore_suppressions:
        return []
    return [path for path in ignore_paths or [] if path.client_supplied is not True]

docs.title: suppression_id(suppression)
docs.text:
Identifier for a suppression given as a dict of its fields.

Shared by AshSuppression.id and the config linter, which reads raw YAML dicts, so the unused-suppressions report and the linter's fixer agree.

Source code in automated_security_helper/models/core.py 
def suppression_id(suppression: Dict[str, Any]) -> str:
    """Identifier for a suppression given as a dict of its fields.

    Shared by ``AshSuppression.id`` and the config linter, which reads raw YAML
    dicts, so the unused-suppressions report and the linter's fixer agree.
    """
    line_start = suppression.get("line_start")
    line_end = suppression.get("line_end")
    line_end_val = line_end if line_end is not None else line_start
    parts = [
        suppression.get("path") or "",
        suppression.get("rule_id") or "*",
        str(line_start) if line_start is not None else "*",
        str(line_end_val) if line_end_val is not None else "*",
    ]
    symbol = suppression.get("symbol")
    if symbol or any(suppression.get(f) for f in PACKAGE_SUPPRESSION_FIELDS):
        parts.append(
            "@".join(suppression.get(f) or "*" for f in PACKAGE_SUPPRESSION_FIELDS)
        )
    # A symbol is a sixth part, and its presence always brings the fifth, so an
    # id's part count says which fields it carries and a symbol can never be
    # read as a package.
    if symbol:
        parts.append(symbol)
    return "|".join(parts)

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This page explains how ASH is put together — the execution model, how plugins are discovered and run, and how findings move through the system. For the domain vocabulary (finding, scanner, reporter, suppression), see Core Concepts.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ASH is a plugin-based security scanning orchestrator. It does not itself analyze code — it drives a collection of third-party scanners (Bandit, Semgrep, Checkov, Grype, cfn-nag, and others), normalizes their heterogeneous output into SARIF, and hands the aggregated results to a pluggable set of reporters.

Three design choices shape the rest of the system:

  • SARIF as the internal interchange format. Every scanner's output is converted to SARIF before anything else touches it. Suppressions, metrics, and reporters all operate on SARIF.
  • Phases as the top-level control flow. Execution is a fixed sequence of phases. Each phase has one job and a stable interface.
  • Everything non-core is a plugin. Scanners, converters, and reporters are all plugins discovered at startup and registered with a central manager.

docs.title: Execution Phases
docs.text:
A scan runs four phases in order:

flowchart LR
    A[Convert] --> B[Scan]
    B --> C[Report]
    C --> D[Inspect]

    style A fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#0969da
    style B fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#0969da
    style C fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#0969da
    style D fill:#f0fff0,stroke:#2da44e

Each phase is a class inheriting from EnginePhase (see automated_security_helper/core/phases/):

  • Convert (convert_phase.py) — transforms input files into formats scanners can read. Jupyter notebooks become Python, archives are extracted, Helm charts are rendered.
  • Scan (scan_phase.py) — runs every enabled scanner against the source and converted directories, collecting SARIF from each.
  • Report (report_phase.py) — hands the aggregated results to every enabled reporter, which writes output files in its requested format.
  • Inspect (inspect_phase.py) — launches the interactive TUI for reviewing findings. Optional; skipped in non-interactive runs.

Phases can be run selectively via the --phases flag. The scan can also be resumed from existing results by running report or inspect alone against a prior output directory.

The ScanExecutionEngine in core/execution_engine.py owns the sequence. It constructs each phase, wires in the PluginContext (shared state including paths, config, and logger), and runs them serially.

docs.title: Plugin Lifecycle
docs.text:
Scanners, converters, and reporters all follow the same lifecycle:

flowchart TD
    A[Startup] --> B[Discover]
    B --> C[Register]
    C --> D[Configure]
    D --> E[Filter enabled]
    E --> F[Execute]
    F --> G[Collect output]

    style B fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#0969da
    style F fill:#fff4e6,stroke:#e36209
  1. Discover. On startup, discover_plugins() walks the Python module path looking for packages in the ash_plugins namespace. Any package exporting ASH_SCANNERS, ASH_CONVERTERS, or ASH_REPORTERS contributes its classes. Built-in plugins are loaded the same way.
  2. Register. The @ash_scanner_plugin, @ash_converter_plugin, and @ash_reporter_plugin decorators register classes with the central ash_plugin_manager.
  3. Configure. When a phase starts, each plugin class is instantiated with its config drawn from the resolved AshConfig. The config is looked up by plugin type and lowercased class name.
  4. Filter. A plugin is skipped if config.enabled is False, if --python-based-plugins-only is set and the plugin isn't Python-only, or if CLI flags (--scanners, --exclude-scanners) exclude it. For scanners these filters are applied before ASH looks for the scanner's tool, so a scanner a filter leaves out is SKIPPED whether or not its tool is installed. A selected scanner whose tool is not found is MISSING.
  5. Execute. Enabled scanners run in parallel via a ThreadPoolExecutor (default) or sequentially if --strategy sequential. Each scanner returns SARIF, which the phase merges into the aggregated results.
  6. Collect. Plugin status (succeeded, failed, skipped, disabled) is recorded on the aggregated results so reporters can surface coverage gaps.

Custom plugins follow the same rules. Point ASH at your package with --ash-plugin-modules my_ash_plugins and your classes will be discovered and treated the same as built-ins.

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Source Code] --> B[Converters]
    B --> C[Converted Files]
    A --> D[Scanners]
    C --> D
    D --> E[Raw Tool Output]
    E --> F[SARIF Normalization]
    F --> G[AshAggregatedResults]
    G --> H[Suppression Filtering]
    H --> I[Reporters]
    I --> J[Output Files]

    style G fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#0969da
    style F fill:#fff4e6,stroke:#e36209

Each scanner wraps an external tool, invokes it against the target, parses the tool's native output (JSON, XML, or custom text), and converts it into SARIF. The SARIF documents from all scanners are merged into a single AshAggregatedResults object (defined in models/asharp_model.py).

Suppressions are applied as a filtering pass over the SARIF runs, not at scanner level. This is why inline suppressions and config-based suppressions produce identical results — both end up as Kind1.inSource entries in the final SARIF, distinguished only by their justification prefix.

Reporters receive the aggregated results and write to the output directory. Because every reporter reads the same SARIF, adding a new output format means writing a reporter — you never touch the scanners.

docs.title: SARIF as the Canonical Format
docs.text:
SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format, OASIS standard) is the internal data model for every finding. Concretely:

  • Every scanner produces SARIF, either natively or via a conversion step inside the scanner plugin.
  • Suppression rules match against SARIF properties (rule ID, file path, line range).
  • Metrics — severity counts, scanner-by-scanner statistics, the metrics table — are computed from SARIF.
  • Reporters consume SARIF and transform it into their output format (HTML, CSV, CycloneDX, OCSF, Security Hub events).

The tradeoff is that SARIF is verbose and not every tool maps cleanly onto it (Grype's CycloneDX-first model is a notable example). The upside is that adding a scanner doesn't force any other component to change, and adding a reporter automatically gets you every scanner's findings.

docs.title: Configuration Resolution
docs.text:
Configuration is resolved at the start of every run. resolve_config() in config/resolve_config.py performs the following, in order:

  1. Start with the default config from default_config.py — all built-in scanners and reporters enabled, conservative ignore paths.
  2. Find a config file by checking the following names in the source directory and .ash/ subdirectory:
.ash.yml      .ash.yaml      .ash.json
ash.yml       ash.yaml       ash.json

The first match wins. If --config is passed explicitly, that file is used directly and no search happens. 3. Merge the config file over the defaults. Values in the file replace defaults; lists replace (not append to) defaults unless the file uses the += append syntax. 4. Apply CLI overrides. --config-overrides values are applied last and win over both the default and the file. They use dot-path syntax:

ash --config-overrides 'scanners.bandit.enabled=false'
ash --config-overrides 'global_settings.ignore_paths+=[{"path": "build/"}]'
5. Validate. The merged dict is parsed into an AshConfig pydantic model. Unknown fields, wrong types, or invalid values raise an error before any scanner runs.

The resolved AshConfig is attached to the PluginContext and passed to every phase and plugin, so runtime behavior is fully determined before the first scanner starts.

docs.title: Building your own container image
docs.text: ASH does not publish a container image to a public registry, and is not planning to. The recommended posture is that the organization running ASH builds the image and hosts it in its own registry.

docs.title: Why you build it yourself
docs.text:
ASH reads your source code. An image that scans your repositories sits in the same trust position as your build tooling, so the question "what is in this image, when did it change, and who approved that change" needs an answer that belongs to you rather than to an upstream publisher.

Building it yourself gives you four things a pulled public image cannot:

  • A known provenance. The image came from a Dockerfile in a commit you can name, built by a pipeline you control.
  • A patching cadence you set. You decide when the base image and the bundled scanner tools move, rather than inheriting whenever an upstream tag was pushed.
  • A scanning surface you can inspect. The image can be scanned, signed, and admitted by the same controls you already apply to your own images.
  • No new external dependency at scan time. Your CI pulls from your registry, so a scan does not fail because a public registry is unavailable or rate-limited.

The tradeoff is real and worth stating plainly: you own the rebuild cadence. An image built once and never rebuilt ages, and ASH's bundled scanners age with it. See Keeping it current.

docs.title: Build it once, host it internally
docs.text:
# Build the image
ash build-image --build-target non-root

# Tag and push to your own registry
docker tag automated-security-helper:non-root \
  my-registry.example.com/security/ash:3.6.0
docker push my-registry.example.com/security/ash:3.6.0

Two build targets exist:

Target Runs as Use when non-root An unprivileged user The default. Prefer it. ci Root The runner's UID/GID mapping makes an unprivileged user impractical

non-root is the default everywhere except Windows. On Windows, container mode (ash --mode container, Invoke-ASH) and ash build-image default to the ci stage, because the output directory is bind-mounted and the runtime there does not map write permissions onto that mount, so the non-root user could not write its reports and logs. Pass --build-target non-root (-BuildTarget non-root) to build the unprivileged image on Windows anyway. Running in CI does not change the default: CI, IsCI, ISCI and CODEBUILD_BUILD_ID play no part, and an explicit --build-target always wins. The stage name is read in any case, as the build reads it: NON-ROOT is non-root, and is built, tagged and checked as non-root. --custom-containerfile builds on ci; with it, --build-target non-root names the custom file's own non-root stage (see Extending the image).

The non-root stage creates its user with the UID and GID of the account running ASH, or with --container-uid and --container-gid. A UID of 0 is root and cannot be that user, and a GID of 0 is root's group, so a non-root build with UID 0 or GID 0 is refused before anything is built, and so is a UID or GID that is not a number. That is the case when ASH itself runs as root, as many CI jobs do (AWS CodeBuild, container-based GitLab and Jenkins jobs): pass --build-target ci there. Another --container-uid and --container-gid work only when the output directory is writable by that UID, since the container runs as that user and writes its reports there; on a root host ASH creates the output directory as root. ./ash refuses it the same way, and so does Invoke-ASH, run as root or given -ContainerUID 0 or -ContainerGID 0; its opt-in is -BuildTarget ci. On Linux and macOS, Invoke-ASH gives the non-root user the caller's own UID and GID (id -u, id -g) unless -ContainerUID or -ContainerGID names another, as ./ash and ash --mode container do, and checks both the same way; on Windows the Dockerfile's defaults apply.

The opt-in for a job that runs as root, such as an AWS CodeBuild build:

ash --mode container --build-target ci        # or: ./ash --build-target ci

Invoke-ASH -BuildTarget ci

Point ASH at your published image with ASH_IMAGE_NAME:

export ASH_IMAGE_NAME="my-registry.example.com/security/ash:3.6.0"
ash --mode container --source-dir .

Tag with the ASH version you built rather than only latest, so a scan result can be traced back to a specific image. A moving latest makes two scans that disagree impossible to explain.

The image's ASH must be the same version as the ASH that runs the scan, or later. Container mode reads the scan's results back only when the ASH in the image records that its run completed, which ASH v3.7.1 and earlier do not do. With an image built from an older ASH, every container scan exits 1 with an error saying the inner run did not complete. Rebuild and republish the image when you upgrade the ASH that runs your scans.

docs.title: Who can write to the image's directories
docs.text:
Who owns each of the image's directories, and who else may write it:

Directory Owner Why /deps, /deps/.semgrep, /deps/.opengrep (offline rules), /ash, /.ash/bin (bundled tools, first on PATH) root, not writable by others Nothing writes there at scan time /deps/.grype (grype's database), /deps/.trivy (trivy's cache, TRIVY_CACHE_DIR) the user the image runs as: root in ci, the unprivileged user in non-root; root in an offline image grype's and trivy's database updates write them at scan time; an offline image never updates them /src, /out writable by every user, with the sticky bit (ci); the unprivileged user (non-root) A run mounts the source and the output here; without those mounts, these two stay writable when the ci image is started under another UID (the database caches do not, see below)

Outside /src, /out and the sticky scratch directories (/tmp, /var/tmp, /run/lock), nothing in the image is writable by every user. Each stage ends by clearing group and other write on anything an installer left that way, such as the lock files uv creates mode 666 in its cache and tool directories and the files some gems ship mode 777 under /var/lib/gems.

An image you extend with --custom-containerfile keeps these modes unless your Dockerfile changes them.

Because only its own user may write the grype and trivy database caches, an image started under a different UID than the one that owns them cannot update the databases: grype or trivy then reports ERROR and the scan fails, rather than scanning against a database it could not refresh. In a non-root image that owner is the UID it was built with (--container-uid, or the host's); in ci it is root, so a ci image has to run as root, which is how ASH's own runner starts it. Build a non-root image with the UID it will run as, or use ci and run it as root. A platform that starts every container under a UID of its own needs an image built for that UID.

docs.title: Which Dockerfile ASH builds
docs.text:
ash build-image and ash --mode container build ASH's own Dockerfile. They never build a Dockerfile found in the directory you run them from or in a directory above it: that file belongs to the project being scanned. Which of ASH's Dockerfiles is used depends on how ASH was installed:

  • Installed from a git URL or a package index. The Dockerfile packaged with ASH, which installs the same ASH revision from git inside the image (--ash-revision-to-install picks another one).
  • Installed from its source tree (an editable install, or pip install <dir> or uvx --from <dir>; the revision is LOCAL). The Dockerfile at the root of that source tree, with the tree as the build context. ASH finds the tree from where the running package is installed, so ash run from a subdirectory of the checkout, or from another project, builds the same image. A package an installer put in a site-packages directory, with its dist-info beside it, is never taken for a clone, whatever other files sit next to it.

A LOCAL revision for an installation with no source tree beside it or recorded for it (for example, ASH installed from a wheel file) is refused before anything is built. Pass --ash-revision-to-install <tag>, reinstall ASH from its source directory, or run an image you already have with --no-build.

docs.title: Which ASH goes into the image
docs.text:
The image installs ASH from source. Which source depends on how the ASH that runs the build was installed:

ASH running the build Source of the image's ASH A clone of the ASH repository, an editable install of one, or pip install <directory> That source tree, the same ASH as the one running. If the directory has since been deleted, or no longer holds ASH's source, the image installs the commit the package build recorded, as in the last row. The directory is trusted by its path, so install from one only you can write, not from under /tmp. From a git URL with a tag or a branch, such as @v3.7.0 or @main That tag or branch of the ASH repository on GitHub, cloned during the build. A git+file:// URL is no different: its ref is cloned from GitHub, not from the repository the URL names. From a git URL with no ref The installed commit, checked out of a clone of the ASH repository on GitHub. Anything else: Homebrew, a wheel or sdist file, an archive URL The commit the package was built from, checked out of a clone of the ASH repository. A package build records it when it runs in a git checkout of ASH. With none recorded (a build from a source tarball), the release tag of the installed version, such as v3.7.0, and a warning that this is a guess: a build of an unreleased commit carries the version of the release before it.

A development or pre-release version has no release tag, so with nothing recorded the build stops before it starts and asks for --ash-revision-to-install. That option overrides the table: pass a tag, a branch, or a full 40-character commit id. --ash-revision-to-install LOCAL builds the running ASH's own source tree, and is refused when there is none, for example for a wheel install.

A commit id, given or recorded, is built only if a branch or a tag of the ASH repository reaches it. Otherwise the Dockerfile's clone step stops with exit status 3, the image build fails, and ash exits with the build's status (1 for a failed docker build). Every branch counts, the ones GitHub and its apps create included, such as the merge queue's gh-readonly-queue/*, Dependabot's dependabot/* and gh-pages, and so does every tag; a pull request's ref (refs/pull/*) does not. GitHub serves a commit that only a fork or a pull request holds under the ASH repository's URL as well, so the id alone does not show that the commit is ASH's. A package built from a commit that is on no branch or tag there yet, a local one for example, records that commit: run the ASH installed from that source tree with --ash-revision-to-install LOCAL, or name a branch instead.

Container mode and ash build-image never build a Dockerfile from the working directory, which is usually the project being scanned. A LOCAL build uses the ASH source tree above, and any other revision uses the Dockerfile packaged with ASH, which clones that revision. ASH v3.0.1 to v3.7.1 could build a Dockerfile they found in or above the working directory and tag the result as ASH's image (automated-security-helper:<target>, or your ASH_IMAGE_NAME), and --no-build runs whatever image has that tag. If you ran one of them in or under a project with its own Dockerfile, remove that image, run ash build-image --force, and push again any copy you host in a registry.

A build whose context is ASH's own source tree builds that tree, whatever the revision. ./ash always builds its own checkout, and the image pipelines under deploy/ build the clone they check out.

A branch, or the floating v3 tag, is cloned again on every build, because it can have moved since the last one. A release tag or a commit id is cloned once, and later builds take that clone from the build cache.

docs.title: Keeping it current
docs.text:
ASH orchestrates external scanners, and their versions are not all pinned. A rebuild can therefore change which findings you get, in both directions — a scanner release can add checks or drop them. cfn-nag is one that is pinned: the image installs it and every gem it depends on from the committed automated_security_helper/assets/Gemfile.lock, with Bundler frozen, so each build of one ASH version installs the same gems. A build whose Gemfile and Gemfile.lock disagree fails at that step instead of resolving new versions. That is an argument for rebuilding on a schedule you choose and reviewing the delta, not for rebuilding as rarely as possible.

A workable cadence:

  • Rebuild when you upgrade ASH, and tag the image with that ASH version.
  • Rebuild on a fixed interval regardless, so base-image CVE fixes land.
  • Compare a scan of a known repository across the old and new image before promoting the new one. A jump in finding counts is usually a scanner version change rather than a change in your code.

docs.title: Air-gapped and offline builds
docs.text:
Building with --offline caches the tool vulnerability databases into the image itself, so a scan needs no network access:

ash build-image --build-target non-root --offline

The build itself still requires network access — that is when the dependencies and databases are fetched. The image keeps trivy's database in TRIVY_CACHE_DIR (/deps/.trivy) and the cfn-guard rules in ASH_CFN_GUARD_RULES_DIR (/usr/share/ash/cfn-guard-rules, owned by root). Only the resulting scan is offline. An offline image's databases are frozen at build time, which makes the rebuild cadence above load-bearing rather than optional.

npm-audit has no database to cache: npm, yarn and pnpm audit a lockfile by asking the registry, so an offline image cannot run it. A scan with the image reports npm-audit MISSING, and exits 1, for a project that has a package-lock.json, npm-shrinkwrap.json, yarn.lock or pnpm-lock.yaml beside a package.json, and SKIPPED for one that has none. Add --exclude-scanners npm-audit to the scan command to scan such a project with the offline image.

An offline image stops passing once grype's database or its rulesets are past their bound. ASH reads each database's own build time after the scan and holds it to a bound: trivy's database 24 hours after it was published, which is trivy's own rule, grype's database 5 days (120h) after it was built, which is grype's own default, and the offline semgrep and opengrep rulesets 30 days after they were downloaded (the build records that time in .ash-rules-fetched-at). Past grype's or a ruleset's bound the scan exits 1. This applies in offline mode exactly as online; before it, an offline scan with a weeks-old database exited 0 with no warning.

trivy's database is the exception. Its bound would fail every trivy scan in the image from a day after the build, so an offline image holds it to warn instead: past 24 hours the scan still passes, and the summary reports, ash.sarif and ash.flat.json all say the trivy database was stale, how old it was, and that the offline image's default let the scan pass. To make it fail the scan in the image too, set content_db_staleness_offline_image_default: false in the ASH config or pass --no-allow-stale-content-db.

A stale trivy database still lacks every advisory published since the build, so refresh the image anyway. Rebuild it with ash build-image --offline, which downloads current databases and rulesets, and move the new image across the air gap: at least every 5 days to keep grype's scans passing (every 30 days, for the rulesets, with scanners.grype.enabled: false), and as often as you want trivy's findings current. Without --force, a build upgrades the OS packages and, offline, downloads a current grype database and current rulesets once per UTC day; with it (--force is --no-cache), on every build. The same holds for ./ash and Invoke-ASH, online or offline. Rebuilds later the same day come from the build cache. The first one on a new day re-runs the Dockerfile's core stage from its apt-get upgrade step down (the OS packages, the scanner tools, the ASH package and, offline, the download), so it needs network access.

On the air-gapped host, scan with the image you moved there instead of rebuilding it: ash scan --mode container --offline --no-build, ./ash --offline --no-build, or Invoke-ASH -Offline -NoBuild. Container mode builds the image before every scan unless told not to, and a build on a new day needs network access. The image has to carry the name ASH runs, automated-security-helper:<build target>, or the one ASH_IMAGE_NAME names.

A docker build of the Dockerfile run by hand gets the same result by passing OFFLINE=YES and, as BUILD_DATE_EPOCH, UTC midnight of the day in epoch seconds: now=$(date +%s); docker build --build-arg OFFLINE=YES --build-arg BUILD_DATE_EPOCH=$((now - now % 86400)) .... Pass BUILD_DATE_EPOCH for an online build too. Without a new value the apt-get upgrade step and the download step are served from the build cache, with the OS packages and databases they held then.

To scan with an image older than that anyway, pass --allow-stale-content-db or set content_db_staleness: warn; the scan passes, and the same reports say which databases were stale and how old they were. See Failing on a stale content database.

docs.title: If you would rather not run a container
docs.text:
--mode local runs ASH as a Python process with no image involved:

uvx git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@v3.7.0 --mode local --source-dir .

This avoids the image question entirely, at a cost: a few of the tools ASH orchestrates cannot be installed through Python packaging alone, so local mode runs a smaller set of scanners than container mode. Check the scanner table in the run summary to see which ones participated rather than assuming parity.

docs.title: If you build per run in CI
docs.text:
Building on every run is supported and is the simplest thing that works, but it is the slowest. On GitHub Actions, ASH passes --cache-from/--cache-to type=gha automatically when ACTIONS_CACHE_URL or ACTIONS_RESULTS_URL is set, with a separate cache scope per build target, so a warm cache skips most of the build. Nothing needs configuring for that.

Even with caching, a registry-hosted image is faster and gives you the provenance story above. Per-run builds are best treated as a starting point rather than a destination.

docs.title: Extending the image
docs.text:
--custom-containerfile builds your own Dockerfile on top of ASH's, with the ASH image passed in as the ASH_BASE_IMAGE build argument:

ash build-image --build-target ci --custom-containerfile ./Dockerfile.internal

Supplying a custom containerfile builds ASH's image at the ci target, so the run-as-non-root configuration is not applied. Securing the final image is then yours to do — set a non-root USER in your own Dockerfile if you need one. To build that, give your Dockerfile a stage named non-root (FROM ${ASH_BASE_IMAGE} AS non-root, followed by the USER it should run as) and pass --build-target non-root: ASH builds its own image at ci and your file at its non-root stage. --build-target non-root with a custom Dockerfile that has no such stage is refused with exit 3 before anything is built, since the image would otherwise run as root without a word.

docs.title: Third-party license files in the image
docs.text:
The image bundles third-party programs that ASH installs from their upstream releases: actionlint, cfn-guard (with the AWS Guard Rules Registry it reads), gitleaks, grype, opengrep, syft, trivy and uv today, and the Python scanners bandit, checkov, cfn-lint, semgrep and zizmor (installed with uv tool install). Each one's license and notice files are in the image under /usr/share/doc/ash/third-party/<tool>/, taken from the exact release the image carries. Beside them, a SOURCE file names the upstream repository, release tag and commit. For a copyleft tool (opengrep is LGPL-2.1), that file also says where the corresponding source is.

/usr/share/doc/ash/third-party/index.json lists every bundled tool with its version, license expression, repository, commit and files. The image build writes it only after checking every entry against the built image, so it describes what is actually installed.

docker run --rm automated-security-helper:non-root cat /usr/share/doc/ash/third-party/index.json

If you redistribute the image, these are the files that go with those programs. Packages installed from Debian carry their own copyright files under /usr/share/doc/<package>/, and Python packages carry their license metadata in their .dist-info directories.

docs.title: CLI Reference (Auto-Generated)
docs.text:
This document is auto-generated from the ASH CLI source code using introspection. Do not edit manually. Regenerate with: uv run python scripts/generate_cli_docs.py

Which CLI reference is authoritative. Two pages describe the CLI: this one and the hand-written CLI Reference. They are not interchangeable, and the split is deliberate rather than accidental:

  • For flag names and aliases, parameter types, defaults, and environment variables, this page wins. Every row here is introspected from the Typer command definitions, and tests/unit/test_generated_docs_freshness.py fails the build if this file and the code disagree. The hand-written page has no such gate and has drifted.
  • For worked examples, exit codes, configuration-override syntax, and narrative guidance, the hand-written page wins. None of that can be introspected, so it is not reproduced here.

The intended end state is a single page: this one, with the hand-written page's narrative content folded in. Until that migration lands, treat a disagreement about a flag between the two pages as a defect in the hand-written page.

docs.title: ash scan
docs.text:
Runs an ASH scan against the source-dir, outputting results to the output-dir.

Flag Type Default Env Var Description --source-dir str ASH_SOURCE_DIR The source directory to scan --output-dir str ASH_OUTPUT_DIR The directory to output results to --scanners List[str] ASH_SCANNERS Specific scanner names to run. Defaults to all scanners. --exclude-scanners List[str] ASH_EXCLUDED_SCANNERS Specific scanner names to exclude from running. Takes precedence over scanners parameter. --ash-plugin-modules List[str] ASH_PLUGIN_MODULES List of Python modules to import containing ASH plugins and/or event subscribers. These are loaded in addition to the default modules. --config-overrides List[str] Configuration overrides specified as key-value pairs (e.g., 'reporters.cloudwatch-logs.options.aws_region=us-west-2'). Supports lists with [item1,item2], append mode with key+=[value], and JSON syntax. See https://awslabs.github.io/automated-security-helper/latest/how-to/configure/ --offline bool False Run scan in offline/airgapped mode. npm-audit does not run offline, because npm, yarn and pnpm audit by asking the registry: a project with a lockfile reports it MISSING, and one without reports it SKIPPED. IMPORTANT: Online access is needed when building ASH to prepare it for usage during a scan! If selecting Offline while performing a build, the ASH container image will be built in offline mode and any typically online-only dependencies like downloadable tool vulnerability databases will be cached in the image itself before publishing for scan usage. --sandbox enum(off, auto, bwrap, firejail, landlock, sandbox-exec) Run every scanner subprocess in an OS-level sandbox: read-only source, writable results directory only, private home and temporary directory, no network unless the scanner needs one (never under --offline). 'auto' picks the best available (Linux: bwrap, firejail, landlock; macOS: sandbox-exec). A scanner that cannot be sandboxed as requested is reported MISSING. Overrides the config file's sandbox.mode; default off. Refused with --mode container (exit 5), which runs the scanners unsandboxed inside the container. See docs/content/docs/scanner-sandbox.md --offline-semgrep-rulesets str p/ci Specify Semgrep rulesets for use in ASH offline mode --strategy enum(sequential, parallel) parallel Whether to run scanners in parallel or sequential --progress/--no-progress, -p/-P bool True Show progress of each job live in the console. Defaults to True. --output-formats, --output-format, --formats, --format, -f List[str] The output formats to use (comma-separated). Available formats: text, flat-json, yaml, csv, html, junitxml, markdown, sarif, ocsf, cyclonedx, spdx, github-ghas, gitlab-sast, gitlab-cyclonedx, unused-suppressions. With the AWS plugin module (ash_aws_plugins) in ash_plugin_modules, also, once enabled: aws-security-hub, bedrock-summary-reporter, cloudwatch-logs, s3. Also accepted, though no reporter writes them: aggregated, dict, asff, custom. --cleanup bool False Clean up 'converted' directory and other temporary files after scan completes. Defaults to False. Note: Scans will always clean up existing files in the output directory before a new scan starts. This parameter only affects the cleanup of the temporary work directory after a scan has completed, typically for inspection of temporary artifacts. --phases List[enum(convert, scan, report, inspect)] The phases to run. Defaults to all phases except inspect. --inspect bool False Enable inspection of SARIF fields after running. This adds the inspect phase to the execution. --use-existing bool False Use an existing ash_aggregated_results.json file in the output-dir. If True, the scan phase will be skipped and reports will be generated from this file. --version bool False Prints version number --mode enum(precommit, container, local, nix) local ASH_MODE Execution mode preset. 'local' (default) runs the scan in this process with the scanner tools installed on this machine. 'precommit' is a local scan that runs only bandit, detect-secrets, checkov, cdk-nag, npm-audit, plus any --scanners, with simplified output and no progress display; in workspace mode it changes only the output. 'container' builds the ASH container image and runs the scan inside it. 'nix' runs the scan inside nix develop, whose shell supplies pinned scanner versions, and always offline. --python-only/--full, --python-based-scanners-only/--all-enabled-scanners, --python-based-plugins-only/--all-enabled-plugins bool False Exclude execution of any plugins or tools that have depencies external to Python. --show-summary bool True Show metrics table and results summary --quiet bool False Hide all log output --log-level enum(QUIET, SIMPLE, ERROR, INFO, ...) INFO Set the log level. --config, -c str ASH_CONFIG The path to the configuration file. By default, ASH looks for the following config file names in the source directory of a scan: ['.ash.yml', '.ash.yaml', '.ash.json', 'ash.yml', 'ash.yaml', 'ash.json'] (each at the root, then in .ash/), then ['.ashrc.toml', '.ashrc.yaml', '.ashrc.yml', '.ashrc.json', 'ashrc.toml', 'ashrc.yaml', 'ashrc.yml', 'ashrc.json'] at the root, then the tool.ash table of pyproject.toml at the root; the first found is used. Alternatively, the full path to a config file can be provided by setting the ASH_CONFIG environment variable before running ASH. --verbose, -v bool False ASH_VERBOSE Enable verbose logging. Any log flag on the command line overrides ASH_VERBOSE. --debug, -d bool False ASH_DEBUG Enable debug logging. Any log flag on the command line overrides ASH_DEBUG. --color bool True Enable/disable colorized output --fail-on-findings bool Enable/disable throwing non-successful exit codes if any actionable findings are found. Defaults to unset, which prefers the configuration value. If this is set directly, it takes precedence over the configuration value. --fail-on-incomplete-scanners bool Exit 1 when a selected scanner did not complete -- ERROR (ran and failed) or MISSING (dependencies unavailable, so it never ran). On by default: under --no-fail-on-incomplete-scanners, a run where nothing ran exits 0, the same code as a clean scan, because no scanner produced any finding. A SKIPPED scanner, one you did not select or one with nothing of its kind to scan, does not trip it by itself, so --scanners and --exclude-scanners both narrow what is gated; but a run in which every scanner is SKIPPED, such as one where no selected scanner had a file to scan, exits 1. Independent of --fail-on-findings, and takes precedence over it when both would fail: a partial scan's findings are real but its clean bill of health is not. Defaults to unset, which prefers the configuration value and then on. Pass --no-fail-on-incomplete-scanners to accept a partial scan's exit code, or --exclude-scanners for a tool you do not have, which records it SKIPPED and says so in the report. --allow-stale-content-db bool Let the scan pass when a scanner's content database (grype's or trivy's vulnerability database, the offline semgrep/opengrep rulesets) is older than its declared bound -- for grype, 120h after the database was built. Without it such a scan exits 1, except for trivy's database in an image built with OFFLINE=YES, which warns by default. With it the scan proceeds and the warning is recorded in the log and in the reports. --no-allow-stale-content-db forces the failure, for that database too. Defaults to unset, which prefers the content_db_staleness config value and then 'fail'; either form of the flag takes precedence over the config. --simple bool False Simplified output mode with minimal logging --ignore-suppressions bool False Ignore all suppression rules and report all findings regardless of suppression status. --honor-ignore-files bool Whether the .gitignore and .ignore files in the scanned tree decide which files are left out of ASH's scan set (the files detect-secrets, cfn-nag, cdk-nag, cfn-lint, cfn-guard, actionlint, zizmor, npm-audit and the converters read). --no-honor-ignore-files scans the files they match too; ASH's own exclusions such as .git still apply. Defaults to unset, which prefers the operator's honor_ignore_files config value and then honoring them. Either form takes precedence over the config. A config file inside the scanned tree cannot set it. The results and summaries record whether the ignore files were honored and how many files they excluded. --min-severity enum(critical, high, medium, low, none) low Minimum severity to trigger non-zero exit code (critical, high, medium, low, none). 'critical' and 'high' are equivalent because SARIF does not distinguish them. Findings below this threshold are still reported but don't affect the exit code. --compact-report bool False Produce a shorter markdown report suitable for PR comments. Omits the severity legend, scan metadata, footer, and rows for scanners that were skipped or had zero findings. --changed-files-only bool False ASH_CHANGED_FILES_ONLY Report only findings in files changed between --base-ref and HEAD, for example on a pull request. Scanners still scan every file; findings located in other files are dropped from every report, the summary counts and the exit code. Findings with no file location are kept. When git cannot list the changes, everything is reported; when nothing changed inside --source-dir, nothing is. Not supported with --mode container, which refuses it (exit 5). --base-ref str origin/main ASH_BASE_REF Git ref to diff against when --changed-files-only is set. --allow-in-tree-tools bool False Let ASH start scanners and other tools found inside the scanned directory, such as an activated in-repo .venv/bin or node_modules/.bin. Off by default: a tool inside the scanned directory is treated as missing. Only this flag (also the allow_in_tree_tools key of --cli-json-input) and the ASH_ALLOW_IN_TREE_TOOLS environment variable (1, true, yes or on) turn it on, never a config file, and ash mcp never does. --shard-index int ASH_SHARD_INDEX Zero-based index of this shard when one scan is split across several executors. Requires --shard-count. A 3-way split uses indices 0, 1 and 2. Each shard runs a disjoint subset of the scanners and records which ones in its results; recombine them with 'ash merge'. --shard-count int ASH_SHARD_COUNT Total number of shards this scan is split across. Requires --shard-index. Balance is by scanner count rather than scanner cost, so counts above about four buy little: wall clock is bounded by the slowest single scanner. --config-from-scanned-repository bool False Apply the limits ASH puts on a repository-written config file to the --config file and every file it extends, wherever they are. Container mode passes this to the scan inside the container when the config is a file the scanned repository wrote (judged by its resolved path and by the name that reached it) but outside --source-dir, where that scan cannot see it. In a workspace scan it marks the --config file that is layered over every project's own config and used alone by a project without one, from planning on. --config-file-from-scanned-repository List[str] Apply the limits ASH puts on a repository-written config file to this one file of the extends chain of the --config file or of the file ASH_CONFIG names. Container mode passes it, once per file, for each file of those chains the scanned repository wrote; the bases of a --config whose whole chain carries --config-from-scanned-repository are passed individually as well, so a mounted base judged on its own is still a marked file. Refused for a file that is in neither chain. --config-file-from-another-checkout List[str] Apply the limits ASH puts on a config file inside a git checkout other than the scanned one to this one file of the extends chain of the --config file or of the file ASH_CONFIG names. The file cannot grant, and still sets what only restricts, as it does on the host: a lowered archive extraction limit, a scanner option that sends no usage data, and a network_scanners list as a limit. Container mode passes it, once per file, for each file of those chains that is in such a checkout, by its path inside the container, where the scan inside cannot see the checkout. Refused for a file that is in neither chain. --ash-config-from-host str Read this file as the file ASH_CONFIG names, for the whole command. Container mode passes it to the scan inside the container, with the path there of the file the host's ASH_CONFIG names, which a local scan reads as its base whatever names the config. Not --config, whose environment variable ASH_CONFIG is. --workspace str ASH_WORKSPACE Path to a '.code-workspace' file whose folders are scanned as separate, independently-scoped projects. Pass 'auto' to use the single '*.code-workspace' file in the current directory. Mutually exclusive with --source-dir. --workspace-config str ASH_WORKSPACE_CONFIG Path to the workspace policy file (severity ceiling, workspace-wide suppressions and ignore paths, additional scanners). Without this, ASH looks for 'ash-workspace.{yaml,yml,json}' in the workspace root or its '.ash' directory; finding none is not an error. Must not be any project's own ASH config: workspace policy governs every project, so reading one project's config as policy would apply its settings to its siblings. --allow-missing-projects bool False In workspace mode, skip project folders that are absent or unreadable instead of failing. Skipped projects are recorded in the plan. Without this, a missing project fails the whole workspace, so a typo or an un-cloned repository cannot pass as a clean scan. --dry-run bool False In workspace mode, print the resolved execution plan and exit without scanning anything. --build/--no-build, -b/-B bool True Whether to build the ASH container image --run/--no-run, -r/-R bool True Whether to run the ASH container image --force bool False Force rebuild of the ASH container image --oci-runner, --oci, --runner, -o str OCI_RUNNER Use the specified OCI runner instead of docker to run the containerized tools --build-target enum(non-root, ci) The ASH image stage to build and run: 'non-root' (an unprivileged user, the default) or 'ci' (root, the default on Windows). CI environment variables do not change it; --custom-containerfile builds on 'ci'. --container-uid, -u str UID to use for the container user --container-gid, -g str GID to use for the container user --ash-revision-to-install str ASH branch, tag or full commit id to install in the container image for usage during containerized scans --custom-containerfile str Path to a custom container definition (e.g. Dockerfile) that you would like to build after the ASH container image builds. This is typically used when building a custom container image for ASH and including custom tooling that ASH does not come with by default. The fully qualified image name for the ASH image is passed in as the ASH_BASE_IMAGE build-arg so you can use it as a base. IMPORTANT: When a custom_containerfile path is provided, the build-target is set to ci so the container run-as configuration is not shifted to the non-root user. If you are using this parameter, you are responsible for securing your final container as appropriate. --custom-build-arg List[str] Custom build arguments to pass to the container build --cli-json-input str Read parameter values from a JSON object: a path, a file:// URI, or '-' for stdin. Keys are parameter names (output_dir) or long flag spellings (--output-dir). Flags given on the command line override the file; the file overrides environment variables. Run with --generate-cli-skeleton for a template. --generate-cli-skeleton bool Print a JSON template for --cli-json-input, listing every parameter of this command with its default, and exit.

docs.title: ash merge
docs.text:
Merges the results of a sharded scan into one unified report.

Flag Type Default Env Var Description --results List[str] required A shard's ash_aggregated_results.json, or a directory containing one. Repeat once per shard. --output-dir str required ASH_OUTPUT_DIR Directory to write the merged results and reports to. --output-formats List[str] Comma-separated report formats to generate. Defaults to the formats the scan's own configuration asks for. --config, -c str ASH_CONFIG The operator's config file. Its values replace the shards' for the settings a shard's recorded config cannot choose, such as where reporters send findings and which off-host reporters run. Its ash_plugin_modules are the plugin modules the merge loads, with any --config-overrides adds; a module only the shards recorded is not loaded. It adds no reporter section the shards did not record; use --config-overrides for that. --config-overrides List[str] Configuration overrides as key-value pairs (e.g., 'reporters.s3.enabled=true'), applied over the shards' recorded config. --min-severity enum(critical, high, medium, low, none) low Minimum severity that counts as actionable for the exit code. --ignore-suppressions bool False Ignore all suppression rules and report every finding regardless of suppression status. Mirrors 'ash scan --ignore-suppressions', so the same tree gives the same verdict sharded or not. --fail-on-findings/--no-fail-on-findings bool Exit non-zero when the merged report has actionable findings. Defaults to the scan configuration's value, then to true. --fail-on-incomplete-scanners/--no-fail-on-incomplete-scanners bool Refuse the merge when a shard completed none of the scanners it owned, and exit 1 when any scanner in the union is ERROR or MISSING, or when every one is SKIPPED, such as when no selected scanner had a file to scan. On by default: under --no-fail-on-incomplete-scanners, a shard whose scanners never ran contributes no findings and the merged report reads as a complete, clean scan. Defaults to the scan configuration's value, then to true; pass --no-fail-on-incomplete-scanners to merge a partial union anyway. --log-level enum(QUIET, SIMPLE, ERROR, INFO, ...) docs.title: ash mcp
docs.text:
Start the ASH MCP server (Model Context Protocol).

Flag Type Default Env Var Description --log-level enum(QUIET, SIMPLE, ERROR, INFO, ...) INFO Set the log level. --verbose/--no-verbose, -v bool False Enable verbose logging --debug/--no-debug, -d bool False Enable debug logging --color bool True Enable/disable colorized output --quiet bool False Hide all log output --transport str stdio Transport: 'stdio' (default), 'streamable-http', or 'sse'. --host str 127.0.0.1 Host to bind for HTTP transports. --port int 8000 Port to bind for HTTP transports. --mount-path str /mcp HTTP path the transport listens on (default: /mcp for streamable-http, /sse for sse). --auth-header-name str Required HTTP header name for single-tenant auth (HTTP transports only). --auth-header-value str Expected value of --auth-header-name. Visible to other local users on the command line; prefer --auth-header-value-file or --auth-header-value-fd. --auth-header-value-file Path Read the expected value of --auth-header-name from this file, once at startup: a regular file, not a symlink, readable by its owner only. One trailing newline is dropped. --auth-header-value-fd int Read the expected value of --auth-header-name from this inherited file descriptor (3 or above), once at startup, then close it. --stateless-http/--no-stateless-http bool False Handle each streamable-HTTP request independently instead of binding it to a server-held session. Required behind a load balancer that may route consecutive requests to different replicas, and by managed runtimes that inject their own Mcp-Session-Id. Only valid with --transport streamable-http. --trust-upstream-session-id bool False Stateless streamable-HTTP only. Declare that a platform in front of ASH issues and authenticates the Mcp-Session-Id header, so it can name the caller's session. Without it a stateless server identifies no session, and tools that need one (source delivery, profiles, the scan registry) refuse. --allowed-host List[str] Host header value to accept, repeatable. Keeps DNS-rebinding protection enabled while allowing a known proxy or load balancer hostname. Required with a non-loopback --host unless --trust-upstream-host-check is given. --session-workspace-ttl int HTTP transports only. Seconds a session workspace (delivered source, uploads, bound profile) may go unused before it is removed. Covers sessions whose end the server cannot see, such as every stateless one. Default: 86400 (24 hours). --trust-upstream-host-check bool False HTTP transports only. Declare that a proxy or platform in front of ASH checks the Host and Origin headers, so ASH serves any. Without it, a non-loopback --host needs --allowed-host or the server refuses to start. Cannot be combined with --allowed-host. --profile List[str] Register a named config profile as NAME=path/to/ash.yaml, repeatable. Clients list them with the list_profiles tool and bind one to their session with select_profile; a bound profile supplies the config for every later call in that session that names none. Each file is loaded and schema-validated now, so a typo fails startup rather than a scan.

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text:
This page provides detailed information about the ASH command-line interface.

Flag tables on this page are hand-maintained

CLI Reference (generated) is introspected from the Typer command definitions and is gated by a freshness test, so it is authoritative for flag names and aliases, parameter types, defaults, and environment variables. This page is authoritative for everything that cannot be introspected: worked examples, exit codes, and configuration-override syntax. If the two disagree about a flag, the generated page is right and this one has a bug — please report it.

docs.title: Common Parameters
docs.text:
These parameters are available across multiple ASH commands:

Parameter Description Default Environment Variable Commands --source-dir Path to the directory containing code to scan Current directory ASH_SOURCE_DIR scan --version Print the installed ASH version and exit scan --ash-revision-to-install ASH branch, tag or full commit id to install in the container image for usage during containerized scans scan --base-ref Git ref to diff against when --changed-files-only is set: a branch, a tag or a commit, optionally followed by ~<n> or ^<n> (origin/main, v1.2.0, HEAD~1). With --changed-files-only, a value that starts with -, holds a character other than letters, digits and . _ / ~ ^ @ { } -, or is not a ref name git check-ref-format --allow-onelevel accepts (main..HEAD, main@{1}) is refused with exit 1 before git runs, and nothing is scanned. Without --changed-files-only the value is not used. origin/main ASH_BASE_REF scan --allow-stale-content-db / --no-allow-stale-content-db Let the scan pass when a scanner's content database is past its declared age bound (for grype, 5 days after it was built), recording a warning in the log and the reports. Without it such a scan exits 1, except for trivy's database in an image built with OFFLINE=YES, which warns by default. Takes precedence over the content_db_staleness config value; see Failing on a stale content database. Unset: the content_db_staleness config value, then fail scan --allow-in-tree-tools Let ASH start scanners and other tools found inside the scanned directory, such as an activated in-repo .venv/bin or node_modules/.bin, and the scanner sandbox's own programs (bwrap, firejail, readlink, true). Without it such a tool is treated as missing and the scanner is reported MISSING with the in-tree path. Only this flag (also the allow_in_tree_tools key of --cli-json-input) and the environment variable, set to 1, true, yes or on, turn it on, never a config file, and ash mcp never does; see Tools inside the scanned directory. Off ASH_ALLOW_IN_TREE_TOOLS scan --sandbox Run every scanner subprocess in an OS-level sandbox: auto, bwrap, firejail, landlock, sandbox-exec or off. A scanner that cannot be sandboxed as requested is reported MISSING. Overrides the sandbox.mode config value. Refused with --mode container (exit 5), which runs the scanners unsandboxed inside the container. See Scanner sandboxing. off (or sandbox.mode) scan --changed-files-only Report only findings in files changed between --base-ref and HEAD. Scanners still scan every file; findings located in other files are dropped from every report, the summary counts and the exit code. When git is not installed, the source directory is not in a git repository, or the diff fails, ASH logs which of these it was and reports every finding. Not supported with --mode container, which refuses it with exit 5 (set through ASH_CHANGED_FILES_ONLY too). See Reporting only changed files. ASH_CHANGED_FILES_ONLY scan --color Enable/disable colorized output scan --compact-report Produce a shorter markdown report suitable for PR comments. scan --container-gid GID to use for the container user scan --container-uid UID to use for the container user scan --custom-build-arg Custom build arguments to pass to the container build scan --custom-containerfile Path to a custom container definition (e.g. scan --fail-on-incomplete-scanners / --no-fail-on-incomplete-scanners Exit 1 when a selected scanner did not complete (ERROR or MISSING), or a converter could not convert some of its inputs. On by default; see An incomplete scan is not a clean scan. --fail-on-incomplete-scanners scan --formats The output formats to use (comma-separated). scan --honor-ignore-files / --no-honor-ignore-files Whether the .gitignore and .ignore files in the scanned tree leave files out of ASH's scan set. --no-honor-ignore-files scans those files too; ASH's own exclusions such as .git still apply. Takes precedence over the honor_ignore_files config value, which a config file inside the scanned tree cannot set. The results and summaries record how many files the ignore files excluded; see Ignore files and the scan set. Unset: the operator's honor_ignore_files, then honored scan --min-severity Minimum severity to trigger non-zero exit code: critical, high, medium, low or none, in any case. critical and high rank the same. Any other value is a usage error. low scan --progress Show progress of each job live in the console. Defaults to True. scan --python-based-plugins-only / --all-enabled-plugins Exclude execution of any plugins or tools that have depencies external to Python. Also spelled --python-only / --full, and --python-based-scanners-only / --all-enabled-scanners; all three name the same option, and the plugins spelling is preferred because the option covers converters and reporters too. scan --runner Use the specified OCI runner instead of docker to run the containerized tools OCI_RUNNER scan --show-summary Show metrics table and results summary scan --simple Simplified output mode with minimal logging scan --output-dir Path to store scan results. Refused, whatever the sandbox mode, when it, a directory or file ASH writes in it, or a directory inside the scanned tree on the way to it is a symlink; see Output directory. .ash/ash_output ASH_OUTPUT_DIR scan, report --config, -c Path to ASH configuration file Discovered ASH_CONFIG scan, config, plugin --config-overrides Override configuration values (can be used multiple times) scan, config, plugin, report --ash-plugin-modules List of Python modules to import containing ASH plugins ASH_PLUGIN_MODULES scan, plugin --mode Execution mode: local, precommit, container or nix. precommit runs only bandit, detect-secrets, checkov, cdk-nag and npm-audit, plus any --scanners, with simplified output; in workspace mode it changes only the output. nix runs the scan inside nix develop, always offline local ASH_MODE scan --debug, -d Enable debug logging False ASH_DEBUG All commands --verbose, -v Enable verbose logging False ASH_VERBOSE All commands --quiet Suppress non-essential output False All commands --no-color Disable colored output False All commands --oci-runner, -o OCI runner to use. Unset by default; ASH uses the first of finch, docker, nerdctl, podman found on PATH first found OCI_RUNNER scan (container mode)

docs.title: Config Overrides Syntax
docs.text:
The --config-overrides parameter allows you to modify configuration values without editing the configuration file:

# Basic usage
ash --config-overrides 'scanners.bandit.enabled=true'

# Multiple overrides
ash \
  --config-overrides 'scanners.bandit.enabled=true' \
  --config-overrides 'global_settings.severity_threshold=MEDIUM'

# Append to lists
ash --config-overrides 'ash_plugin_modules+=["my_ash_plugins"]'

# Complex values using JSON syntax
ash --config-overrides 'global_settings.ignore_paths+=[{"path": "build/", "reason": "Generated files"}]'

The key is applied exactly as written, so a key that would name a setting nothing reads is refused, with exit code 3. That is a key with a dot-separated part that is empty (a..b, or a leading or trailing .), a part that holds whitespace (a space, a tab, a no-break space), or a part that holds a character that does not print, as Python's str.isprintable() decides it. The last covers the zero-width space, the byte order mark and the bidirectional controls, such as U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE and U+2066 LEFT-TO-RIGHT ISOLATE, which can make one key display as another. It also covers the zero-width non-joiner (U+200C), the zero-width joiner (U+200D) and the soft hyphen (U+00AD). Some languages need those in text, but no configuration key holds one. Only the key is checked this way: a value may hold spaces.

docs.title: Passing parameters as JSON
docs.text:
ash scan, ash build-image, ash report, and ash merge accept --cli-json-input, which reads the command's parameters from a JSON object instead of, or as well as, flags. It follows the AWS CLI's --cli-input-json convention.

# Write a template listing every parameter of the command with its default
ash scan --generate-cli-skeleton > scan-params.json

# Run with it. A path, a file:// URI, and - (stdin) are all accepted
ash scan --cli-json-input scan-params.json
ash scan --cli-json-input file://scan-params.json
cat scan-params.json | ash scan --cli-json-input -

# Flags on the command line win over the file
ash scan --cli-json-input file://scan-params.json --strategy sequential

{
  "source_dir": "./src",
  "scanners": ["bandit", "semgrep"],
  "strategy": "sequential",
  "offline": true,
  "config_overrides": ["global_settings.severity_threshold=LOW"]
}

Keys. A key is either the parameter name, which is what --generate-cli-skeleton writes (source_dir, output_formats), or one of the option's long flag spellings (--source-dir, --formats). The negative half of a boolean pair is not a key: write "offline": false, not "--no-offline": true. Every parameter the command takes is accepted, and both the accepted keys and the skeleton are read from the command's own option definitions, so a newly added flag is available here without further changes. Use the subcommand form; bare ash --cli-json-input ... is rejected as an unknown option.

Values. A list parameter takes a JSON array; every other parameter takes a single string, number, or boolean. null means "not provided", which is how the skeleton marks a parameter whose default is computed at run time. Each value is converted and checked by the same parameter type the flag uses, so an invalid value fails just as the equivalent flag would, and the error names the JSON key.

Precedence, highest first:

  1. A flag or positional argument given on the command line.
  2. A value in the --cli-json-input document.
  3. The parameter's environment variable, such as ASH_SOURCE_DIR.
  4. The parameter's default.

The document ranks above environment variables because it is named on this invocation's command line. A list given on the command line replaces the document's list for that parameter rather than extending it, so --scanners checkov with "scanners": ["bandit"] in the file runs only checkov.

Interaction with --config and --config-overrides. The document is resolved while the command line is parsed, before ASH reads any configuration. It only supplies parameter values: "config" in the document is the value of --config, and "config_overrides" is the list --config-overrides would have built. After that, configuration is resolved exactly as it is for flags: the configuration file is loaded, then each override is applied in order. A --config-overrides flag on the command line replaces the document's config_overrides list as a whole.

Errors. The command exits 5 without running when the document cannot be read, is not valid JSON, is not a JSON object, repeats a key, names a key the command does not have (the message lists the valid ones), sets one parameter under two spellings, or holds a value the parameter's type rejects. Exit 5 is the usage-error code, the same code an invalid flag produces.

Security. The document is parsed as JSON and nothing else. No value is evaluated, and no environment-variable or ~ expansion is applied, which matches how a flag's value is treated once the shell has handed it over. Relative paths in values are relative to the working directory, as they are for flags.

docs.title: Core Commands
docs.text:
ASH v3 provides several core commands:

ash [command] [options]

docs.title: Available Commands
docs.text: Command Description scan Run security scans on source code (default command) merge Recombine the results of a sharded scan into one report config Manage ASH configuration plugin Manage ASH plugins report Generate reports from scan results dependencies Install dependencies for ASH plugins inspect Inspect and analyze ASH outputs and reports build-image Build the ASH container image get-genai-guide Write the GenAI Integration Guide for AI assistants mcp Start the Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for AI tools

docs.title: Scan Command
docs.text:
The scan command is the primary command for running security scans. If no command is specified, ASH defaults to the scan command.

ash [options]

docs.title: Scan Options
docs.text: Option Description Default Environment Variable --source-dir Path to the directory containing code to scan Current directory ASH_SOURCE_DIR --output-dir Path to store scan results .ash/ash_output ASH_OUTPUT_DIR --mode Execution mode: local, precommit, container or nix. precommit runs only bandit, detect-secrets, checkov, cdk-nag and npm-audit, plus any --scanners, with simplified output; in workspace mode it changes only the output. nix runs the scan inside nix develop, always offline local ASH_MODE --config, -c Path to ASH configuration file Discovered from the source directory ASH_CONFIG --config-overrides Override configuration values --ash-plugin-modules List of Python modules to import containing ASH plugins ASH_PLUGIN_MODULES --scanners Specific scanner names to run All enabled scanners ASH_SCANNERS --exclude-scanners Specific scanner names to exclude None ASH_EXCLUDED_SCANNERS --output-formats, -f Output formats (comma-separated). Run ash scan --help for the list this build accepts; the help text is derived from the code, so it cannot go stale. The reporter names are also tabulated in Output formats The config's output_formats, else every enabled reporter --strategy Whether to run scanners in parallel or sequential parallel --log-level Set the log level INFO --fail-on-findings Exit with non-zero code if findings are found From config --ignore-suppressions Ignore all suppression rules and report all findings False --honor-ignore-files/--no-honor-ignore-files Whether the scanned tree's .gitignore and .ignore files leave files out of ASH's scan set. A config file inside the scanned tree cannot set it; see Ignore files and the scan set From operator config, then honored --offline Run in offline mode (container mode only) False --offline-semgrep-rulesets Semgrep rulesets for offline mode p/ci --build/--no-build, -b/-B Whether to build the ASH container image True --run/--no-run, -r/-R Whether to run the ASH container image True --build-target Container build target: non-root or ci (runs as root). CI environment variables do not change it non-root (ci on Windows) --oci-runner, -o OCI runner to use. Unset by default; ASH uses the first of finch, docker, nerdctl, podman found on PATH first found OCI_RUNNER --python-only/--full Use only Python-based plugins False --cleanup Clean up temporary files after scan False --use-existing Use existing results file False --phases Phases to run: convert, scan, report, inspect convert,scan,report --inspect After the scan, analyze the SARIF fields in this scan's output directory and write the result to its analysis/ directory False --shard-index Zero-based index of this shard when one scan is split across several executors. Requires --shard-count None ASH_SHARD_INDEX --shard-count Total number of shards the scan is split across. Requires --shard-index None ASH_SHARD_COUNT --workspace Path to a .code-workspace file, or auto to find the one in the current directory. Mutually exclusive with --source-dir None ASH_WORKSPACE --workspace-config Path to the workspace policy file. Defaults to ash-workspace.{yaml,yml,json} in the workspace root or its .ash directory None ASH_WORKSPACE_CONFIG --allow-missing-projects Skip workspace projects that are absent or unreadable False --dry-run Print the resolved workspace plan and exit without scanning False --allow-in-tree-tools Let ASH start tools found inside the scanned directory; see Common Parameters False ASH_ALLOW_IN_TREE_TOOLS

docs.title: Running a scan in a container
docs.text:
--mode container, the ./ash wrapper and Invoke-ASH in utils/ash_helpers.ps1 run the scan inside the ASH image with these bind mounts:

Mount Host path Access /src --source-dir read-only /out --output-dir read-write /ash-config/... --config (or ASH_CONFIG), when outside --source-dir read-only /ash-workspace-config/... the workspace policy, when outside the workspace root read-only /ash-env-config/... the file ASH_CONFIG names, when outside --source-dir read-only

The source is mounted read-only wherever the output directory is, including the default .ash/ash_output inside the source directory: the scan inside the container writes only to /out. An output directory that is the source directory itself, or a directory above it, would hold the source tree at /out, writable, so --mode container, ./ash and Invoke-ASH refuse it with exit 3 before anything is built or mounted (compared by real path, so a link to the source counts). Use an output directory inside the source or outside it.

The output directory must not be a symlink or be reached through one, because the scan inside the container would write wherever the link leads. --mode container, ./ash and Invoke-ASH refuse with exit 3, before the directory is created or mounted, an output directory that is a symlink, wherever it is, and any symlink between the source directory and it (a committed .ash -> /some/host/dir, for the default .ash/ash_output). --no-run is refused too, since the output directory is created either way. Links at or above the source directory are your own spelling and are not examined. This is the rule a sandboxed local scan applies (see Scanner sandbox).

The config file named with --config (or ASH_CONFIG) is the one the scan inside the container reads. One inside --source-dir is read through /src. One outside it is mounted read-only under /ash-config, together with the files its extends chain names, each where the file that extends it names it (relative to the config's directory, the parent of .ash/ for a file in .ash/), so the bases resolve inside to the files the host reads, including a base the host reaches through a link; only those files are mounted, not the directory. A relative --config is resolved against the working directory on the host, as a local scan resolves it, and the scan inside is given the file's path in the container, never the path as typed, so it cannot name a different file under /src. The config file the scan inside will use, whether named with --config, named by ASH_CONFIG, or found in --source-dir, is read on the host the way a local scan reads it, before anything is built, run, mounted or cleared. One that a local scan would refuse refuses the run with exit 3 and the same message (Invalid configuration: ...): a file that is missing or empty, a directory or another file that is not a regular file, unreadable, not UTF-8, not valid YAML, JSON or TOML (YAML aliases included), or not a valid config, and a name in --source-dir that is a link to nothing. --config-overrides are applied to it the same way, so one that does not parse, or sets a value the config does not accept, refuses the run too. Options of a scanner or reporter plugin are left to the scan inside, which loads the plugin from the image. --mode nix reads the file the same way before it enters its shell. --no-run builds an image and scans nothing, so its config is not read. An extends entry anywhere in the chain that names its base by absolute path refuses the run with exit 3 before the container starts: inside the container that path is not the same file. A --config named inside the scanned tree whose real path, with every link on the way resolved, is outside that tree is refused with exit 3 too, and so is a config file ASH cannot read itself. A config outside --source-dir whose extends chain includes a file inside it is refused with exit 3 as well: a chain is read whole through /src, for a config inside --source-dir, or mounted whole from outside it. A file of the chain inside the scanned checkout may extend only files inside that checkout. Inside the container an extends entry is followed as written, from where the extending file is mounted, so an entry whose written path leaves the config's directory (../cfg/base.yaml from cfg/ash.yaml), or that climbs out with .. after a link to a directory at another depth, would place its base outside /ash-config: the run is refused with exit 3 before anything is built, naming the entry. So is a chain where two files would be mounted at one container path, or one file at a path another file of the chain needs as a directory. A config the scanned repository wrote keeps the limits a local scan gives it (see Settings a repository's config cannot choose): when the config or a file it extends is inside the scanned tree (the git checkout holding --source-dir) or is reached through a symlink that sits in it, but outside --source-dir itself, where the scan inside the container cannot see that, the host passes it --config-from-scanned-repository (./ash and Invoke-ASH do the same for the config file, following its path one link at a time as the host does). When only files the config extends are in the scanned tree, the host marks each of those on its own (--config-file-from-scanned-repository), so the config, as on the host, keeps the sandbox settings it writes itself and its bases grant nothing. A file inside some other git checkout (an ops repository beside the scanned one, say), or reached through a symlink that sits in one, is not the scanned tree's, but it cannot grant either: the host marks each such file of the --config chain and of ASH_CONFIG's chain on its own (--config-file-from-another-checkout; a file already marked as the scanned tree's keeps that mark alone), and the scan inside limits it as the host does. Such a file still sets what only restricts: a lowered archive extraction limit, a scanner option that sends no usage data, and a network_scanners list as a limit. The scan inside reads those from the mounted file, so no value travels in the mark. ./ash (for the --config file and the ASH_CONFIG file) and Invoke-ASH (for the ASH_CONFIG file) pass the same mark for the file they mount, on the host's judgment: a .git entry that is a file, a link or a directory holding HEAD, at the file's directory or above it, found from the name as given, from the real path, or from where a link the name goes through sits (a relative name is read from the physical working directory, and ./ash also reads it from the directory $PWD names, as the host does). In a directory that group members or others can write, such an entry counts only when root, the directory's owner or the user running the script owns it. A file already marked as the scanned tree's keeps that mark alone. When they cannot make the judgment (./ash needs ls to read the owner of a link or the mode of a directory only in the rare case the shell's own ownership test does not settle it; Invoke-ASH needs ls and id on the path when its PowerShell runs on a .NET without File.GetUnixFileMode, as PowerShell 7.0 to 7.2 do, and PowerShell 7.3 and later need neither), they refuse with exit 3 and start nothing. In workspace mode the host marks a --config from another git checkout this way, and the workspace scan inside limits it as a local workspace scan does. One in the checkout around the workspace root, or reached through a link there, is refused with exit 3 before anything is built or mounted: keep --config, and every file it extends, outside every git checkout. A config inside the workspace root is refused as in a local workspace scan, because the operator's config may not be one of the workspace's files, and one outside every checkout is the operator's. ./ash and Invoke-ASH scan one directory and refuse a --workspace passed through to ash with exit 3; use ash --mode container --workspace.
