Only when there is none there does it look for uv on PATH and in the directories above.

A scan finds what --bin-path installed somewhere else only when ASH_BIN_PATH names that directory for the scan too. Nothing is remembered between runs, so ash dependencies install ends by printing the line that sets it, in absolute form, for POSIX shells and for PowerShell:

  export ASH_BIN_PATH=/home/me/tools/ash-bin    (POSIX shells)
  $env:ASH_BIN_PATH = '/home/me/tools/ash-bin'    (PowerShell)

It prints nothing when a scan in the same environment looks there anyway: the directory is the (absolute) ASH_BIN_PATH, or ~/.ash/bin with ASH_BIN_PATH unset.

docs.title: Python packages
docs.text:
Some plugins need Python packages in ASH's own environment: cdk-nag needs aws-cdk-lib, cdk-nag and constructs, and the ferret-scan community plugin needs ferret-scan. ash dependencies install adds them with the installer that owns that environment:

  • In an environment uv tool install created, it runs uv pip install --no-config --python <ASH's interpreter>. A later uv tool upgrade or uv tool install --force rebuilds that environment without them: run ash dependencies install --tool cdk-nag again after either one, or add --with for each package to the uv tool install command you install ASH with.
  • In an environment where pip is importable (pip, pipx, python -m venv), it runs <ASH's interpreter> -m pip install.
  • Anywhere else, including uvx and a uv venv without pip, it runs uv pip install --no-config --python <ASH's interpreter>. uvx builds a new environment when its cache entry is gone or ASH changes; add --with for each package to the uvx command to keep them.

With neither pip nor uv available, the plugin's row is FAILED and the message says what to install.

docs.title: uv settings
docs.text:
Every uv subcommand except uv tool reads uv.toml and pyproject.toml's [tool.uv] from the working directory and its parents (uv pip, uv venv, uv python, uv run and the rest). The ones ASH runs itself are uv pip install (above), the dry run that checks a tool found on PATH, and uv cache dir (below). It runs the first two with --no-config, because the working directory is usually the repository being scanned and its configuration must not choose what ASH installs.

An install command a plugin declares gets UV_NO_CONFIG=1 when it runs uv (as uv, uv.exe, uv.bat, uv.cmd, or python -m uv however Python's options are spelled: -Im uv, -muv and -m uv.__main__ count), unless it is a uv tool command or uvx. That keeps uv from reading configuration files, and nothing more: such a command still runs in the working directory, where uv finds the project and its .venv (a uv pip command can use a Python interpreter the repository put there, and uv run or uv sync creates .venv and uv.lock in it). In a plugin, declare python -I -m uv rather than python -m uv: -m puts the working directory first on sys.path, so a declared python -m uv run from the repository runs a uv.py the repository carries, and -I leaves the working directory off. -I also skips user site-packages, so where uv is installed only there (pip install --user uv), declare python -P -m uv instead (Python 3.11+): -P leaves the working directory off and keeps the user site.

For the commands with --no-config or UV_NO_CONFIG=1, your own and the system uv.toml are not read either; UV_* environment variables still apply (UV_INDEX_URL, UV_EXTRA_INDEX_URL, UV_OFFLINE and the rest), and so does a file named by UV_CONFIG_FILE, which uv reads even with --no-config:

UV_CONFIG_FILE=~/.config/uv/uv.toml ash dependencies install --tool cdk-nag

The uv tool install, uv tool run and uv tool list commands ASH runs for bandit, checkov, semgrep and nbconvert get no flag. uv ignores project files for uv tool commands, so the scanned repository cannot configure them, and they read your user uv.toml (~/.config/uv/uv.toml, %APPDATA%\uv\uv.toml on Windows) and the system one (/etc/uv/uv.toml), where an index mirror is usually set. A cache-dir there moves their cache. ASH runs uv cache dir from the filesystem root (/, or the system drive's root on Windows), where only an administrator can put a uv.toml, and without UV_PROJECT or UV_WORKING_DIR, which would send uv to read a uv.toml elsewhere. So it names that same cache and never one that a scanned repository's uv.toml, or one in a shared temporary directory, chose. Give cache-dir and UV_CACHE_DIR as absolute paths: uv resolves a relative one against each command's own working directory, so the cache uv cache dir names from / is not the one the tools used.

docs.title: Inspect Command
docs.text:
The inspect command allows you to analyze ASH outputs and reports.

ash inspect [subcommand] [options]

docs.title: Inspect Subcommands
docs.text: Subcommand Description sarif-fields Analyze SARIF fields across different scanners findings Interactive TUI to explore findings

docs.title: Inspect Options
docs.text: Option Description Default Environment Variable --output-dir Directory containing scan results .ash/ash_output ASH_OUTPUT_DIR --config, -c Path to configuration file Discovered ASH_CONFIG --debug, -d Enable debug logging False ASH_DEBUG --verbose, -v Enable verbose logging False ASH_VERBOSE --no-color Disable colored output False

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Analyze SARIF fields
ash inspect sarif-fields

# Explore findings interactively
ash inspect findings

docs.title: Build-Image Command
docs.text:
The build-image command builds the ASH container image and then, unless --no-run is given, scans the current directory with it.

ash build-image [options]

It takes only the options below; any other argument is a usage error. To scan with scan options, such as --scanners or --min-severity, use ash scan --mode container, which builds the image the same way and accepts every scan option.

docs.title: Build-Image Options
docs.text: Option Description Default Environment Variable --build-target Container build target: non-root or ci (runs as root). CI environment variables do not change it non-root (ci on Windows) --offline Build for offline use False --offline-semgrep-rulesets Semgrep rulesets for offline mode p/ci --oci-runner, -o OCI runner to use. Unset by default; ASH uses the first of finch, docker, nerdctl, podman found on PATH first found OCI_RUNNER --debug, -d Enable debug logging False ASH_DEBUG --verbose, -v Enable verbose logging False ASH_VERBOSE --no-color Disable colored output False

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Build the default image
ash build-image

# Build for CI environments
ash build-image --build-target ci

# Build for offline use
ash build-image --offline --offline-semgrep-rulesets p/ci

# Build using a specific OCI runner
ash build-image --oci-runner podman

docs.title: Get-GenAI-Guide Command
docs.text:
The get-genai-guide command writes the ASH GenAI Integration Guide to a file. The guide tells AI assistants and LLMs how to work with ASH scan results.

ash get-genai-guide [options]

The guide ships with ASH, so the command writes the copy that belongs to the installed version and needs no network access. Every installation carries one: a wheel or sdist, an install from a git URL, a clone of the repository (where the command writes docs/content/docs/genai-steering-guide.md), and the container images that ash build-image, ash scan --mode container, ./ash and Invoke-ASH build. A package built from a source tree without docs/ has none, and there the command exits 1 and names --from-github. --from-github downloads the guide from GitHub instead: the main branch's, or that of the branch or release tag --branch names.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This guide provides AI assistants with: - Instructions on using correct output formats (JSON vs HTML) - Proper suppression creation with correct YAML syntax - Working with CycloneDX SBOM for dependency analysis - Configuration file schema and structure - Common pitfalls and known issues - Integration patterns and examples - Pre-tested jq queries for efficient result querying

docs.title: Get-GenAI-Guide Options
docs.text: Option Description Default --output, -o Output path for the GenAI integration guide ash-genai-guide.md --from-github Download the guide from GitHub instead of writing the installed copy off --branch, -b Branch or tag to download from with --from-github main

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Write to the default location (ash-genai-guide.md)
ash get-genai-guide

# Write to another location
ash get-genai-guide -o /path/to/guide.md

# Write to the current directory under another name
ash get-genai-guide --output genai-integration.md

docs.title: Installation for AI Coding Tools
docs.text:
For Kiro (Global - Recommended): 

# Install globally for all Kiro workspaces
mkdir -p ~/.kiro/steering
ash get-genai-guide -o ~/.kiro/steering/ash-integration.md

# Kiro will automatically load this as steering context

For Kiro (Project-Specific): 

# Install for current project only
mkdir -p .kiro/steering
ash get-genai-guide -o .kiro/steering/ash-integration.md

For Cline (VS Code): 

# Add to project root for Cline to reference
ash get-genai-guide -o .cline/ash-guide.md

# Or add to VS Code workspace settings
mkdir -p .vscode
ash get-genai-guide -o .vscode/ash-integration-guide.md

For Claude Desktop / MCP Clients: 

# Save to a dedicated documentation folder
mkdir -p ~/Documents/ai-guides
ash get-genai-guide -o ~/Documents/ai-guides/ash-integration.md

# Then reference in your prompts:
# "Please read the ASH integration guide at ~/Documents/ai-guides/ash-integration.md"

For Amazon Q CLI: 

# Add to project documentation
mkdir -p docs/ai-guides
ash get-genai-guide -o docs/ai-guides/ash-integration.md

# Reference in .q/config if supported

For Cursor: 

# Add to .cursorrules or project docs
ash get-genai-guide -o .cursor/ash-guide.md

# Or add to project root
ash get-genai-guide -o ASH_INTEGRATION_GUIDE.md

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
For Users: - Download and provide to AI assistants as context - Share with team members using AI coding tools - Include in documentation for AI-assisted workflows

For AI Assistants: - Learn correct ASH result processing patterns - Avoid common mistakes (parsing HTML, incorrect suppressions) - Use efficient queries and proper data formats - Understand ASH configuration and suppression syntax

docs.title: Guide Contents
docs.text:
The guide includes: - Quick reference for key files and locations - Critical rules for GenAI tools - File structure and output directory layout - Working with ash_aggregated_results.json - Working with CycloneDX SBOM - Configuration file schema - Creating suppressions properly - Common pitfalls and solutions - Integration patterns (CI/CD, analysis, reporting) - MCP server integration guidelines - Scanner-specific notes - Performance optimization tips - Troubleshooting guide

For more information, see the GenAI Integration Guide documentation.

docs.title: MCP Command
docs.text:
The mcp command starts the Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, which enables AI assistants to interact with ASH programmatically.

ash mcp

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The MCP server provides a standardized interface for AI assistants to: - Run security scans programmatically - Retrieve scan results with filtering options - Monitor scan progress in real-time - Manage multiple concurrent scans - Access scan result files and paths

A scan started through the MCP server never runs a tool from inside the scanned or delivered directory: ASH_ALLOW_IN_TREE_TOOLS and --allow-in-tree-tools are not honored by ash mcp. See Tools inside the scanned directory.

docs.title: MCP Server Features
docs.text:
• Real-time Progress Tracking: Monitor scan progress with streaming updates
  • Background Scanning: Start scans and continue other work while they run
  • Multiple Scan Management: Handle concurrent scans with unique identifiers
  • Comprehensive Error Handling: Detailed error messages and recovery suggestions
  • Configuration Support: Full support for ASH configuration files and environment variables
  • Result Filtering: Filter results by severity, scanner, or response size

docs.title: MCP Options
docs.text:
Option Description Default --transport Transport to serve on: stdio, streamable-http, or sse stdio --host Host to bind for HTTP transports 127.0.0.1 --port Port to bind for HTTP transports 8000 --mount-path HTTP path the transport listens on. With --transport sse, an unchanged default becomes /sse /mcp --auth-header-name Required HTTP header name for single-tenant auth. Must be set with --auth-header-value None --auth-header-value Expected value of --auth-header-name None --stateless-http / --no-stateless-http Handle each streamable-HTTP request independently instead of binding it to a server-held session --no-stateless-http --trust-upstream-session-id Stateless streamable-HTTP only: a platform in front of ASH issues and authenticates Mcp-Session-Id, so the header names the caller's session False --allowed-host Host header value to accept. Repeatable. Required with a non-loopback --host unless --trust-upstream-host-check is given None --session-workspace-ttl Seconds a session workspace may go unused before it is removed. HTTP transports only 86400 --trust-upstream-host-check A proxy or platform in front of ASH checks Host and Origin, so ASH checks neither. HTTP transports only; not with --allowed-host False --profile Register a config profile as NAME=path/to/ash.yaml. Repeatable. Each file is loaded and validated at startup, and one that fails stops the server with exit 3. See Config profiles None --log-level Set the log level INFO --verbose / --no-verbose, -v Enable verbose logging --no-verbose --debug / --no-debug, -d Enable debug logging --no-debug --quiet / --no-quiet Hide all log output --no-quiet --color / --no-color Enable/disable colorized output --color

Setting --auth-header-name without --auth-header-value, or the reverse, is rejected: partial auth configuration would look configured and enforce nothing.

--profile is the only way a profile is registered. Clients see the names with the list_profiles tool and bind one to their session with select_profile; a bound profile supplies the config for every later call in that session that names none. A profile file that does not load, has an unknown top-level key, or repeats a name stops the server from starting, with exit code 3. See Config profiles.

Everything this command writes goes to stderr. On the stdio transport stdout is the JSON-RPC channel, so one human-readable line there makes the client fail to parse the stream.

docs.title: Session Handling and Host Allowlisting
docs.text:
--stateless-http makes the server handle each request on its own instead of binding it to a session the server is holding. Two situations require it: a load balancer that may route consecutive requests from one client to different replicas, where the next request reaches a replica that never saw the session; and managed runtimes that inject their own Mcp-Session-Id, which a stateful server refuses as a session it did not issue. The difference is observable — given a session id the server never issued, a stateful server answers 404 and a stateless one answers 200.

A stateless server issues no session, so by default its callers have no session identity: the Mcp-Session-Id they send is client-chosen and is ignored, and the tools that need a session (source delivery, select_profile, the scan registry tools) refuse with error_type: session_identity_required. Pass --trust-upstream-session-id when a platform in front of ASH issues and authenticates that header, as Bedrock AgentCore Runtime does; the header then names the caller's session. See Session identity.

The flag is only valid with --transport streamable-http, and passing it on another transport is refused rather than ignored. stdio has a single implicit session and sse holds an open connection per client, so neither has a session to make stateless; silently dropping the flag would leave you running a stateful server and finding out only when a request landed on the wrong replica in production. --no-stateless-http is indistinguishable from the default, so it is accepted on every transport.

--allowed-host is repeatable and names the Host header values the server will accept. The MCP SDK enables DNS-rebinding protection automatically when the bind address is 127.0.0.1, localhost or ::1; bind anywhere else and that autodetect leaves protection off, so the server would answer any Host and any Origin. ASH refuses that: a non-loopback --host without --allowed-host exits 5, a usage error, with an error naming --allowed-host and --trust-upstream-host-check. --allowed-host keeps protection on for a non-loopback bind, because supplying it replaces the SDK's autodetect with an explicit allowlist. That is the right posture behind a proxy whose hostname you know:

ash mcp --transport streamable-http --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --stateless-http \
  --allowed-host ash-mcp.internal.example.com

On a loopback bind without --allowed-host, ASH accepts only the server's own origin: Host 127.0.0.1, localhost or [::1] with the --port it is bound to, and those as http:// origins. The SDK's own check would accept them on any port. On --port 80 the names are accepted without the port as well, as clients write them. --port 0 lets the system choose: ASH binds first and accepts the port it got, which the startup message prints.

The Origin allowlist is left empty rather than mirroring the host list. Origin is a browser-supplied header, and an MCP server reached through a proxy has no reason to trust one.

--trust-upstream-host-check is the explicit alternative when a proxy or platform in front of ASH checks Host and Origin and cannot give ASH a fixed list of names, as on Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. With it ASH checks neither header. It is refused together with --allowed-host, which says the opposite, and on stdio.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: The MCP server is typically configured in AI assistant clients (Amazon Q CLI, Claude Desktop, Cline) rather than run directly. See the MCP Server Guide for detailed setup instructions.

docs.title: Configuration Example
docs.text:
For Amazon Q CLI (~/.aws/amazonq/mcp.json): 

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ash": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": [
        "--from=git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper@v3.7.0",
        "ash",
        "mcp"
      ],
      "disabled": false,
      "autoApprove": []
    }
  }
}

For more information, see: - MCP Server Guide - MCP Tools Reference - MCP Filtering Guide - Using ASH with MCP Tutorial

docs.title: Additional Environment Variables
docs.text:
ASH supports additional environment variables that don't directly map to command-line parameters:

Variable Description Default ASH_IMAGE_NAME Name of the ASH container image automated-security-helper:<build-target> OCI_RUNNER OCI runner to use instead of auto-detection first of finch, docker, nerdctl, podman on PATH OCI_RUNNER_WRAPPER Command prefix to wrap the OCI runner invocation ASH_OFFLINE Run in offline mode ASH_DEBUG Enable debug logging ASH_DEBUG_SHOW_LOCALS Show each frame's local variables in a traceback. They can include secrets; see below unset ASH_VERBOSE Enable verbose logging ASH_BASE_IMAGE_OVERRIDE Registry to fetch the Dockerfile's base image from unset (the Dockerfile's own ARG BASE_IMAGE) ASH_BASE_OCI_LAYOUT Verified OCI layout to build the base image from, with no registry call unset ASH_ALLOW_IN_TREE_TOOLS Let ASH start tools found inside the scanned directory, as --allow-in-tree-tools does: 1, true, yes or on. Ignored by ash mcp unset

docs.title: ASH_DEBUG_SHOW_LOCALS
docs.text: Set to YES, 1 or TRUE, a traceback in the console log, and the one printed for an uncaught error, lists each frame's local variables. It is for debugging on your own machine. Those variables can include secrets from the config and from the environment, so never set it in CI or anywhere the output is shared. On a CI runner ASH ignores it: when GITHUB_ACTIONS, TF_BUILD, AZURE_PIPELINES, TEAMCITY_VERSION, JENKINS_URL, CODEBUILD_BUILD_ID, GITLAB_CI, BUILDKITE, CIRCLECI, TRAVIS, APPVEYOR, BITBUCKET_BUILD_NUMBER or bamboo_buildKey is set, to any value, an empty one included, or CI is set to anything but 0 or false (true, 1, ...), no locals are shown, and the scan logs one warning saying the variable was ignored. A developer whose shell exports CI=1 gets no locals either.

docs.title: ASH_BASE_IMAGE_OVERRIDE
docs.text:
When set, this replaces the Dockerfile's ARG BASE_IMAGE default for the duration of the build, as --build-arg BASE_IMAGE=<value>. Every build entrypoint honours it: the Python CLI (ash build-image and ash scan --mode container), the ./ash shell entrypoint, and Invoke-ASH in utils/ash_helpers.ps1.

It exists for one reason. ECR Public meters anonymous pulls by monthly data volume as well as by rate, and a CI runner drawing from a shared egress pool can find that volume already spent by someone else. ASH's CI pre-pulls the base image and, when ECR Public refuses, sources it from Docker Hub instead, then sets this variable to the Docker Hub reference so the build asks the registry that actually answered. Tagging the fallback image locally under the ECR name is not sufficient: nerdctl, finch, and docker buildx on a docker-container driver all resolve FROM against the registry and never consult the local image store.

Set it yourself if you mirror the base image into a registry of your own. A digest-suffixed reference is accepted and recommended:

export ASH_BASE_IMAGE_OVERRIDE="my-registry.example.com/python@sha256:<digest>"
ash build-image

An explicit --custom-build-arg BASE_IMAGE=... takes precedence over this variable.

docs.title: ASH_BASE_OCI_LAYOUT
docs.text:
<layout dir>@sha256:<manifest digest>: an OCI image layout holding the Dockerfile's base image, and the digest of the manifest for this machine's architecture inside it. ASH's CI sets it after restoring the base image from the Actions cache and verifying every blob against the Dockerfile's ARG BASE_IMAGE_DIGEST, so that a warm CI run makes no registry call for the base image at all. You do not normally set it yourself.

What each entrypoint does with it depends on the builder:

Builder What ASH passes docker buildx build (docker-container builder) --build-context ash-base-image=oci-layout://<dir>@<digest> and --build-arg BASE_IMAGE=ash-base-image nerdctl, finch --build-context ash-base-image=oci-layout://<dir>, --build-arg BASE_IMAGE=ash-base-image and --pull=false plain docker build, podman nothing: these read the base image from their local image store, where the CI step placed it

A value that is not <dir>@sha256:<64 hex> stops the build with an error rather than being ignored. When it applies, it takes the place of ASH_BASE_IMAGE_OVERRIDE; an explicit --custom-build-arg BASE_IMAGE=... still takes precedence over both.

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text:
Every ash command exits with one of these codes. --help exits 0, as does --version on ash and ash scan.

Code Meaning Returned by 0 Success. For a scan or a merge: no actionable findings at or above the threshold every command 1 The command failed, or the scan is incomplete: a selected scanner is ERROR or MISSING, a rule could not be evaluated, a content database is stale, or a merge was refused. Also a scan run on the host (local, precommit or nix mode) of a directory whose path is not UTF-8, refused before it writes anything every command (any unexpected error exits 1) 2 Actionable findings at or above the threshold ash, ash scan, ash merge, ash build-image 3 Invalid configuration or refused input, including, for the ash config commands, a named config file that does not exist or cannot be read, and a configured ash_plugin_modules entry that fails to import (or, for the checks, one no installed package provides). Also, in container mode, a directory to scan or an output directory whose path holds a comma, a double quote or a line break, or is not UTF-8, refused before any container runtime call (--no-run, which mounts nothing, is not refused); ./ash refuses such a path with 3 too ash, ash scan, ash build-image, ash report, ash merge, ash dependencies install, ash plugin list, ash config validate, lint, get, update and validate-plugin-dependencies, ash mcp 4 Workspace definition or policy error; nothing was scanned ash and ash scan in workspace mode, or given a workspace-only option without --workspace 5 Usage error: the command line was refused and nothing ran, including a --source-dir that does not exist, is not a directory or cannot be entered, and an --output-dir that is a file, cannot be created, cannot be entered or cannot be written (see Usage errors) every command, ./ash and Invoke-ASH 130 Stopped with Ctrl-C every command, at any point: while the CLI loads, while the command runs, and while it reports an unexpected error

Code 4 is distinct from code 2 on purpose. Code 2 means a scan ran and found issues; code 4 means the workspace definition could not be used and no project was scanned at all.

docs.title: Container and nix mode
docs.text:
In container and nix mode ASH runs a second ASH, the inner run, and computes the exit code from the results it writes. It reads those results back only when the inner run recorded that it completed, with the ID the outer process gave it (ASH_OUTER_RUN_ID). Otherwise the exit code is 1, whatever the inner run's own status was, and the error says the inner run did not complete and names the results file. A container image built from an ASH older than the one running the scan records no completion, so a --no-build run of such an image, or an image built with --ash-revision-to-install naming an older release, exits 1 this way; rebuild the image from this ASH. When the inner run refused its reports, the exit code is 1 with the inner run's own message. A container status that is not a verdict (3, 4, or the runner's own, such as 125 or 137) is returned as is, without reading any results back.

ash mcp also exits 2 when the server stops on a scanner error, and ash dependencies install for a --tool it cannot select or a --plugin-type that is none of the three. In container mode (and with ash build-image), a status the container runtime reports, such as 125 for a container that could not start or 137 for one that was killed, is passed through unchanged.

A scan stopped with Ctrl-C exits 130 in every mode: local, container and Nix. It prints that it was interrupted, and no completion line, results table or verdict. In container and Nix mode the interrupt is passed on to the container runtime or the Nix shell, which has 5 seconds to stop before it is killed. A second Ctrl-C during those 5 seconds kills it at once. On Windows the console passes a Ctrl-C to the runtime as well, since the two share it; when ASH is attached to no console, it ends the runtime at once instead. ash build-image stopped with Ctrl-C also exits 130 and says it was interrupted. Every other command stopped with Ctrl-C while it runs exits 130 too. Stopped while the CLI loads, before the command runs, or while it reports an unexpected error, any command exits 130 as well and prints nothing more: neither the error nor a traceback of the interrupt. A shell script that runs ash in a loop sees 130 as an exit status, not as an interrupt, and goes on to the next iteration unless it checks for it, for example with ash scan ... || [ $? -ne 130 ] || break.

The ./ash wrapper script in the repository exits 3 when it refuses its own arguments or environment, before it builds or runs anything: no container runner found or an OCI_RUNNER of only whitespace, an option given without a value or with an empty or blank one, a --source-dir or --output-dir whose path holds a newline, a carriage return, a comma or a double quote (a runtime reads --mount as CSV, so it cannot take any of them; a relative --output-dir counts the working directory's path, and is refused before it is created) or bytes that are not UTF-8, an ASH_IMAGE_NAME that starts with - or holds a character other than A-Z, a-z, 0-9 and . _ : / @ -, a --build-target that starts with - or holds one other than A-Z, a-z, 0-9 and . _ -, a --workspace or --workspace-config (the wrapper scans one directory, so run ash --mode container --workspace <file> instead), when it builds the image, an ASH_BASE_IMAGE_OVERRIDE held to the same characters as an image name or a malformed ASH_BASE_OCI_LAYOUT, or, with OCI_RUNNER_WRAPPER set, a GITHUB_ACTIONS, TF_BUILD or TEAMCITY_VERSION that holds a newline. A registry named by a bracketed IPv6 literal, such as [::1]:5000, is refused as well, since [ and ] are not among the image-name characters; name the registry by a host name instead. Those characters are the same in every locale, and Invoke-ASH holds an image name and ASH_BASE_IMAGE_OVERRIDE to them as well, with the same message; it reads ASH_BASE_IMAGE_OVERRIDE when it starts, even with -NoBuild. ash scan --mode container holds ASH_IMAGE_NAME to them too, with the same message and exit 3, before it builds or runs anything; an empty one names the default image. When it builds, it holds ASH_BASE_IMAGE_OVERRIDE to them as well, with the wrappers' message and exit 3, before the build starts: a value of only whitespace is refused, and only an empty one is unset. Both refusals write a tab, a newline or a carriage return in the value as \x09, \x0a or \x0d, so each stays on one line. With --no-run, which only builds the image, the two directories are neither checked nor created and the runner variables are not read, so those refusals do not apply. The exceptions to exit 3 are the usage errors ash itself refuses with 5, refused with 5 and the text ash scan gives: an explicit --sandbox other than off, as ash scan --mode container --sandbox refuses it, even next to a --workspace, whichever comes first; a --source-dir that does not exist, is not a directory, or cannot be entered; and an --output-dir that is a file, cannot be created, or cannot be entered or written. A command line that reaches ash inside the container is refused there with 5, as above. The other two wrappers follow the same rule: utils/ash_helpers.sh returns 3 when it cannot find the checkout, and Invoke-ASH in utils/ash_helpers.ps1 sets $LASTEXITCODE to 3 and throws for each refusal its help lists, or to 5 for the same usage errors. PowerShell's own errors in reading Invoke-ASH's parameters, such as a parameter given no value, are not Invoke-ASH refusals; its help gives the catch form that turns them into exit 1.

docs.title: Usage errors
docs.text:
ASH exits 5 when something on the command line is wrong. It refuses before any scanner runs, and writes no report. Exactly these exit 5:

  • An unknown command or option, or an argument the command does not take, for any command. ash scan --fail-on-finding (for --fail-on-findings) is refused rather than run without the gate it names.
  • An option given to ash before a subcommand that does not take it, as in ash --source-dir src report. An option the subcommand does take is passed to it, as though written right after the subcommand name, so ash --output-dir out report reads out. An option set through its environment variable, such as ASH_SOURCE_DIR, is not affected.
  • A missing required option, such as ash merge without --output-dir or --results.
  • A value an option does not accept: a value outside its choices (--mode, --strategy, --output-formats, --build-target, --min-severity, ash mcp --transport), or a number that is not one (--shard-index first).
  • A name ASH does not know: a --scanners list that names no registered scanner, in a single scan or a workspace scan; an ash report --format that no reporter answers to, whether or not there are results to report. Two selections exit 2 instead: an ash dependencies install --tool name that it has no plugin for, or whose plugin type --plugin-type leaves out, and a --plugin-type that is none of converter, scanner and reporter.
  • Options that cannot be combined: --shard-index without --shard-count or the reverse, a --shard-index outside 0 to --shard-count minus one, either with --workspace, a --scanners list that --exclude-scanners cancels out, and ash mcp's --stateless-http without --transport streamable-http, --auth-header-name without --auth-header-value or the reverse, --quiet with --verbose or --debug, a non-loopback --host with neither --allowed-host nor --trust-upstream-host-check, --allowed-host together with --trust-upstream-host-check, and --trust-upstream-host-check on a loopback --host or on --transport stdio.
  • A path that names nothing usable: a --source-dir (or ASH_SOURCE_DIR) that does not exist, is not a directory, or cannot be entered, for ash scan and the ash config commands that take it; an ash scan --output-dir that is a file, cannot be created, or is there but cannot be entered or written; an ash merge --results that does not exist or is neither a file nor a directory; and a --cli-json-input file that cannot be read, along with a document in it that ASH cannot use. A missing --output-dir is not refused: it is created.

The directory refusals read the same from ash, ./ash, Invoke-ASH and the MCP server's scan tools, which name the case and the path as given, and no option: Source directory does not exist: <path>, Source directory is not a directory: <path>, Source directory cannot be entered: <path>, Output directory is not a directory: <path>, Output directory cannot be entered: <path>, Output directory cannot be created: <path> (<reason>) and Output directory cannot be written: <path> (<reason>), whose reason is the system's own text for the error, such as Not a directory for a file on the way to it, Permission denied or Read-only file system. Whether an output directory that is there can be written is found by making a file in it, under a name of its own, and deleting it, before anything else is written there; the permission bits alone miss ACLs and read-only mounts. The wrappers put ERROR: before them. A source directory cannot be entered when its entries cannot be both listed and opened (it lacks read or search permission), and also when it is under a directory that cannot be searched, whether or not it is there: the system denies such a path, which is not the same as not finding it.

These are not usage errors, because the command line is right and what it asks for is not there yet, or the problem is the machine's. They exit 1: --use-existing when the output directory holds no results, ash report when it holds none, an ash merge --results directory holding no results file or more than one, and --mode nix on a machine without Nix. So do ash config validate, lint, update and validate-plugin-dependencies given no --config in a directory with no config file.

A config path that names no readable file is not a usage error either: it names the configuration to use, and that configuration cannot be used. ash config validate, lint, get, update and validate-plugin-dependencies exit 3 for a --config, an ASH_CONFIG or a path argument that does not exist, is a directory, or cannot be read, as they do for a file a scan refuses. So do ash scan and ash report for an ASH_CONFIG or a --config that does not exist, and ash config validate, lint and get checking another file while ASH_CONFIG names a file that does not exist, since a scan with that environment refuses it. An empty ASH_CONFIG counts as unset; one of only whitespace is refused.

Usage errors have a code of their own because click, the library ASH's command line is built on, exits 2 for them, and 2 is ASH's code for actionable findings: a CI gate would read a mistyped flag as a scan that found problems. Workspace-mode refusals keep code 4, including --dry-run or --workspace-config without --workspace and --workspace combined with --source-dir.

Container mode and --mode nix run a second ASH, inside the image or the Nix shell. When that inner ASH exits 3, 4 or 5 before scanning, the outer ash exits with the same code and names its meaning.

docs.title: An incomplete scan is not a clean scan
docs.text:
Zero findings has two causes and they are not the same answer: nothing was wrong, or nothing was checked. The exit code used to be derived from finding counts alone, so both produced 0. A machine without cfn-nag, grype and syft installed reported those three as MISSING and exited 0, indistinguishable from a run where all ten scanners ran clean.

ASH now exits 1 for that case and prints which scanners did not run:

$ ash scan
ERROR    Scan incomplete: cfn-nag (MISSING), grype (MISSING), syft (MISSING)

Two statuses count as incomplete:

  • ERROR — the scanner ran and failed: its tool exited with a code the scanner does not accept, its results could not be read, or its content database does not exist. Whatever results file the tool left is not graded.
  • MISSING — the scanner's dependencies were unavailable, so it never ran.

SKIPPED does not. A skipped scanner is one you did not select, which is also how sharding divides work between executors: each shard excludes the scanners its siblings own, and those land as SKIPPED. Gating on SKIPPED would fail every shard of a healthy sharded scan. A scanner with nothing to scan in the project is SKIPPED as well, whether or not its tool is installed: cdk-nag and cfn-nag with no CloudFormation template among the scanned files, npm-audit with no lockfile beside a package.json. With files to scan and no tool, it is MISSING.

A run in which every scanner is SKIPPED still exits 1, because it scanned nothing. A scanner with nothing of its kind to scan is SKIPPED too, so this is also what happens when no selected scanner had a file to scan: a scan whose config ignores every file, or --scanners bandit on a tree with no Python file. The error says so:

$ ash scan --scanners detect-secrets
ERROR    No selected scanner had a file to scan: detect-secrets was SKIPPED with nothing to scan, so this run has shown the target to be neither clean nor dirty. The config's global_settings.ignore_paths ('**') leaves every path it matches out of what the scanners read, which can leave them nothing to scan; narrow it to have those files scanned. To accept a run that scanned nothing, set fail_on_incomplete_scanners: false or pass --no-fail-on-incomplete-scanners.

The ignore_paths sentence appears only when the config sets ignore_paths. A run whose scanners were all SKIPPED for another reason, such as --scanners naming a scanner this platform does not support, reports Scan ran no scanners with the list of scanners and their statuses.

ash merge reaches the same verdict over the union of its shards. With --no-fail-on-incomplete-scanners such a run exits 0.

Converters count too. A notebook nbconvert could not convert (it exited non-zero, timed out or wrote no output) and a .zip, .tar or .gz file that is not an archive Python can read are recorded under converter_results.<name>.failed_inputs, and the scan exits 1 naming the converter and the files:

ERROR (1) Exiting because conversion was incomplete: 1 converter(s) did not process the files they were given
  jupyter: could not convert 1 input: notebooks/report.ipynb

Other errors are recorded too, as <Type>: <message>. A converter that crashed, and one whose tool is missing while it had inputs, also make the scan incomplete. A .gz that is one compressed file rather than a tarball, such as data.json.gz, is decompressed and scanned, and is a failed input only when it cannot be decompressed. ash merge combines every shard's failed inputs, and workspace mode reports them per project in incomplete_converters. When a scanner is incomplete as well, the message names the scanners only; the converter failures are then in ash.log and in the results file.

Narrowing a run selects rather than fails. --scanners bandit, --exclude-scanners grype and --python-only record the scanners you left out as SKIPPED, so they do not trip the gate. That was not always true of --scanners: the scan phase used to validate a scanner's dependencies before checking whether it had been selected, so on a host without cfn-nag, grype and syft a --scanners bandit run reported those three MISSING while the six left-out scanners whose tools were present reported SKIPPED — the status depended on whether the tool happened to be installed rather than on what you asked for.

A scanner that scanned no file is not PASSED. semgrep, opengrep and bandit record how many files they scanned. When their exclusions left out every file there was to scan (semgrep's and opengrep's --exclude patterns, or Python files bandit was not told to exclude but did not scan), the scanner is ERROR and the message gives the count; when there was nothing to scan, it is SKIPPED.

Two more things worth knowing:

  • It takes precedence over --fail-on-findings. A run with both actionable findings and an incomplete scanner exits 1, not 2, because clearing the findings that were reported would not make the scan complete.
  • It is independent of --fail-on-findings in the other direction too: fail_on_findings: false still reports an incomplete scan, since it says nothing about whether the scanners ran.

--no-fail-on-incomplete-scanners (config: fail_on_incomplete_scanners: false) accepts a partial scan's exit code. Reach for it last. If a tool cannot be installed on a platform, excluding its scanner is the better answer: the run then records SKIPPED and the report says which scanners were not part of it, where false returns to a 0 that carries no such information.

ash merge uses the same vocabulary over the union of a sharded run: 0 clean, 1 the merge was refused so the union's findings are unknown, 2 findings at or above the threshold, 5 a usage error. See Merge Exit Codes. A shard's own exit code is not the verdict for a sharded run — see Sharding.

Workspace mode applies the gate per project, so ash --workspace and ash --source-dir <one project> agree about whether that project's scan happened. A project that completed with a scanner at ERROR or MISSING is reported with scan_incomplete: true and the scanner named in incomplete_scanners, and the run exits 1. A scanner at ERROR only because its content database is stale is named in stale_content_databases instead, as a single scan's results name it. A project whose conversion was incomplete (a converter that crashed, one that could not convert some of its inputs, a converter tool that was absent with inputs to convert, or an archive refused for an extraction limit) is reported the same way, with the converter and the reason in incomplete_converters, exactly as ash --source-dir <project> fails on it; the MCP workspace tools report the same rows in each project's incomplete_converters. --no-fail-on-incomplete-scanners applies per project as well, and it clears only the verdict: incomplete_scanners and incomplete_converters still name what did not run, because turning the gate off accepts the risk rather than asserting the scan was complete. Each project's inputs_not_scanned names the inputs its scanners found and did not scan (an offline npm-audit's lockfiles), with workspace-relative paths, and the merged summaries and the console list them.

An incomplete project outranks findings, as in a single-project scan: a workspace where project A is incomplete and project B has actionable findings exits 1, not 2. B's findings are still in the results file (exceeds_threshold and the counts) and in every summary, so a gate that has to block on findings whatever else happened should read them there. Exit 4 is unaffected, because it means no project was attempted at all.

docs.title: A scan against a stale database is not a clean scan
docs.text:
A vulnerability database only describes the advisories published before it was built. Measured with grype 0.111.0 under ASH's offline settings, a database built 10 days earlier scanned with exit 0 and no warning. ASH now reads each content database's own build time after its scanner runs and exits 1 when it is past the declared bound (grype 120h, trivy 24h, the offline semgrep and opengrep rulesets 30 days). In an image built with OFFLINE=YES, a stale trivy database warns instead; see Failing on a stale content database:

$ ash scan --offline
ERROR    Content database grype-db (grype) is stale: built 2026-09-21T13:13:21Z,
         10d 0h old, past its 120h bound (grype's own bound); age read from `built`
         in `grype db status -o json`. The scan fails: ...

This does not depend on --fail-on-incomplete-scanners, and it takes precedence over --fail-on-findings the same way. --allow-stale-content-db (config: content_db_staleness: warn) lets the scan pass and records the warning in the summary reports, the SARIF and ash.flat.json instead. Workspace mode applies it per project, reporting the project scan_incomplete: true. See Failing on a stale content database for the bounds, where each comes from, and how to refresh each database.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: This page explains the domain model behind ASH — the key abstractions and how they fit together.

docs.title: Finding
docs.text: A finding is a single security issue detected by a scanner. Each finding has a rule ID, severity level, source location (file and line), and a message describing the problem. Internally, ASH represents all findings in SARIF format regardless of which scanner produced them.

docs.title: Scanner
docs.text:
A scanner is a plugin that analyzes source code, configuration files, or container images for a specific class of vulnerabilities. Each scanner wraps an external tool (like Bandit, Checkov, or Grype), invokes it against the target, and translates its output into SARIF findings. ASH ships with built-in scanners and supports community-contributed ones.

ASH runs a scanner's tool from outside the directory it is scanning. A copy inside it, such as one in the project's .venv/bin or node_modules/.bin that uv run ash or npm run put first on PATH, is skipped; with no other copy the scanner is MISSING, and its missing_reason names the in-tree path. --allow-in-tree-tools or ASH_ALLOW_IN_TREE_TOOLS=1 allows in-tree tools for one run, the scanner sandbox's own programs included. A configuration file cannot turn this on, and ash mcp never does. See Tools inside the scanned directory.

docs.title: Converter
docs.text:
A converter transforms input files into a format that scanners can process. For example, a converter might extract files from a ZIP archive, convert Jupyter notebooks to Python scripts, or render Helm charts into Kubernetes manifests. Converters run before scanners in the pipeline.

The Jupyter converter runs nbconvert outside the scanned tree on a copy named notebook.ipynb, so a notebook whose name contains glob or format characters, such as [x].ipynb, converts, and the result is named after the original. A file a converter could not convert, such as a notebook nbconvert failed on or a .zip, .tar or .gz file that is not an archive Python can read, is recorded in converter_results.<name>.failed_inputs and makes the scan incomplete, which exits 1 by default as a scanner that did not run does. ash merge combines every shard's failed inputs, and workspace mode reports them per project. A .gz that is one compressed file rather than a tarball, such as data.json.gz, is decompressed and scanned, and is a failed input only when it cannot be decompressed. See Inputs a converter could not convert.

docs.title: Reporter
docs.text: A reporter takes the aggregated SARIF findings and produces output in a specific format. Built-in reporters generate HTML dashboards, CSV spreadsheets, SARIF files, CycloneDX SBOMs, and OCSF events. AWS reporters can push findings to Security Hub, CloudWatch Logs, or S3.

docs.title: Suppression
docs.text: A suppression is a rule that hides a known-accepted finding from results. Suppressions can be config-based (defined in .ash-config.yml by rule ID, file path, or pattern) or inline (a code comment like # ash-ignore:rule-id placed next to the flagged line). Suppressed findings are still recorded but marked as suppressed in the output.

docs.title: Configuration trust
docs.text: ASH's configuration can come from the operator who runs it, from the repository being scanned, or, under the MCP server, from a client. Everything the operator sets applies: the defaults, a config file outside the scanned tree, --config-overrides, --ash-plugin-modules, and the profiles the MCP server registers. A config file inside the scanned tree cannot choose what ASH installs or imports, a scanner's own config files, the sandbox's grants, where reporters send findings or the credentials they use, or a plugin package that sends data off the host; those come from the operator. A config file an MCP client delivered is limited the same way, and may not change a field the session's runtime-override policy (denied_paths) denies either. So is a profile the client patched with select_profile, and so are the MCP workspace tools' config_overrides: the allowlist decides which keys a client may change, not whose the values are. Its suppressions and ignore paths apply, and its scanner exclusions are applied as suppressions, but every finding any of them hides is kept in the results, suppressed and marked client-supplied. See Settings a repository's config cannot choose and Config files in delivered source.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text:
ASH processes code in four sequential phases:

  1. Convert — transform input files into scannable formats
  2. Scan — run all enabled scanners against the (converted) source
  3. Report — generate output files from the collected findings
  4. Inspect — launch an interactive UI for reviewing results (optional)

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
ASH supports four execution modes:

  • Local — runs scanners directly on the host using UV-managed tool installations
  • Container — runs inside a Docker container with all tools pre-installed
  • Pre-commit — a local scan limited to bandit, detect-secrets, checkov, cdk-nag and npm-audit, with simplified output; it scans the whole source directory, not only staged files
  • Nix — runs the scan inside nix develop, with every scanner at a pinned version, always offline

docs.title: Output directory
docs.text:
A scan writes to an output directory: .ash/ash_output in the directory ASH runs from unless --output-dir names another, which is inside the scanned directory when you scan the one you are in. Before a scan ASH clears analysis, reports, scanners and converted there, then writes its logs, results and reports, and a sandboxed scan mounts the directory. So ASH refuses, whatever the sandbox mode and before writing anything, an output directory when any of these is a symlink or a directory junction:

  • the output directory itself;
  • a directory inside the scanned tree on the way to it, however either path is spelled (an in-tree output directory whose real path is outside the tree is refused too);
  • analysis, reports, scanners or converted under it;
  • a file ASH writes there by a fixed name: ash.log, ash.log.jsonl, ash_aggregated_results.json, ash-ignore-report.txt, ash-scan-set-files-list.txt;
  • in workspace mode, projects/, each projects/<key> and .workspace-spool.

The error names the link; pass --output-dir with a directory that is not a link. This applies to local, container, nix, workspace and MCP scans, and ash report and ash merge refuse a linked output or reports directory the same way. A link above an output directory outside the scanned tree, such as /tmp on macOS, is your own spelling and is accepted. See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: SARIF
docs.text: SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format) is the internal data model. Every scanner produces SARIF output, every suppression rule matches against SARIF properties, and every reporter consumes SARIF as input. This common format lets ASH treat all scanners uniformly regardless of their native output format.

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows how findings flow through the system:

flowchart LR
    A[Source Code] --> B[Convert]
    B --> C[Scan]
    C --> D[SARIF Findings]
    D --> E[Suppression Filtering]
    E --> F[Reporters]
    F --> G[Output Files]

    style A fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333
    style D fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#0969da
    style G fill:#f0fff0,stroke:#2da44e

Source code enters the pipeline, converters prepare it, scanners produce SARIF findings, suppression rules filter out accepted issues, and reporters write the final output in the requested formats.

docs.title: Configuration Overrides
docs.text: ASH supports runtime configuration overrides through the --config-overrides CLI parameter. This allows you to modify configuration values without editing the configuration file.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
ash --config-overrides 'reporters.markdown.options.include_detailed_findings=true'

You can specify multiple overrides by using the parameter multiple times:

ash \
  --config-overrides 'reporters.cloudwatch-logs.options.aws_region=us-west-2' \
  --config-overrides 'global_settings.severity_threshold=LOW'

docs.title: Supported Value Types
docs.text:
The configuration override system automatically converts values to appropriate types:

  • Strings: 'key=value'
  • Numbers: 'key=123' or 'key=3.14'
  • Booleans: 'key=true' or 'key=false'
  • Null: 'key=null' or 'key=none'
  • Lists: 'key=[item1, item2, item3]' or 'key=["item1", "item2", "item3"]'
  • Dictionaries: 'key={"subkey1": "value1", "subkey2": "value2"}'

docs.title: List Append Mode
docs.text:
You can append to existing lists by adding a + at the end of the key path:

# Add a new plugin module without replacing existing ones
ash --config-overrides 'ash_plugin_modules+=["my_ash_plugins"]'

docs.title: Complex Structures
docs.text:
For complex structures, you can use JSON syntax:

# Add a new ignore path
ash --config-overrides 'global_settings.ignore_paths+=[{"path": "build/", "reason": "Generated files"}]'

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
1. Change severity threshold: 

    ash --config-overrides 'global_settings.severity_threshold=LOW'

  2. Enable a specific scanner: 

    ash --config-overrides 'scanners.bandit.enabled=true'

  3. Configure AWS region for CloudWatch Logs reporter: 

    ash --config-overrides 'reporters.cloudwatch-logs.options.aws_region=us-west-2'

  4. Replace the list of plugin modules: 

    ash --config-overrides 'ash_plugin_modules=["automated_security_helper.plugin_modules.ash_aws_plugins"]'

  5. Add a plugin module to the existing list: 

    ash --config-overrides 'ash_plugin_modules+=["automated_security_helper.plugin_modules.custom_plugin"]'

  6. Configure multiple scanner options: 

    ash \
  --config-overrides 'scanners.bandit.options.confidence_level=high' \
  --config-overrides 'scanners.bandit.options.ignore_nosec=true'

docs.title: Configuration Management
docs.text: ASH provides several ways to manage your configuration:

docs.title: Configuration File
docs.text:
ASH uses YAML configuration files by default. ash config init creates .ashrc.yaml in your project directory; an existing .ash/.ash.yaml keeps working. You can also use JSON (.ashrc.json) or TOML (.ashrc.toml, or a [tool.ash] table in pyproject.toml). The Configuration Guide lists every name ASH looks for, in order.

A basic configuration file looks like this:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper/refs/heads/main/automated_security_helper/schemas/AshConfig.json
project_name: my-project
global_settings:
  severity_threshold: MEDIUM
  ignore_paths:
    - path: 'tests/test_data'
      reason: 'Test data only'
scanners:
  bandit:
    enabled: true
    options:
      confidence_level: high
reporters:
  markdown:
    enabled: true
    options:
      include_detailed_findings: true

docs.title: JSON Schema Support
docs.text:
ASH provides a JSON schema for configuration files, which enables validation and auto-completion in compatible editors. Add this line at the top of your YAML file:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper/refs/heads/main/automated_security_helper/schemas/AshConfig.json

docs.title: Configuration Commands
docs.text: ASH provides several commands to manage your configuration:

docs.title: Initialize a Configuration
docs.text:
Create a new configuration file:

ash config init

This creates a default configuration file, .ashrc.yaml, in the current directory.

docs.title: View Current Configuration
docs.text:
View the current configuration:

ash config get

You can also apply overrides when viewing the configuration:

ash config get --config-overrides 'scanners.bandit.enabled=false'

docs.title: Update Configuration
docs.text:
Update an existing configuration file:

ash config update --set 'scanners.bandit.enabled=false' --set 'global_settings.severity_threshold=LOW'

You can use the same syntax as --config-overrides, including list operations:

# Add a new ignore path
ash config update --set 'global_settings.ignore_paths+=[{"path": "build/", "reason": "Generated files"}]'

# Preview changes without writing to file
ash config update --set 'scanners.semgrep.enabled=false' --dry-run

docs.title: Validate Configuration
docs.text:
Validate your configuration file:

ash config validate

You can also validate with overrides:

ash config validate --config-overrides 'scanners.bandit.options.confidence_level=high'

docs.title: Custom Plugins
docs.text:
You can add custom plugins to ASH by specifying them in the ash_plugin_modules list. Each entry must be a dotted path of Python identifiers inside ASH's plugin namespace: under automated_security_helper. or ash_plugins, or a top-level package named ash_plugins or ending in _ash_plugins (my_ash_plugins, acme_ash_plugins). A name outside that namespace, such as my_plugins, ASH's plugin root automated_security_helper.plugin_modules, or a namespace package (a directory with no __init__.py) refuses the scan with exit code 3 before any module is imported.

ash_plugin_modules:
  - my_ash_plugins

Or using the override:

ash --config-overrides 'ash_plugin_modules+=["my_ash_plugins"]'

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Configuration overrides are applied after loading the configuration file
  • Overrides work with both default and explicit configurations
  • An override that cannot be parsed, or that produces a configuration failing validation, stops the run with exit code 3 (invalid config or refused input). Nothing is scanned, because continuing would mean scanning with settings you did not choose. Note that a top-level key ASH does not recognise is still ignored rather than rejected, for compatibility with configuration files written against other ASH versions.
  • For complex values, use valid JSON syntax
  • Environment variables can be referenced in YAML configuration files using !ENV ${VAR_NAME} or !ENV ${VAR_NAME:default_value} syntax. VAR_NAME must begin with ASH_, or be one of AWS_REGION, AWS_DEFAULT_REGION or AWS_PROFILE. A reference to any other name is left in the configuration exactly as written and a warning names it; ASH does not read the variable. The names are matched exactly, so write them in upper case. An ASH_ name that ends in _KEY, _TOKEN, _SECRET, _PASSWORD, _CREDENTIAL, _CREDENTIALS or _HEADER_VALUE, in any case, and ASH_MCP_AUTH_HEADER_VALUE, is left as written the same way: a configuration file does not read a variable named for a credential. The warning names the variable, never its value.

In YAML, an unquoted value that starts with ${ is resolved with or without the !ENV tag; a quoted one ('${VAR_NAME}') only with it. In a TOML file every string value that starts with ${ is resolved. A JSON configuration file is never interpolated.

ASH reads the configuration file it finds in the directory it is scanning, so which variables that file may name is ASH's decision rather than the file's. To reference a variable of your own, give it an ASH_ prefix — ASH_MY_BUCKET rather than MY_BUCKET — and set it under that name wherever you run ASH.

A reference with no default, ${VAR_NAME}, reads the variable too. When the variable is not set, the configuration is refused with exit code 3 and the error names the variable, since there is no value to use; write ${VAR_NAME:None}, or another default, for a variable that may be unset. A variable that is set to an empty string resolves to nothing either way. This holds in YAML, TOML and pyproject.toml alike.

Write one reference per value, at its start. A reference runs to the last } in the value, so text after it is kept only if it contains no }: ${ASH_REPORT_PREFIX:scans}/ash resolves to the variable, or scans, followed by /ash. When the text after it does contain a }, it is read as part of the reference. With a default, as in ${ASH_PREFIX:scans}/{run}, the default becomes scans}/{run, and the whole value is replaced by the variable when it is set; without one, as in ${ASH_PREFIX}/{run}, the value is left as written. A reference after other text is not resolved, and neither is a second reference.

The scan, and the reports it renders, use the value. What ASH writes of the configuration holds the reference as the file wrote it instead: the ash_config a scan records in ash_aggregated_results.json, the merged results, what an off-host reporter sends, ash config get, and the MCP get_config tool, which shows <from ${VAR_NAME}>. Debug output names a section's keys, never its values. A reference whose variable is unset records the default the file wrote. ash merge and ash report do not read the environment for a recorded reference. A field that takes a fixed choice, such as global_settings.severity_threshold, cannot hold one, so they exit 3 and name the field until you supply it, as in --config-overrides 'global_settings.severity_threshold=MEDIUM' or in the file that --config (or ASH_CONFIG) names, for both commands. A field that holds a list, such as output_formats, needs the whole list: an override that appends with += adds to the list the configuration holds and does not supply the field. A config file in the working directory supplies nothing. ash merge over several shards refuses once, naming each such field with its reference and every shard and results file that recorded it, and both commands word a refusal over several fields the same way. A boolean or a number field cannot hold one either, and the results file that records one there is refused.

Under the MCP server, a configuration file an MCP client delivered may not use !ENV at all, whatever the name, and for a remote client neither may any other file outside ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS and the session's own config/ directory, a scan target's own config included; see Config files in delivered source.

docs.title: Configuration Guide
docs.text: ASH v3 uses a YAML configuration file to control its behavior. This guide explains how to configure ASH for your project.

docs.title: Configuration File Location
docs.text:
ASH reads its configuration from one source. When --config (or the ASH_CONFIG environment variable) names a file, that file is used. Otherwise ASH looks in the source directory in this order and uses the first source it finds:

  1. .ash.yml
  2. .ash/.ash.yml
  3. .ash.yaml
  4. .ash/.ash.yaml
  5. .ash.json
  6. .ash/.ash.json
  7. ash.yml
  8. .ash/ash.yml
  9. ash.yaml
  10. .ash/ash.yaml
  11. ash.json
  12. .ash/ash.json
  13. .ashrc.toml
  14. .ashrc.yaml
  15. .ashrc.yml
  16. .ashrc.json
  17. ashrc.toml
  18. ashrc.yaml
  19. ashrc.yml
  20. ashrc.json
  21. pyproject.toml

Items 1-12 are checked per filename, not per directory: for each name ASH checks the source directory and then its .ash/ subdirectory, so .ash.yml in the source directory beats .ash/.ash.yaml. Items 13-21 are checked in the source directory only. A pyproject.toml counts only when it has a [tool.ash] table; one without that table is not a config source. The lists come from ASH_CONFIG_FILE_NAMES, ASH_RC_FILE_NAMES and ASH_PYPROJECT_FILE_NAME in automated_security_helper/core/constants.py.

Sources are never merged. If more than one exists, ASH logs which one it used and logs a warning naming each one it ignored, once. The scan repeats each of those warnings under "CONFIGURATION WARNING" in its summary and records it in the results as a config_warning entry of validation_checkpoints, because the settings in an ignored source are not applied; ash merge keeps one copy of a warning every shard recorded. The names in items 1-12 are deprecated in favor of an ashrc file or [tool.ash], and the warning says so when one of them shadows a newer source. They still take precedence, so adding a [tool.ash] table to a repository that already has .ash/.ash.yaml does not change which settings a scan uses until the older file is removed.

Scan results are written to .ash/ash_output whichever source is used.

You can also specify a custom configuration file path using the --config option:

ash --config /path/to/my-config.yaml

In a single-directory scan, that file replaces discovery, so the repository's own config is not read. In workspace mode (ash --workspace) it is layered over each project's own config instead: every field it sets is final for every project, and a project's config fills only the fields it leaves unset. See The operator's config.

docs.title: A config file that cannot be loaded stops the scan
docs.text:
ASH uses its built-in default configuration only when there is no config file at all: none named and none found in the source directory. A config file that is named or found and cannot be loaded stops the scan with exit code 3 before any scanner runs, and the message names the file. That covers:

  • a file named by --config, ASH_CONFIG, the config argument of run_ash_scan() or an MCP tool's config_path that does not exist, and an empty --config "". An empty ASH_CONFIG counts as unset;
  • a named or discovered file that is not valid YAML, JSON or TOML, is not UTF-8, cannot be read, is larger than 1 MiB, uses a YAML alias (*name), or is a directory, FIFO, device or other non-regular file. A syntax error, and an alias, names its line. A file that is not a regular file is refused without being read, so a FIFO or /dev/zero at a config name does not stall the scan. A leading UTF-8 byte order mark is accepted in YAML, JSON and TOML alike. Aliases are refused in every YAML ASH reads as configuration (config files, extends bases, workspace policy files, MCP profiles and a client's override_yaml), because a few hundred bytes of nested aliases expand to gigabytes when the config is written into the results; an anchor (&name) that nothing refers to is accepted;
  • a dangling symbolic link at one of the names above, for example .ash/.ash.yaml linked to a shared file that is not checked out. It is not treated as "no config";
  • a pyproject.toml that cannot be read at all, when it would be the source ASH uses: ASH cannot tell whether it holds a [tool.ash] table;
  • a config name ASH cannot look for, such as one inside an .ash/ directory that cannot be searched: ASH cannot tell whether the file is there.

Scanning with the defaults instead would run without the file's suppressions, ignore paths, thresholds and sandbox settings, and report the scan as completed. The same applies to ash report, ash plugin list, ash dependencies install, ash config get and ash config wizard (each exits 3; the wizard leaves the file as it was rather than rewriting it from the defaults), to workspace mode (see Workspace mode), and to the MCP server: scan_directory refuses such a file, and an empty config_path, before it starts a scan, a workspace scan's session profile that does not load is reported as an invalid configuration (exit code 3), and get_config (with or without raw) returns an error instead of the default configuration, with error_category file_not_found for a file that does not exist and invalid_format for one that does not load. A config file outside the session's allowed config roots is refused as outside them before anything reads it, so the response says nothing about its contents. That includes a config source found in the scanned directory: a pyproject.toml, a config file or an .ash/ directory that is a symbolic link out of the roots is refused before discovery opens it, with the same response whether its target is missing, unreadable or readable.

docs.title: Configuring ASH in pyproject.toml
docs.text:
[tool.ash] holds the same settings as .ashrc.yaml, written as TOML, and is validated by the same schema:

[tool.ash]
project_name = "my-service"
fail_on_findings = true

[tool.ash.global_settings]
severity_threshold = "MEDIUM"
ignore_paths = [{ path = "tests/fixtures/**", reason = "Test fixtures" }]

[[tool.ash.global_settings.suppressions]]
rule_id = "B101"
path = "tests/**"
reason = "assert is expected in tests"

[tool.ash.scanners.bandit]
enabled = true

A validation error names the table and its line, for example pyproject.toml [tool.ash] (line 12). String values beginning with ${ are resolved from the environment by the same rule as in YAML, including the limit on which variable names may be read; see the !ENV notes in Configuration Overrides. ash config update, ash config wizard, ash config lint --fix and the suppression dialog in ash inspect edit YAML and JSON (a .json config is written back as JSON), so they refuse a TOML file rather than rewrite it; edit [tool.ash] by hand.

A pyproject.toml that is not valid TOML is skipped, unless its text declares a [tool.ash] table, in which case the scan fails instead of running with the default configuration. One that cannot be read at all (a dangling link, no permission) fails the scan when it would be the source ASH uses; behind a higher-precedence file it is only logged.

docs.title: Creating a Configuration File
docs.text:
The easiest way to create a configuration file is to use the config init command:

ash config init

This creates .ashrc.yaml in the current directory with every setting at its default. It is one of the newer names discovery reads (items 13-21 above), so its discovery warning does not apply to it. When the directory already has a config source, such as .ash/.ash.yaml or a [tool.ash] table, ash config init refuses instead of adding a second one, because sources are never merged; keep using the existing file, or pass --config to write somewhere else. Existing files under the older names keep working. ash config wizard without --config edits the config a scan would use, or creates .ashrc.yaml, and ash inspect findings saves suppressions to .ashrc.yaml when there is no config yet.

docs.title: Configuration Structure
docs.text:
The ASH configuration file has the following main sections:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper/refs/heads/main/automated_security_helper/schemas/AshConfig.json
project_name: my-project
global_settings:
  severity_threshold: MEDIUM
  ignore_paths: []
fail_on_incomplete_scanners: true
converters:
  # Converter plugins configuration
scanners:
  # Scanner plugins configuration
reporters:
  # Reporter plugins configuration
output_formats: []  # Empty writes every enabled reporter
ash_plugin_modules: []

docs.title: Naming the project
docs.text: project_name names the project in the reports: the HTML, Markdown and text reports, metadata.project in ash.flat.json, metadata.project_name in ash_aggregated_results.json, and the SPDX document's root package. Without it the name is the ASH_PROJECT_NAME environment variable, else ash-scan. In workspace mode each project's reports carry that project's label instead.

docs.title: Failing on an incomplete scan
docs.text:
fail_on_incomplete_scanners is a top-level key, and it is on by default. ASH exits 1 when a scanner you selected did not complete — status ERROR (it ran and failed) or MISSING (its dependencies were unavailable, so it never ran) — and prints which ones.

It is on rather than off because a scanner recorded ERROR or MISSING produces no findings, so with the gate off that scan reports the exit code of a clean one. That is the one failure a reader cannot see: the crash is visible in the log, the false all-clear is not. A host that genuinely cannot provide a scanner's tool says so once, with the key below or --no-fail-on-incomplete-scanners, and keeps its old exit codes.

It selects on status, so it covers a failure only once that failure has reached the status. A tool's own failure does reach it: a scanner whose tool exits with a code outside the codes that scanner accepts for a completed run is ERROR, whatever its results file holds, and the row records the exit code and the tool's stderr. A failed tool can still leave a results file behind (semgrep writes SARIF holding only error notifications when it cannot read its rules, grype a zero-byte report when it cannot load its database), and "found nothing" and "never scanned" look the same in it, so that file is not read. The accepted codes per scanner are in Scanner exit codes. A results file ASH cannot read as SARIF is ERROR too, whatever the exit code, as is an empty results file, SARIF with no run, and a scanner result that carries nothing to grade (a dict with no status, severity_counts or findings, a dict whose status does not say its tool completed, or a list or string from a scanner's own scan()); none of them can show that the target is clean. The scanners ASH ships write SARIF with one run even when there is nothing for them to scan. So is a scanner whose tool reports that its content database does not exist; see Failing on a stale content database.

With the key off, an ERROR scanner no longer fails the scan: the exit code comes from the findings alone, so a scan whose only problem is a failed scanner exits 0, the same code as a clean scan. That is what turning the gate off means, and the summary table still shows the ERROR row.

It covers converters too: a converter that crashed, one that could not convert some of its inputs (converter_results.<name>.failed_inputs), and one whose tool is missing while it had inputs make the scan exit 1, as an incomplete scanner does, in ash merge and per project in workspace mode as well.

SKIPPED scanners are ones you did not select and never trip it, which is what keeps a sharded scan working: each shard excludes the scanners its siblings own, and those are recorded as SKIPPED. Narrowing a run with --scanners, --exclude-scanners or --python-only also records the scanners you left out as SKIPPED, whether or not their tools are installed, so selecting a subset does not fail the gate.

A scanner with nothing to scan in the project is SKIPPED too, whether or not its tool is installed: cdk-nag and cfn-nag when no scanned file is a CloudFormation template, npm-audit when no package.json has a lockfile (package-lock.json, npm-shrinkwrap.json, yarn.lock or pnpm-lock.yaml) beside it. A JSON or YAML file ASH cannot read counts as a possible template. A file that does not parse as a template is read again with unknown YAML tags and JSON comments allowed, and counts when that yields a document with Resources, or when its text contains AWSTemplateFormatVersion or a Type: AWS:: resource type, as a damaged template does. So an mkdocs.yml with !!python/name: tags, a Helm chart's templates and a tsconfig.json with comments leave cdk-nag and cfn-nag SKIPPED, as they do with the tools installed, and a truncated template leaves them MISSING. A scanner that has files to scan and no tool is still MISSING, and still fails the gate. The row's skipped_reason or missing_reason in ash_aggregated_results.json says which.

To accept a partial scan's exit code, set it to false:

fail_on_incomplete_scanners: false

Prefer excluding the scanner whose tool you do not have. false makes ASH exit 0 for a scan where nothing ran, which is the same code as a scan where everything ran and found nothing; excluding the scanner records it as SKIPPED and says so in the report, so the next reader can see what was and was not measured.

It is independent of fail_on_findings in both directions. fail_on_findings: false still reports an incomplete scan, and when both would fail the exit code is 1 rather than 2, because clearing the findings that were reported would not make the scan complete. See An incomplete scan is not a clean scan.

docs.title: Failing on a stale content database
docs.text:
content_db_staleness is a top-level key, and it defaults to fail. After each scanner that matches against a content database, ASH reads that database's own build time and compares it to the bound declared for it in automated_security_helper/utils/content_databases.py. Past the bound, the scan exits 1 and names the database, when it was built, how old it is, the bound, and how to refresh it. This happens in online and offline mode alike.

Database Scanner Bound Where the bound comes from Age read from grype-db grype 120h (5 days) grype's own default, db.max-allowed-built-age built in grype db status -o json trivy-db trivy-repo, unless its scanners list leaves out vuln, and trivy 24h trivy's own rule: a database is current until its NextUpdate, which the published database sets 24h after UpdatedAt VulnerabilityDB.UpdatedAt in trivy version --format json semgrep-offline-rules semgrep (offline only) 720h (30 days) ASH's own choice; semgrep has no staleness notion for local rules .ash-rules-fetched-at in $SEMGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR, else the oldest rules file's mtime opengrep-offline-rules opengrep (offline only) 720h (30 days) ASH's own choice; opengrep has no staleness notion for local rules .ash-rules-fetched-at in $OPENGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR, else the oldest rules file's mtime

A database whose build time cannot be read is treated as stale, because an unmeasurable database is not evidence of a fresh one. So is a database whose build time is more than 15 minutes ahead of the host's clock: its age cannot be measured, and the message says so.

A database the tool reports does not exist at all (grype's database does not exist, no VulnerabilityDB from trivy, no rules files in the offline rules directory) also makes that scanner ERROR, under fail and warn alike: the scan had nothing to match against, so its zero findings are not a result. warn relaxes the age bound for a database that exists.

Under fail, a scanner whose result is clean and whose database is stale is recorded ERROR, not PASSED, in its scanner row, ash.flat.json and the summary table, with the stale database named. A scanner that found something keeps FAILED, because its findings are real. The scan reports that ERROR once, as the stale database with how to refresh it: it is not listed again as an incomplete scanner, it counts as a scanner that ran, and ash merge merges its shard and then exits 1 on the stale database.

To let one scan run against a stale database, pass --allow-stale-content-db, or set:

content_db_staleness: warn

Under warn the scan proceeds, and the warning is written to the log and into the reports: a ### Stale content databases section in ash.summary.md, a STALE CONTENT DATABASES section in ash.summary.txt, a toolConfigurationNotifications entry with descriptor id ASH-CONTENT-DB-STALE on the scanner's invocation in ash.sarif, and a content_databases list in ash.flat.json with stale: true and enforced: false. A reader of any of those can see the scan ran against an out-of-date database.

To relax one database without relaxing the others, for example while an upstream publisher is not publishing, name it in content_db_staleness_overrides:

content_db_staleness: fail
content_db_staleness_overrides:
  - database: trivy-db        # a name from the table above
    policy: warn
