  }
]
  • The flat-json and CSV reports show the finding with is_suppressed: true and that justification in suppression_justification, and the GitLab SAST report includes it in the finding's solution.
  • Like any suppressed finding, it does not count toward fail_on_findings. --ignore-suppressions turns it back into an ordinary, unmarked finding, whether a suppression entry, an ignore path or a scanner exclusion hid it: the files under a client-supplied ignore path or exclusion were scanned, and the flag skips the step that suppresses and marks their findings.

docs.title: Temporarily Disabling Suppressions
docs.text:
To temporarily ignore all suppressions and see all findings, use the --ignore-suppressions flag:

ash --ignore-suppressions

This is useful when you want to:

  • Verify if previously suppressed issues have been fixed
  • Get a complete view of all security findings in your codebase
  • Perform a comprehensive security review

When this flag is used, ASH processes all findings as if no suppressions were defined, and that includes ignore_paths. Every scanner reads the files under an ignore path, the converters convert the archives and notebooks there, and their findings are reported as ordinary findings. The same holds for an ignore path or scanner exclusion an MCP client's config supplied (see Suppressions an MCP client's config supplied). Expect a slower scan when an ignore path leaves out a large part of the tree. In container mode the flag is passed to the scan inside the container.

ASH's own output directory is not an ignore path. Findings located there, outside its converted work directory, are left out of the results with or without the flag.

docs.title: Expiring Suppressions
docs.text:
Suppressions and ignore paths both take an optional expiration, and it works the same way on each, and on the scanner options that take the same entries (bandit excluded_paths, checkov skip_path, syft exclude):

  1. The date is YYYY-MM-DD, written as a quoted string ('2027-06-30'). Any other format refuses the configuration, and the scan exits with code 3.
  2. The entry applies until that date, read on the local clock of the host running the scan; in container mode that clock is UTC, because the ASH image sets TZ=UTC. On the expiration date itself the entry no longer applies: an expired suppression's findings count again, and the files an expired ignore path excluded are scanned again. (A content_db_staleness_overrides entry is different: it stops applying at 00:00 UTC on its date, whatever the host's time zone.)
  3. For the 30 days before the date, every scan logs a warning that names the entry. From the date on, one warning at the start of each scan lists every ignore path and suppression that has expired, so a scan whose result changed says why. ash config lint reports expired entries, and malformed dates, by the same rule.
global_settings:
  ignore_paths:
    - path: 'vendor/legacy-sdk/**'
      reason: 'Vendored copy, removed by the SDK upgrade'
      expiration: '2027-06-30'

An expired entry stays in the configuration file, and in the ash_config section of ash_aggregated_results.json; only its effect stops. Remove it or move its date.

This helps ensure that temporary exceptions don't become permanent security gaps.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always provide a reason: Document why the finding is being suppressed
  2. Use expiration dates: Set an expiration date for temporary suppressions
  3. Be specific: Use symbol, or line numbers, to limit the scope of suppressions. A symbol keeps pointing at the same code when lines move
  4. Regular review: Periodically review suppressions to ensure they're still valid
  5. Document approvals: Include reference to security review or approval in the reason

docs.title: Identifying Unused Suppressions
docs.text:
ASH automatically tracks which suppressions are actually being applied to findings and generates a report of unused suppressions. This helps you maintain a clean configuration by identifying:

  • Suppressions for files that no longer exist
  • Suppressions for findings that have been fixed
  • Suppressions that are no longer applicable due to code changes

docs.title: Unused Suppressions Report
docs.text:
After each scan, ASH generates two reports for unused suppressions:

  1. JSON Report: .ash/ash_output/reports/ash.unused-suppressions.json
  2. Markdown Report: .ash/ash_output/reports/ash.unused-suppressions.md (human-readable)

docs.title: JSON Report Format
docs.text:
{
  "summary": {
    "total_suppressions": 10,
    "used_suppressions": 7,
    "unused_suppressions": 3
  },
  "unused_suppressions": [
    {
      "path": "src/old_file.py",
      "rule_id": "B201",
      "line_start": 42,
      "line_end": 42,
      "reason": "False positive - debug mode only in development",
      "expiration": "2026-12-31"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Markdown Report Format
docs.text: The markdown report provides a human-readable summary with: - Overall statistics (total, used, unused counts) - Percentage of unused suppressions - Detailed list of each unused suppression - Recommendations for cleanup

docs.title: Reviewing Unused Suppressions
docs.text:
Check the summary after a scan:

# View summary statistics
jq '.summary' .ash/ash_output/reports/ash.unused-suppressions.json

# View all unused suppressions
jq '.unused_suppressions' .ash/ash_output/reports/ash.unused-suppressions.json

# Or view the markdown report
cat .ash/ash_output/reports/ash.unused-suppressions.md

docs.title: Cleaning Up Unused Suppressions
docs.text:
For each unused suppression, determine the appropriate action:

  1. File no longer exists: Remove the suppression from your configuration
  2. Finding was fixed: Remove the suppression as it's no longer needed
  3. Path/rule/line/symbol mismatch: Update the suppression to match the current code structure. An entry whose symbol was renamed or removed lands here
  4. Still needed: Verify the suppression is correctly configured (check path, rule_id, line numbers)

Example cleanup workflow:

# 1. Run scan
ash --mode local

# 2. Check for unused suppressions
cat .ash/ash_output/reports/ash.unused-suppressions.md

# 3. Edit configuration to remove unused suppressions
vim .ashrc.yaml  # your ASH config file; `ash config validate` prints which one a scan uses

# 4. Re-run scan to verify
ash --mode local

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
The unused suppressions reporter is enabled by default. To customize its behavior, add to your ASH config file (.ashrc.yaml in a new project):

reporters:
  unused-suppressions:
    enabled: true  # Set to false to disable
    options:
      output_format: "json"  # "json" or "markdown"

docs.title: Integration with CI/CD
docs.text:
You can use the unused suppressions report in your CI/CD pipeline:

# Check if there are unused suppressions
UNUSED_COUNT=$(jq '.summary.unused_suppressions' .ash/ash_output/reports/ash.unused-suppressions.json)

if [ "$UNUSED_COUNT" -gt 0 ]; then
  echo "Warning: $UNUSED_COUNT unused suppressions found"
  echo "Review: .ash/ash_output/reports/ash.unused-suppressions.md"
  # Optionally fail the build
  # exit 1
fi

docs.title: Suppressions in GitLab Security Dashboard
docs.text: When using the GitLab SAST reporter, ASH handles suppressed findings in a way that integrates with GitLab's Security Dashboard:

docs.title: Default Behavior
docs.text:
By default, suppressed findings are included in the GitLab SAST report (ash.gl-sast-report.json) with two modifications:

  • Severity is downgraded to Info — suppressed findings won't trigger alerts or block pipelines
  • The suppression reason is added to the solution field — GitLab admins can see why the finding was suppressed

This approach provides an audit trail: security teams can see that a finding was detected and deliberately suppressed, and use GitLab's built-in vulnerability dismissal workflow to close it.

docs.title: Dismissing Suppressed Findings in GitLab
docs.text:
Once suppressed findings appear in the GitLab Security Dashboard as Info-level vulnerabilities:

  1. Navigate to Security & Compliance > Vulnerability Report
  2. Filter by severity Info to find suppressed findings
  3. Select the finding and click Dismiss
  4. Choose a reason: "Acceptable risk", "False positive", or "Used in tests"
  5. Paste the ASH suppression reason from the solution field as the dismissal comment

Once dismissed, GitLab tracks the dismissal across future scans — the finding won't reappear as active even if ASH reports it again.

For automation, GitLab's REST API supports programmatic dismissal:

curl --request POST \
  --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/:id/vulnerabilities/:vulnerability_id/dismiss" \
  --data "comment=Suppressed by ASH: <reason>"

docs.title: Excluding Suppressed Findings
docs.text:
If you prefer suppressed findings to not appear in the GitLab Security Dashboard at all, set exclude_suppressed: true in your ASH configuration:

reporters:
  gitlab-sast:
    enabled: true
    options:
      exclude_suppressed: true

With this option, suppressed findings are omitted entirely from the GitLab SAST report. This results in a cleaner dashboard but removes the audit trail from GitLab.

docs.title: Troubleshooting UV Tool Installation
docs.text: This guide helps resolve common issues with UV tool installation in ASH (Automated Security Helper).

docs.title: Check Installation Status
docs.text:
# Check if UV is available
uv --version

# List installed UV tools
uv tool list

# Check specific tool installation
uv tool run bandit --version
uv tool run checkov --version
uv tool run semgrep --version

The tools ASH runs with uv tool use uv's cache, which a cache-dir in your own or the system uv.toml moves (see uv settings). Run the cache commands below from / (on Windows, from the system drive's root, cd $env:SystemDrive\), as ASH does. A uv.toml or pyproject.toml [tool.uv] in the current directory or its parents changes the cache they name, and anyone who can write that directory or a parent, /tmp on a shared host included, could choose what they clean or change the owner of. Only an administrator can put such a file in /.

docs.title: Enable Debug Logging
docs.text:
export ASH_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG
ash --mode local

Look for log messages with these tags: - [INSTALLATION_START] - Installation beginning - [INSTALLATION_PROGRESS] - Installation progress - [INSTALLATION_SUCCESS] - Successful installation - [INSTALLATION_FAILED] - Installation failure - [INSTALLATION_ERROR] - Installation error - [INSTALLATION_SKIP] - Installation skipped

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text: UV tool validation failed - UV is not available but required

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
ASH uses the uv installed with it first: the uv executable beside the Python interpreter that runs ASH (in its Scripts directory on a Windows Python outside a virtual environment). Only when that is missing does it look on PATH, in the ASH bin directory and in /usr/local/bin. Check both:

# The interpreter running ASH; uv should be in the same directory
head -1 "$(command -v ash)"
which uv
uv --version

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Option A: Install UV via pip 

pip install uv

Option B: Install UV via official installer 

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
source ~/.bashrc  # or restart terminal

Option C: Install UV via package manager 

# macOS with Homebrew
brew install uv

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt update && sudo apt install uv

# Arch Linux
pacman -S uv

Option D: Use pre-installed tools 

# Install tools system-wide as fallback
pip install bandit checkov semgrep

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text: Tool installation timed out after 300 seconds for bandit

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
• Check network connectivity
  • Check if PyPI is accessible
  • Monitor installation progress

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Option A: Increase timeout 

# ASH config file (.ashrc.yaml in a new project)
scanners:
  bandit:
    options:
      install_timeout: 600  # 10 minutes

Option B: Check network connectivity 

# Test PyPI connectivity
curl -I https://pypi.org/

# Test specific package availability
curl -I https://pypi.org/project/bandit/

Option C: Use offline mode 

export ASH_OFFLINE=true
ash --mode local

Option D: Pre-install tools 

# Pre-install before running ASH
uv tool install bandit
uv tool install checkov
uv tool install semgrep

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
Tool installation failed for bandit with exit code 1
No matching distribution found for bandit>=2.0.0

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
# Check available versions
pip index versions bandit

# Test version constraint manually
uv tool install "bandit>=1.7.0,<2.0.0"

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Option A: Fix version constraint syntax 

# Correct syntax
tool_version: ">=1.7.0,<2.0.0"

# Common mistakes to avoid
tool_version: ">= 1.7.0, < 2.0.0"  # Extra spaces
tool_version: ">=1.7.0 <2.0.0"     # Missing comma

Option B: Use broader version ranges 

# Instead of exact version
tool_version: "==1.7.5"

# Use minimum version
tool_version: ">=1.7.0"

Option C: Check version availability 

# List available versions
pip index versions bandit
pip index versions checkov
pip index versions semgrep

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text: Offline mode is enabled (ASH_OFFLINE=true) but tool 'bandit' is not available

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
# Check if tools are pre-installed
which bandit
which checkov
which semgrep

# Check UV tool installation
uv tool list

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Option A: Pre-install tools with UV 

# Install tools before enabling offline mode
uv tool install bandit
uv tool install checkov
uv tool install semgrep

# Then enable offline mode
export ASH_OFFLINE=true

Option B: Install tools system-wide 

pip install bandit checkov semgrep

Option C: Use UV cache in offline mode 

# Set UV offline mode
export UV_OFFLINE=1
export ASH_OFFLINE=true

Option D: Disable offline mode temporarily 

unset ASH_OFFLINE
ash --mode local

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
Permission denied: '/usr/local/bin/uv'
[Errno 13] Permission denied: '/home/user/.local/share/uv'

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
The uv cache commands on this page run from /, with UV_PROJECT and UV_WORKING_DIR unset (env -u), as ASH runs them: a uv.toml in the current directory, its parents, or a directory those variables name can choose another cache. The Cache Management section of the UV tool installation guide explains why and has the PowerShell form.

# Check UV installation location
which uv
ls -la $(which uv)

# Check UV cache directory permissions, asking from /
UV_CACHE="$(cd / && env -u UV_PROJECT -u UV_WORKING_DIR uv cache dir --color never)"
ls -ld "$UV_CACHE"
ls -la "$UV_CACHE"

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Option A: Fix UV permissions 

# If UV is installed system-wide
sudo chown $(whoami) $(which uv)

# If cache directory has permission issues: find it, check that it is the
# directory you expect, and only then change its owner
UV_CACHE="$(cd / && env -u UV_PROJECT -u UV_WORKING_DIR uv cache dir --color never)"
ls -ld "$UV_CACHE"
sudo chown -R "$(whoami)" "$UV_CACHE"

Option B: Install UV in user directory 

# Reinstall UV for current user
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Option C: Use virtual environment 

python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install uv

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
Failed to download package: Connection timeout
SSL certificate verification failed

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
# Test direct connectivity
curl -I https://pypi.org/

# Check proxy settings
echo $HTTP_PROXY
echo $HTTPS_PROXY

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Option A: Configure proxy for UV 

export HTTP_PROXY=http://proxy.company.com:8080
export HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.company.com:8080
export NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1

Option B: Use trusted hosts 

# For pip fallback
pip install --trusted-host pypi.org --trusted-host pypi.python.org bandit

Option C: Use offline mode with pre-downloaded packages 

# Download packages on a machine with internet
uv tool install bandit
uv tool install checkov
uv tool install semgrep

# Copy UV cache to offline machine (asked from /: the cache ASH's tools read)
tar -czf uv-cache.tar.gz "$(cd / && env -u UV_PROJECT -u UV_WORKING_DIR uv cache dir --color never)"
# Transfer and extract on offline machine

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
No space left on device
OSError: [Errno 28] No space left on device

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
# Check disk space
df -h

# Check UV cache size
du -sh "$(cd / && env -u UV_PROJECT -u UV_WORKING_DIR uv cache dir --color never)"

# Check specific tool sizes
uv tool list

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Option A: Clean UV cache 

(cd / && env -u UV_PROJECT -u UV_WORKING_DIR uv cache clean)

Option B: Move UV cache to larger disk 

# Set custom cache directory (an absolute path: uv resolves a relative one
# against each command's own working directory)
export UV_CACHE_DIR=/path/to/larger/disk/uv-cache

Option C: Free up disk space 

# Remove unused packages
pip uninstall <unused-packages>

# Clean system package cache
sudo apt clean  # Ubuntu/Debian
brew cleanup    # macOS

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
Another uv process is already running
Lock file conflict during installation

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
# Check for running UV processes
ps aux | grep uv

# Check for lock files
find /tmp -name "*uv*lock*" 2>/dev/null

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Option A: Wait for other processes 

# Wait for other UV processes to complete
wait

Option B: Kill stuck processes 

# Find and kill stuck UV processes
pkill -f "uv tool"

Option C: Remove lock files 

# Remove stale lock files (use with caution)
rm -f /tmp/*uv*lock*

docs.title: Bandit Issues
docs.text:
Symptoms: 

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'bandit.formatters.sarif'

Solution: 

# Ensure SARIF extra is installed
scanners:
  bandit:
    options:
      tool_version: ">=1.7.0"  # SARIF support requires 1.7.0+

docs.title: Checkov Issues
docs.text:
Symptoms: 

checkov: command not found after installation

Solution: 

# Verify installation
uv tool run checkov --version

# Check PATH
echo $PATH | grep -o '[^:]*uv[^:]*'

docs.title: Semgrep Issues
docs.text:
Symptoms: 

Semgrep rules download failed in offline mode

Solution: 

# Pre-download rules for offline use
export SEMGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR=/path/to/rules/cache
semgrep --config=auto --download-rules

docs.title: Debug Installation Process
docs.text:
# Enable maximum verbosity
export ASH_LOG_LEVEL=TRACE
export UV_VERBOSE=1

# Run with debug output
ash --mode local 2>&1 | tee ash-debug.log

docs.title: Manual Installation Testing
docs.text:
# Test manual UV tool installation
uv tool install --verbose bandit

# Test tool execution
uv tool run bandit --help

# Test with specific version
uv tool install "bandit>=1.7.0,<2.0.0"

docs.title: Environment Validation
docs.text:
# Check Python environment
python --version
which python

# Check UV environment
uv --version
uv tool dir
(cd / && env -u UV_PROJECT -u UV_WORKING_DIR uv cache dir)

# Check system resources
df -h
free -h
ulimit -a

docs.title: Configuration Validation
docs.text:
# Validate ASH configuration
ash --validate-config

# Check scanner configuration
ash --list-scanners

# Test specific scanner
ash --scanner bandit --dry-run

docs.title: 1. Pre-Installation in CI/CD
docs.text:
# GitHub Actions example
- name: Setup UV and Tools
  run: |
    curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
    uv tool install bandit
    uv tool install checkov
    uv tool install semgrep

docs.title: 2. Health Checks
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
# health-check.sh

echo "Checking UV installation..."
uv --version || exit 1

echo "Checking tool installations..."
uv tool run bandit --version || exit 1
uv tool run checkov --version || exit 1
uv tool run semgrep --version || exit 1

echo "All tools are ready!"

docs.title: 3. Monitoring and Alerting
docs.text:
# Monitor installation success rates
grep "INSTALLATION_SUCCESS\|INSTALLATION_FAILED" ash.log | \
  awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c

docs.title: 4. Backup Strategies
docs.text:
# Backup UV cache for offline use
tar -czf uv-cache-backup.tar.gz "$(cd / && env -u UV_PROJECT -u UV_WORKING_DIR uv cache dir --color never)"

# Backup tool installations
uv tool list > installed-tools.txt

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text:
If you continue to experience issues:

  1. Check ASH Documentation: Review the main documentation for configuration examples
  2. Enable Debug Logging: Use ASH_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG for detailed error information
  3. Check UV Documentation: Visit UV documentation for UV-specific issues
  4. Report Issues: Create an issue with:
  5. ASH version
  6. UV version
  7. Operating system
  8. Complete error logs
  9. Configuration files (sanitized)

docs.title: Useful Commands for Issue Reports
docs.text:
# System information
uname -a
python --version
uv --version

# ASH information
ash --version
ash --list-scanners

# Configuration
cat .ashrc.yaml  # your ASH config file; `ash config validate` prints which one a scan uses

# Recent logs (sanitize sensitive information)
tail -100 ash.log

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Common issues you may hit while running ASH, with the cause and fix for each. For UV-specific installation problems, see Troubleshooting UV Tool Installation.

docs.title: Semgrep Login Prompt During Scan
docs.text:
Symptom

ash pauses mid-scan with a prompt like:

Enter your Semgrep registry token, or hit ENTER to skip login:

The scan hangs or fails in CI because stdin is not interactive.

Cause

Semgrep is trying to authenticate to the Semgrep App registry to fetch rulesets. This happens when registry-hosted rules (e.g. p/ci, p/owasp-top-ten) are in use and no token is configured.

Fix

Provide a token via the SEMGREP_APP_TOKEN environment variable:

export SEMGREP_APP_TOKEN=your-token-here
ash --mode local

Or run in offline mode with pre-cached rulesets:

ash --mode container --offline

Or disable the Semgrep scanner if you don't need it:

ash --config-overrides 'scanners.semgrep.enabled=false'

docs.title: cfn-nag Fails Because Ruby Is Missing
docs.text:
Symptom

cfn-nag skipped: Ruby gem 'cfn-nag' is not installed

Or a bundle: command not found error during scan setup.

Cause

cfn-nag is a Ruby gem. Local mode requires a system Ruby installation and the gem on the PATH. Fresh systems (and minimal CI images) often don't have Ruby.

Fix

Install Ruby and the gem:

# macOS
brew install ruby
gem install cfn-nag

# Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt install ruby-full
gem install cfn-nag

Or switch to container mode, which bundles Ruby and cfn-nag:

ash --mode container

docs.title: Grype Cannot Fetch Vulnerability Database
docs.text:
Symptom

failed to load vulnerability db: failed to download: unable to fetch latest.json

Cause

Grype downloads a vulnerability database from toolbox-data.anchore.io on startup. In corporate networks this often fails behind a proxy or TLS inspection gateway.

Fix

Set proxy environment variables before running ASH:

export HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.corp.example:8080
export HTTP_PROXY=http://proxy.corp.example:8080
export NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1
ash --mode local

For air-gapped environments, pre-populate the Grype database cache and run in offline mode:

# On a connected machine
grype db update
# Copy ~/.cache/grype to the air-gapped host

ash --mode container --offline --no-build

--no-build runs the image already on the host. Without it container mode rebuilds the image first, and the first build on a new UTC day upgrades the OS packages and downloads the databases again, which needs network access.

In local mode, ASH reads grype's database from GRYPE_DB_CACHE_DIR when it is set, else from $XDG_CACHE_HOME/grype/db when XDG_CACHE_HOME is an absolute path, else ~/.cache/grype/db (~/Library/Caches/grype/db on macOS). The container image sets GRYPE_DB_CACHE_DIR to /deps/.grype. A db.cache-dir in a grype config is not used, and when the grype config ASH passes to grype sets it, ASH logs a warning naming the file:

The grype config at .grype.yaml sets db.cache-dir, which ASH does not use: grype reads its database from the directory ASH refreshes and checks the age of. Set GRYPE_DB_CACHE_DIR to move it.

To keep the database somewhere else, set GRYPE_DB_CACHE_DIR instead.

A grype run with no database at all is recorded ERROR, not PASSED with no findings: grype exits 1 when it cannot load its database, and ASH also asks grype for the database's status after the scan. When grype reports database does not exist, the scanner is ERROR whatever content_db_staleness or --allow-stale-content-db says, and its error says how to create the database.

docs.title: A Scanner Is ERROR With an Exit Code It Does Not Accept
docs.text:
Symptom

A scanner's row is ERROR, and its error names the tool's exit code:

Failed to execute semgrep scanner on source: SemgrepScanner scan failed: its tool exited with code 7, which this scanner does not accept as a completed run, so its results file is not graded (exit code 7: not an accepted exit code; success_exit_codes=[0, 1]). No stderr captured; checked .ash/ash_output/scanners/semgrep/source/SemgrepScanner.stderr.log, which the tool did not write. .ash/ash_output/scanners/semgrep/source/results_sarif.sarif reports: Invalid YAML file ...

Cause

The tool reported that it failed. Each scanner accepts the exit codes its tool uses for a run that completed, with or without findings, and nothing else. A failed tool can still leave a results file (semgrep exits 7 and writes SARIF holding only error notifications when it cannot read a rule configuration; grype exits 1 and writes a zero-byte report when it cannot load its database), so ASH does not read the file of a run with any other code: an empty or error-only file would otherwise be graded PASSED with no findings. A tool ended by a signal shows as 128 + N (129 for SIGHUP, 130 for SIGINT, 137 for SIGKILL). 127 is a tool the OS could not start, or a run ASH itself failed to carry out (the scanner's errors name ASH's error).

Scanner Accepted exit codes What the tool uses other codes for bandit 0, 1 (issues found) 2: any error (bandit/cli/main.py) checkov 0, 1 (failed checks) 2: the run crashed (checkov/main.py) grype 0, 2 (a match at or above --fail-on) 1: any error, such as a database it cannot load (cmd/grype/cli/cli.go) semgrep 0, 1 (findings) 2: fatal; 3 and up: specific failures, 7 for a rule configuration it cannot read (semgrep/error.py) opengrep 0, 1 the same values as semgrep (src/osemgrep/core/Exit_code.ml) trivy, trivy-repo 0 1: any error (cmd/trivy/main.go) syft 0 1: any error (cmd/syft/main.go) ferret-scan 0, 3 (coverage cut short under fail_on_incomplete: the findings are reported and the row is ERROR, as its target counts as failed) 1: any error snyk-code 0, 1 (issues found) 2: an error; 3: no supported project (src/cli/exit-codes.ts)

trivy exits 0 for a run with findings unless its exit-code setting names another code. ASH passes --exit-code=0 to trivy and trivy-repo, which outranks an exit-code in the operator's trivy config and TRIVY_EXIT_CODE (measured with trivy 0.75.0), and neither scanner reads a trivy.yaml from the scanned directory, so a run with findings exits 0 and a nonzero exit only ever means trivy failed. ASH decides the scan's exit code from the findings itself.

cfn-nag, npm audit, detect-secrets and cdk-nag are not in this table. cfn-nag exits with its count of failing violations and is judged per template; npm audit exits 1 both for advisories and for errors and is judged by whether it wrote a report; detect-secrets and cdk-nag run in ASH's own worker processes.

Fix

Read what the message quotes, and fix what the tool reported: its stderr, or, when it wrote none (semgrep and opengrep report a rule file they cannot read only in their SARIF), the error-level notifications from its results file, which the message names. The full text is in the <Scanner>.stderr.log, the <Scanner>.stdout.log and the results file under scanners/<name>/<target>/ in the output directory; the message names the ones the tool wrote. For semgrep and opengrep under --offline, see Seeding the semgrep and opengrep rule cache. For grype, see Grype Cannot Fetch Vulnerability Database.

The scan exits 1 for an ERROR scanner while fail_on_incomplete_scanners is on, which is the default. With it off, the exit code comes from the findings alone, so a scan whose only problem is the failed scanner exits 0; see Failing on an incomplete scan.

docs.title: Container Image Build Fails
docs.text:
Symptom

ash build-image exits with a Docker or Podman error — network timeout, no space left on device, or an apt-get failure mid-build.

Cause

Most common causes, in order:

  1. Disk pressure on the Docker daemon's storage (layers, volumes, old images)
  2. Network reachability to package mirrors (pip, apt, Alpine)
  3. A stale intermediate image left from a previous failed build

Fix

Free space and rebuild from scratch:

docker system prune -af
ash build-image --force

If the network is the issue, check that the daemon can reach the registries you need (often the host can but the container build context cannot). Configure proxies in ~/.docker/config.json or /etc/containers/containers.conf for Podman.

docs.title: "Scanner Dependencies Not Satisfied"
docs.text:
Symptom

A scanner is skipped with a warning like:

Scanner 'checkov' skipped: required tool 'checkov' not found on PATH

Cause

Local mode requires each scanner's underlying tool to be installed and resolvable. If the tool isn't present, the scanner self-disables rather than failing the entire run.

ASH searches only the absolute entries on PATH, plus its own bin directory. An entry that is relative (bin, .) or empty names a directory under the working directory, usually the repository being scanned, so ASH skips it: a tool reachable only through such an entry is reported as not found, and a command naming it fails with exit 127 and a reason that names the copy ASH did not run. If the tool is installed in a project directory such as node_modules/.bin, add that directory to PATH by its absolute path.

Fix

Install the missing tool. Most tools are Python packages installable via uv tool install:

uv tool install checkov
uv tool install bandit

Or run in container mode, which bundles every supported scanner:

ash --mode container

Or explicitly exclude the scanner if you don't need it:

ash --exclude-scanners checkov

docs.title: Docker Permission Denied on Socket
docs.text:
Symptom

permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket at unix:///var/run/docker.sock

Cause

The user running ash is not in the docker group, so they can't talk to dockerd over the default socket.

Fix

Add your user to the docker group (requires logout/login to take effect):

sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
newgrp docker

Or use Podman instead, which runs rootless by default:

ash --mode container --oci-runner podman

docs.title: Windows Path Separator Errors
docs.text:
Symptom

On Windows, paths like C:\Users\me\project fail config validation, or suppressions configured with Windows-style paths don't match.

Cause

ASH uses forward slashes internally for path patterns (matching SARIF conventions). Config files that mix \ and / can fail to match the files they target.

Fix

Use forward slashes in config paths, even on Windows:

global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - rule_id: RULE-123
      path: src/example.py   # not src\example.py

ASH v3 runs natively on Windows PowerShell and cmd. WSL2 is not required. If you do use WSL2, run ASH inside the Linux side rather than crossing the /mnt/c boundary — file I/O there is an order of magnitude slower.

docs.title: uv or uvx Not Found
docs.text:
Symptom

ash: command not found

Or:

Error: uvx not found on PATH

Cause

ASH is installed via uv tool install, but UV itself isn't on the PATH, or a previous UV installation left stale shims.

Fix

Install UV and ensure its bin directory is on your PATH:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
source ~/.bashrc   # or ~/.zshrc, ~/.profile, etc.

Verify:

uv --version
uvx --version

If ash still can't be found after UV is installed, reinstall it:

uv tool install --force git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@v3

For deeper diagnostics, see Troubleshooting UV Tool Installation.

docs.title: Scan Completes With No Findings
docs.text:
Symptom

The run exits cleanly and a report is generated, but total_findings is 0 for a codebase you expect to have findings in.

Cause

One of three things:

  1. --source-dir points somewhere that doesn't contain your code (e.g. the repo root when the code lives in a subdirectory).
  2. A broad .gitignore or .ignore file, or an ASH ignore_paths entry, is excluding everything the scanners would look at.
  3. Every scanner that would produce findings is disabled or excluded.

Fix

Confirm the source directory:

ash --source-dir ./src --debug

Check how many files the repository's ignore files removed. The scan metadata in ash.summary.txt and ash.summary.md has an Ignore files: line with the total, and metadata.ignore_file_exclusions.by_ignore_file in ash_aggregated_results.json gives the count for each .gitignore and .ignore. To scan the files they exclude, pass --no-honor-ignore-files; see Ignore files and the scan set.

Check for overly broad ignore paths in your config:

global_settings:
  ignore_paths:
    - path: "**/*"        # this will hide everything
      reason: "..."

List which scanners actually ran and their status with --debug, then look for:

Scanner 'bandit' status: SKIPPED

If a scanner you expected is skipped, check dependencies and the scanners.<name>.enabled config flag.

docs.title: Sandbox Settings in a Config File Are Ignored
docs.text:
Symptom

Under --sandbox, a scanner gets no network, or cannot read a path listed in sandbox.extra_read_paths, and the log has a warning like:

Ignoring sandbox.network_scanners from the config built on /home/me/dotfiles/ash.yaml: the file is inside a git checkout or the scanned directory, so someone other than the operator may have written it, and it cannot grant sandbox access. ...

Cause

sandbox.network_scanners, sandbox.extra_read_paths, sandbox.read_path_scanners and sandbox.env_scanners grant access, and a config file inside any git checkout cannot set them, because someone who can push to that checkout could have written it. That includes a config you keep in a checkout of your own, such as an ops or dotfiles repository. For a scanned directory outside any checkout, a config file inside that directory cannot set them either. Under the MCP server, a file a client delivered and named as config_path cannot set them wherever it is, and the warning says that an MCP client supplied the file.

Fix

Pass the setting on the command line:

ash --sandbox auto --config-overrides 'sandbox.network_scanners=[grype,trivy-repo]'

Or move the config file somewhere outside every git checkout and outside the scanned directory, and pass it with --config. Such a file can extend the repository's own config: it keeps the sandbox settings it writes itself, and the warning then names the repository's file. What the file inherits from its bases, or adds with patch, is dropped, so write each grant in the file itself. A mode its own patch sets counts as the mode it wrote.

docs.title: A Plugin Module From a Config File Is Not Imported
docs.text:
Symptom

Ignoring ash_plugin_modules entries 'my_plugins' (it is at /home/me/tools/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/my_plugins, and it is inside the git checkout at /home/me/tools) from .ash/.ash.yaml: ...

Cause

A config file the scanned repository could have written imports only installed modules outside every git checkout and the scanned directory. A virtualenv inside a git checkout counts as inside it.

Fix

Name the module with --ash-plugin-modules my_plugins, or install it into an environment outside every git checkout and outside the scanned directory.

docs.title: A Sandboxed Scanner Does Not Get a Path or Variable Its Options Name
docs.text:
Symptom

my-scanner's settings ask for host paths the default policy does not allow, and those settings can come from the scanned repository, so the sandbox does not grant them. ...

or, for detect-secrets:

Not reading the detect-secrets baseline /opt/baselines/.secrets.baseline: it is outside the source tree, and under the sandbox a file outside the tree is read only for a scanner named in sandbox.read_path_scanners. Candidates the baseline would have marked are reported.

Cause

A scanner's options can come from the scanned repository, so under --sandbox the paths and environment variables they name are granted only to scanners the operator lists in sandbox.read_path_scanners or sandbox.env_scanners.

Fix

Name the scanner, and put the file's directory in sandbox.extra_read_paths:

ash --sandbox auto \
  --config-overrides 'sandbox.read_path_scanners=[detect-secrets]' \
  --config-overrides 'sandbox.extra_read_paths=[/opt/baselines]'

A path outside the source tree has to be inside a sandbox.extra_read_paths entry whether ASH reads it, as it does detect-secrets' baseline, or a plugin scanner reads it inside the sandbox:

ash --sandbox auto \
  --config-overrides 'sandbox.read_path_scanners=[my-scanner]' \
  --config-overrides 'sandbox.extra_read_paths=[/opt/my-scanner-rules]'

docs.title: Landlock Is Unavailable on an Older Kernel
docs.text:
Symptom

With --sandbox landlock, every scanner is recorded MISSING with a reason like:

Landlock ABI 2 is below 3 (Linux 6.2), so it cannot stop a scanner from truncating files it may only read, and the source tree would not be read-only

With --sandbox auto on a machine without a working bubblewrap or firejail, the scanners are recorded MISSING with the same reason in the list of backends auto tried.

Cause

Landlock controls truncation only from ABI 3, which Linux 6.2 introduced. On an older kernel a scanner could truncate files in the source tree, so ASH does not use Landlock there.

Fix

Install bubblewrap and use --sandbox bwrap (or auto, which tries it first), run on a kernel with Landlock ABI 3 or later, or use container mode.

docs.title: A Scanner Is MISSING Because It Was Found Only Inside the Scanned Tree
docs.text:
Symptom

A scanner you have installed is reported MISSING, and the scan exits 1 with a line like:

Found only inside the scanned tree, so not run: bandit (/home/me/repo/.venv/bin/bandit). To use them, install it outside the scanned tree, or set ASH_ALLOW_IN_TREE_TOOLS=1 or pass --allow-in-tree-tools to allow tools from the tree.

The scanner's row in ash_aggregated_results.json carries the same reason in missing_reason.

Cause

ASH does not start tools from inside the directory it scans. uv run ash scan . puts the repository's .venv/bin first on PATH, and npm run puts node_modules/.bin there, so a scanner installed as a project dependency is a file in the repository being scanned. ASH skips it and uses the next copy on PATH; with no other copy the scanner is MISSING. The programs the scanner sandbox starts (bwrap, firejail, readlink, true) are found the same way.

Fix

Install the scanner outside the repository, for example with uv tool install bandit, a system package or Homebrew, and run ASH as usual.

Or, if you trust the repository's tools, allow them for this run:

ash scan --allow-in-tree-tools
# or
ASH_ALLOW_IN_TREE_TOOLS=1 ash scan

ASH then logs a warning naming each in-tree tool it uses. A repository's .ash/.ash.yaml cannot turn this on, and ash mcp ignores both, so for MCP use install the scanners outside the repository. See Tools inside the scanned directory.

docs.title: The Scan Stops Because Something in the Output Directory Is a Symlink
docs.text:
Symptom

The scan exits 3 before any scanner runs, with a message like:

ERROR (3) The output directory /home/me/out is a symlink. ASH does not write to, clear or mount its output directory through a link, whatever the sandbox mode. Pass --output-dir with a directory that is not a link, or replace the link with a directory.

The first sentence names the link; it can be a directory on the way to the output directory, a working directory such as .ash/ash_output/reports, or a file such as .ash/ash_output/ash.log. Over MCP the message ends with a remedy for the MCP caller instead.

Cause

Before a scan ASH removes and recreates analysis, reports, scanners and converted under the output directory, writes its logs and results there, and a sandboxed scan mounts it, so each of these has to be a real directory or file. ASH checks this in every sandbox mode and in local, container, nix, workspace and MCP scans, and ash report and ash merge check the same links below the current directory. In workspace mode a link at projects/ or .workspace-spool stops the whole run, and a link at projects/<key> fails that project with the same message; over MCP, run_ash_workspace_scan refuses the whole call for either. See Output directory for the full list.

Fix

Point --output-dir at a real directory:

ash scan --output-dir "$HOME/ash-output"

or replace the link with a directory. A link above an output directory outside the scanned tree, such as /tmp on macOS, is your own spelling and is accepted.

docs.title: The Scan Exits 1 Because Conversion Was Incomplete
docs.text:
Symptom

ERROR (1) Exiting because conversion was incomplete: 1 converter(s) did not process the files they were given
  jupyter: could not convert 1 input: notebooks/report.ipynb

Cause

A converter could not convert some of its inputs, so the scanners never saw those files in converted form: nbconvert exited non-zero, timed out or wrote no output for a notebook, or a .zip, .tar or .gz file is not an archive Python can read. Each is recorded under converter_results.<converter>.failed_inputs in ash_aggregated_results.json, with the reason. A .gz that is one compressed file rather than a tarball, such as data.json.gz, is decompressed and scanned, and is a failed input only when it cannot be decompressed. A Git LFS pointer named like an archive is reported as not scanned and does not fail the scan. ash merge combines every shard's failed inputs, and workspace mode reports them per project in incomplete_converters.

A notebook's name is not the cause: nbconvert reads its notebook argument as a glob pattern and its output name as a format string, so ASH converts a copy named notebook.ipynb and names the result after the original, and [x].ipynb or {a,b}.ipynb convert. cfn-nag likewise is given a copy of each template named template.json, template.yaml or template.yml, so a template's name does not change how it is scanned, on Windows too.

Fix

Read the reason in failed_inputs, or rerun with --debug to see nbconvert's own error output. Then fix or remove the notebook or archive, exclude it with ignore_paths, disable the converter if its inputs are not wanted, or accept the partial scan with --no-fail-on-incomplete-scanners.

docs.title: An Archive Makes the Scan Incomplete
docs.text:
Symptom

The scan exits 1 with Exiting because conversion was incomplete, naming the archive converter and one or more .zip, .tar or .gz files, or the summary lists an archive under "Converter inputs not scanned".

Cause

One of three things, named in converter_results.archive in ash_aggregated_results.json:

  1. The archive is over an extraction limit: its refused_inputs record names the limit, such as max_total_bytes.
  2. The archive cannot be read (damaged, truncated, a tar cut off between members, empty, or a .tar.gz that is not a tarball): it is in failed_inputs.
  3. The file is a Git LFS pointer rather than the archive, because the checkout did not fetch the LFS objects. This is reported but does not fail the scan.

Fix

For a limit, raise it as the operator; a config file inside the scanned tree cannot raise it:

ash scan --config-overrides 'converters.archive.options.max_total_bytes=4294967296'

For an archive that cannot be read, replace it with an intact copy, or exclude it with global_settings.ignore_paths if its contents need not be scanned.

For an LFS pointer, fetch the LFS objects before the scan: git lfs pull, or lfs: true on the CI checkout step. See Archive Converter.

docs.title: A Scanner Is ERROR Because a Path Below the Output Directory Is a Symlink
docs.text:
Symptom

A scanner row is ERROR, and its error ends with:

.ash/ash_output/scanners/detect-secrets/source/results_sarif.sarif was not written: .ash/ash_output/scanners/detect-secrets/source/results_sarif.sarif is a symlink, and ASH does not write through a symlink below its output directory

Cause

ASH found a symlink at a path it writes below its output directory, or at a directory on the way to it, and did not write through it. This holds with and without --sandbox. With a sandbox, a symlink anywhere below the scanner's results directory before the scanner starts is refused the same way. The default output directory is inside the scanned tree, so the link usually came with the repository.

An error that ends with <n> names refer to it, and ASH does not write to a file below its output directory that another name refers to is the same refusal for a hard link: the file at that path is also reachable under another name, possibly outside the output directory, so ASH did not change it. Archives can carry hard links.

Fix

Remove the link, or pass an --output-dir outside the scanned tree.

docs.title: UV Tool Installation Guide
docs.text: This guide covers the enhanced UV tool installation functionality in ASH (Automated Security Helper), which provides explicit tool installation for Python-based security scanners.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ASH now supports explicit UV tool installation for Python-based security scanners including:

  • Bandit - Python source code security analyzer
  • Checkov - Infrastructure as Code (IaC) security scanner
  • Semgrep - Static analysis tool for finding bugs and security issues

The enhanced installation system provides:

  • Explicit Installation: Tools are installed upfront rather than on-demand
  • Version Control: Specify exact version constraints for reproducible scans
  • Offline Mode Support: Works with cached tools and pre-installed dependencies
  • Enhanced Error Handling: Comprehensive logging and fallback mechanisms
  • Performance Optimization: Leverages UV's caching for faster subsequent installations

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text: tool_version is the operator's setting. Set it in a config file outside the scanned tree or with --config-overrides; a value in the scanned repository's own config is ignored with a warning unless it equals the operator's. See Settings a repository's config cannot choose.

docs.title: Bandit Scanner Configuration
docs.text:
scanners:
  bandit:
    enabled: true
    options:
      tool_version: ">=1.7.0,<2.0.0"  # Version constraint for installation
      install_timeout: 300             # Installation timeout in seconds
      confidence_level: "all"
      ignore_nosec: false

docs.title: Checkov Scanner Configuration
docs.text:
scanners:
  checkov:
    enabled: true
    options:
      tool_version: ">=3.2.0,<4.0.0"  # Version constraint for installation
      install_timeout: 300             # Installation timeout in seconds
      frameworks: ["all"]
      offline: false

docs.title: Semgrep Scanner Configuration
docs.text:
scanners:
  semgrep:
    enabled: true
    options:
      tool_version: ">=1.125.0"        # Version constraint for installation
      install_timeout: 300             # Installation timeout in seconds
      config: "auto"
      metrics: "auto"

docs.title: 1. Explicit Installation Process
docs.text:
When a scanner is initialized, the following workflow occurs:

  1. UV Availability Check: Verify that UV is available on the system
  2. Tool Status Check: Check if the tool is already installed via UV
  3. Installation Attempt: If not installed, attempt explicit installation with version constraints
  4. Validation: Validate that the installed tool is functional
  5. Fallback: If installation fails, fall back to pre-installed tools or existing validation

docs.title: 2. Installation Commands
docs.text:
The system generates UV tool installation commands automatically:

# Basic installation
uv tool install bandit

# With version constraint
uv tool install "bandit>=1.7.0,<2.0.0"

# With package extras (for enhanced functionality)
uv tool install "bandit[sarif,toml]>=1.7.0,<2.0.0"

# In offline mode
uv tool install --offline "bandit>=1.7.0,<2.0.0"

These read your user and system uv.toml (an index mirror set there applies) and not the scanned repository's: uv ignores project files for uv tool commands. The uv pip commands ASH runs carry --no-config. See uv settings in the CLI reference.

docs.title: Supported Version Constraint Formats
docs.text:
# Exact version
tool_version: "==1.7.5"

# Minimum version
tool_version: ">=1.7.0"

# Version range
tool_version: ">=1.7.0,<2.0.0"

# Compatible release
tool_version: "~=1.7.0"

# Latest version (default)
tool_version: null

docs.title: Default Version Constraints
docs.text:
Each scanner has sensible default version constraints:

  • Bandit: >=1.7.0,<2.0.0 (SARIF and TOML support)
  • Checkov: >=3.2.0,<4.0.0 (Improved stability)
  • Semgrep: >=1.125.0 (Enhanced performance)

docs.title: Enabling Offline Mode
docs.text:
Set the ASH_OFFLINE environment variable:

export ASH_OFFLINE=true
ash --mode local

Or configure in scanner options:

scanners:
  checkov:
    options:
      offline: true

docs.title: Offline Mode Behavior
docs.text:
In offline mode:

  1. Installation Skipping: UV tool installation attempts are skipped
  2. Pre-installed Detection: System searches for pre-installed tools
  3. Cache Usage: Leverages UV's local cache when available
  4. Clear Error Messages: Provides helpful guidance for offline limitations

docs.title: Offline Mode Environment Variables
docs.text:
# Enable ASH offline mode
export ASH_OFFLINE=true

# Enable UV offline mode (for tool execution)
export UV_OFFLINE=1

# Specify Semgrep rules cache directory
export SEMGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR=/path/to/cached/rules

docs.title: 1. UV Not Available
docs.text:
Error: UV tool validation failed - UV is not available but required

ASH looks for uv in this order: the uv installed with ASH, in ASH's own environment (ASH depends on the uv package, so a pip, pipx, uv tool or uvx install has one beside the Python interpreter that runs ASH, or in that interpreter's Scripts directory on Windows, even when that directory is not on PATH), then PATH, the ASH bin directory (~/.ash/bin or ASH_BIN_PATH) and /usr/local/bin. The error means none of them has a uv, which happens when ASH was installed without its dependencies.

Solution: 

# Install UV using pip
pip install uv

# Or using homebrew (macOS)
brew install uv

# Or using the official installer
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

docs.title: 2. Installation Timeout
docs.text:
Error: Tool installation timed out after 300 seconds

Solutions: - Increase timeout in configuration: 

scanners:
  bandit:
    options:
      install_timeout: 600  # 10 minutes
- Check network connectivity - Use offline mode with pre-installed tools

docs.title: 3. Version Conflicts
docs.text:
Error: Tool installation failed with exit code 1

Solutions: - Check version constraint syntax - Verify tool version availability - Use broader version ranges: 

tool_version: ">=1.7.0"  # Instead of exact version

docs.title: 4. Offline Mode Issues
docs.text:
Error: Offline mode is enabled but tool 'bandit' is not available

Solutions: - Pre-install tools manually: 

uv tool install bandit
- Install tools system-wide: 
pip install bandit checkov semgrep
- Disable offline mode temporarily

docs.title: Logging and Diagnostics
docs.text:
The installation system provides structured logging with tags:

  • [INSTALLATION_START]: Installation initiation
  • [INSTALLATION_PROGRESS]: Progress updates
  • [INSTALLATION_SUCCESS]: Successful installation
  • [INSTALLATION_FAILED]: Installation failure
  • [INSTALLATION_ERROR]: Unexpected errors
  • [INSTALLATION_SKIP]: Installation skipped (offline mode, already installed)

Enable debug logging for detailed diagnostics:

export ASH_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG
ash --mode local

docs.title: Caching Benefits
docs.text:
UV's built-in caching provides significant performance improvements:

  • First Installation: Downloads and caches tool and dependencies
  • Subsequent Installations: Uses cached artifacts (50-90% faster)
  • Cross-Project Sharing: Cache shared across different ASH projects

docs.title: Cache Management
docs.text:
Run these from / (on Windows, from the system drive's root), as ASH does, with UV_PROJECT and UV_WORKING_DIR unset. A cache-dir in a uv.toml or pyproject.toml [tool.uv] in the current directory or its parents, or in the directory either variable names, changes the cache they act on, so whoever can write that directory, /tmp on a shared host included, could choose what uv cache clean removes. Only an administrator can put such a file in /. A cache-dir in your own or the system uv.toml, or UV_CACHE_DIR, moves the cache for ASH's tools and for these commands alike when it is an absolute path. uv resolves a relative one against each command's working directory, so (cd / && uv cache clean) would act on a directory under /, not on the cache the tools used:

# View cache size
(cd / && env -u UV_PROJECT -u UV_WORKING_DIR uv cache size)

# Check cache location
(cd / && env -u UV_PROJECT -u UV_WORKING_DIR uv cache dir)

# Clean cache if needed
(cd / && env -u UV_PROJECT -u UV_WORKING_DIR uv cache clean)

In PowerShell, remove the two variables first (this changes the current session), then run each command from the system drive's root:

Remove-Item Env:UV_PROJECT, Env:UV_WORKING_DIR -ErrorAction Ignore
Push-Location "$env:SystemDrive\"; uv cache size; Pop-Location
Push-Location "$env:SystemDrive\"; uv cache dir; Pop-Location
Push-Location "$env:SystemDrive\"; uv cache clean; Pop-Location

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use Version Ranges: Allows cache reuse across compatible versions
  2. Pre-install in CI: Install tools in CI setup phase for faster builds
  3. Shared Cache: Use shared cache directories in containerized environments
  4. Concurrent Scans: Installation system handles concurrent scanner initialization

docs.title: Custom Installation Commands
docs.text:
For advanced use cases, you can define custom installation commands:

# In custom scanner implementation
def _get_tool_version_constraint(self) -> str:
    return ">=1.7.0,<2.0.0"


def _get_tool_package_extras(self) -> List[str]:
    return ["sarif", "toml", "yaml"]

docs.title: Retry Configuration
docs.text:
Configure installation retry behavior:

retry_config = {
    "max_retries": 3,
    "base_delay": 1.0,
    "max_delay": 60.0,
}

docs.title: Progress Monitoring
docs.text:
For long-running installations, progress monitoring is automatically enabled:

def progress_callback(message: str):
    print(f"Installation progress: {message}")


# Progress updates every 10 seconds for installations > 60 seconds

docs.title: From On-Demand to Explicit Installation
docs.text:
If you're upgrading from a previous version of ASH:

  1. No Configuration Changes Required: Explicit installation is enabled by default
  2. Optional Version Pinning: Add tool_version to scanner configurations for reproducibility
  3. Timeout Adjustment: Increase install_timeout if you experience timeout issues
  4. Offline Mode: Configure offline mode if running in air-gapped environments

docs.title: Backward Compatibility
docs.text:
The enhanced installation system maintains full backward compatibility:

  • Existing Configurations: Continue to work without changes
  • Fallback Mechanisms: Falls back to pre-installed tools if UV installation fails
  • Legacy Behavior: On-demand installation still available as fallback

docs.title: Basic Configuration
docs.text:
# ASH config file (.ashrc.yaml in a new project)
scanners:
  bandit:
    enabled: true
  checkov:
    enabled: true
  semgrep:
    enabled: true

docs.title: Advanced Configuration with Version Control
docs.text:
# ASH config file (.ashrc.yaml in a new project)
scanners:
  bandit:
    enabled: true
    options:
      tool_version: ">=1.7.5,<1.8.0"
      install_timeout: 600
      confidence_level: "medium"

  checkov:
    enabled: true
    options:
      tool_version: ">=3.2.5,<3.3.0"
      install_timeout: 300
      frameworks: ["terraform", "cloudformation"]

  semgrep:
    enabled: true
    options:
      tool_version: ">=1.125.0,<2.0.0"
      install_timeout: 450
      config: "p/security-audit"

docs.title: Offline Mode Configuration
docs.text:
# ASH config file (.ashrc.yaml in a new project)
scanners:
  checkov:
    enabled: true
    options:
      offline: true
      frameworks: ["terraform"]

  semgrep:
    enabled: true
    options:
      offline: true
      config: "p/ci"  # Use cached rules

docs.title: CI/CD Integration
docs.text:
# GitHub Actions example
- name: Setup UV
  run: |
    # The installer puts uv in ~/.local/bin, not under ~/.cargo; UV_INSTALL_DIR pins it.
    curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | UV_INSTALL_DIR="$HOME/.local/bin" sh
    echo "$HOME/.local/bin" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"

- name: Pre-install Security Tools
  run: |
    uv tool install "bandit>=1.7.0,<2.0.0"
    uv tool install "checkov>=3.2.0,<4.0.0"
    uv tool install "semgrep>=1.125.0,<2.0.0"

- name: Run ASH Security Scan
  run: |
    ash --mode local

docs.title: 1. Version Management
docs.text:
• Pin Major Versions: Use ranges like >=1.7.0,<2.0.0 to avoid breaking changes
  • Regular Updates: Periodically update version constraints for security patches
  • Testing: Test version updates in development before production deployment

docs.title: 2. Performance Optimization
docs.text:
• Pre-installation: Install tools during environment setup rather than scan time
  • Cache Sharing: Use shared UV cache directories in containerized environments
  • Concurrent Scans: Leverage concurrent scanner initialization for faster startup

docs.title: 3. Error Handling
docs.text:
• Timeout Configuration: Set appropriate timeouts based on network conditions
  • Fallback Planning: Ensure pre-installed tools are available as fallbacks
  • Monitoring: Monitor installation success rates and adjust configurations

docs.title: 4. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Version Pinning: Pin tool versions for reproducible security scans
  • Repository configuration is not read: uv tool commands ignore project files, and ASH runs uv pip with --no-config and uv cache from the filesystem root, so a scanned repository's uv.toml or [tool.uv] cannot point uv at its own packages
  • Offline Mode: Use offline mode in secure environments with limited network access
  • Tool Verification: Regularly validate that installed tools are functional

docs.title: Troubleshooting Checklist
docs.text:
When experiencing installation issues:

  1. Check UV Installation: uv --version
  2. Verify Network Connectivity: Can reach PyPI and tool repositories
  3. Check Disk Space: Ensure sufficient space for tool installation and cache
  4. Review Logs: Enable debug logging for detailed error information
  5. Test Manual Installation: Try installing tools manually with UV
  6. Check Version Constraints: Verify version constraint syntax and availability
  7. Consider Offline Mode: Use offline mode with pre-installed tools if needed
  8. Update Configuration: Adjust timeouts and retry settings as needed

docs.title: Streamable-HTTP MCP Deployment Guide
docs.text:
This guide covers running the ASH MCP server over the streamable-HTTP transport so remote clients can drive scans against their own source trees and configs. It is the deployment counterpart to the local stdio transport documented in ASH MCP Server Guide.

The behaviour described here lands under Track 10 of the ASH v3.x refactor (sections 10.1 through 10.7 in tasks/todo.md).

docs.title: When to use streamable-HTTP vs stdio
docs.text:
ASH ships two MCP transports:

  • stdio (default). A single client (typically an IDE or a local agent) launches ash mcp as a subprocess and speaks JSON-RPC over the child's stdin/stdout. One process per user, no network surface, no auth needed. This is what ash mcp does today and remains the recommended setup for individual developer machines.
  • streamable-HTTP. The MCP server is bound to a TCP port and accepts connections from remote clients. Each connection gets its own session workspace, its own selected config profile, and its own optional source-upload pipeline. Use this when you need a deployable, multi-tenant ASH service — for example, a shared scanner for CI runners, a hosted scanner an external agent can drive, or any setup where the client and the scanner run on different hosts.

Pick stdio for local single-user IDE integration. Pick streamable-HTTP when ASH must be reachable over the network.

docs.title: Starting the server
docs.text:
The full invocation form (Track 10.1):

ash mcp \
  --transport streamable-http \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8000 \
  --mount-path /mcp \
  --allowed-host ash-mcp.example.com \
  --auth-header-name x-ash-token \
  --auth-header-value-file /etc/ash/mcp-token \
  --profile default=/etc/ash/default.yaml \
  --profile strict=/etc/ash/strict.yaml

Flags:

  • --transport streamable-http — selects the streamable-HTTP transport. Other accepted values: stdio (default) and sse (legacy, not covered here).
  • --host — bind address. Use 127.0.0.1 for loopback-only deployments and 0.0.0.0 when fronted by a reverse proxy. Any address other than 127.0.0.1, localhost or ::1 needs --allowed-host or --trust-upstream-host-check, or the server refuses to start with the usage-error code; see Host and Origin checking.
  • --allowed-host — a Host header value the server accepts, repeatable: the name clients use to reach it, such as the proxy's hostname. ASH checks Host against this list and accepts no Origin header.
  • --trust-upstream-host-check — a proxy or platform in front of ASH checks Host and Origin, so ASH checks neither. For a platform that restricts Host itself and cannot be given an allowlist in advance, such as Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. Refused together with --allowed-host, and refused with a loopback --host (127.0.0.1, localhost, ::1), where ASH accepts only its own origin; behind a proxy on the same host, pass --allowed-host with the name the proxy forwards. Both refusals exit with the usage-error code.
  • --port — TCP port. Defaults are deliberately omitted; pick an explicit port that matches your proxy/firewall config.
  • --mount-path — path under which the FastMCP app is mounted. Defaults to /mcp. Clients must connect to http(s)://host:port<mount-path>.
  • --auth-header-name with --auth-header-value-file PATH, --auth-header-value-fd N or --auth-header-value VALUE — single-tenant header gate. Connections missing this header (or carrying a wrong value) are rejected before any tool dispatch. See Auth for how each form passes the value.
  • --stateless-http — handle each request on its own instead of binding it to a server-held session, for a load balancer or a platform such as AgentCore. A stateless server issues no session; see Session identity.
  • --trust-upstream-session-id — stateless only: a platform in front of ASH issues and authenticates Mcp-Session-Id, so the header names the caller's session. See Session identity.
  • --session-workspace-ttl SECONDS — how long a session workspace may go unused before the server removes it (default 86400). See Session lifecycle.
  • --profile NAME=path/to/ash.yaml — register a config profile under NAME. Repeatable. The YAML is loaded and validated through AshConfig.from_file at startup, with its extends chain (bases must stay in the profile's directory); bad profiles fail fast and the server refuses to start, including one whose file or any of whose bases has an unknown top-level field. See Config profiles.

The server logs the bound address and the registered profile names on startup. It does not log header values or profile contents.

docs.title: Host and Origin checking
docs.text:
The MCP SDK protects against DNS rebinding by checking the Host and Origin headers, and it turns that check on by itself only when the app is built for 127.0.0.1, localhost or ::1. For any other bind address, including 0.0.0.0, ::, a routable address and 127.0.0.2, the check would be off and the server would answer any Host and any Origin. ASH therefore refuses to start a non-loopback bind unless the operator says how Host is checked:

  • --allowed-host NAME (repeatable): ASH checks Host against the names given. Use the name clients and your proxy send.
  • --trust-upstream-host-check: something in front of ASH checks Host and Origin, and ASH checks neither.

On a loopback bind with no --allowed-host, the server accepts only its own origin: Host 127.0.0.1:PORT, localhost:PORT or [::1]:PORT, where PORT is --port, and the same as http:// origins. The SDK's own loopback check accepts those names on any port; ASH accepts the bound port only. A request with no Origin header, which is what every non-browser MCP client sends, needs only the right Host. On port 80 the names without a port (127.0.0.1, http://localhost) are accepted too, because clients leave out the default port. With --port 0 the system picks the port: ASH binds the socket first, builds the server for the port it got, and prints it at startup.

If you build the app yourself with build_streamable_http_app or build_sse_app on a loopback host without allowed_hosts, pass port= the port the server listens on; the builders refuse to build one without it (or with 0), because an app built for another port answers 421 to every request.

The refusal names both options. The Terraform container entrypoint passes --trust-upstream-host-check only when ASH_MCP_TRUST_UPSTREAM_HOST_CHECK=true, ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS is empty and the bind is not loopback; the AgentCore module sets it. With neither variable set, an image bound to 0.0.0.0 refuses to start.

docs.title: Session identity
docs.text:
Source delivery, a bound profile and the scan registry all belong to a session, so the server has to know which session a call is part of. It decides that from the transport, never from a header alone:

Transport The caller's session stdio the single local client (__default__), with local trust sse the session the server issued for the event stream, named once in the message URL's session_id; an Mcp-Session-Id header on a message is ignored, and a URL that names session_id twice names no session streamable-HTTP, stateful the Mcp-Session-Id the server issued at initialize; a value it did not issue is ignored streamable-HTTP, --stateless-http none: the server issues no session and the header is client-chosen streamable-HTTP, --stateless-http --trust-upstream-session-id the Mcp-Session-Id header, which the operator declares a platform in front of ASH issues and authenticates

Every caller on a network transport is remote, whatever headers it sends: it is confined to the operator's grants (ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS, ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS) plus its own session workspace, and never gets stdio's local trust. Local trust goes only to a caller ASH knows is the local client: ash mcp on stdio, or a program that drives the server through the MCP SDK's in-memory client inside automated_security_helper.cli.mcp.session_identity.serving_local_client(). Any other tool call that reaches the server with no HTTP request behind it, including an in-memory client outside that block, has no session identity.

ASH_MCP_TRANSPORT is an operator override on top of that: set to streamable-http or sse, it makes every caller in the process remote, in-process ones included. It is read stripped and in any case; empty, or only whitespace, it is unset. A value that names no transport (http or streamable_http, say) is treated as remote by an in-process caller, and ash mcp and python -m automated_security_helper.cli.mcp_server refuse to start with it, with exit 5 (a usage error), rather than serve with the override in an unknown state.

ASH_CONFIG is the operator's config for every scan the server runs without a config of its own. The server loads it at startup, the way it loads each --profile. When it names a path that is not a file (missing, or a directory), or a file the server can't read, parse or validate, ash mcp refuses to start on every transport (exit 3) with an error naming ASH_CONFIG and the path. Unset or empty, scans use the built-in default.

A caller with no session can still use the tools that take a path, inside the operator's grants. The tools that need a session refuse it with error_type: session_identity_required and an error naming --trust-upstream-session-id: set_source_git, set_source_zip_chunk, set_source_zip_finalize, clear_source, select_profile, list_active_scans, get_scan_progress, cancel_scan, and run_ash_scan, with or without source_dir: a scan it started could be neither followed nor cancelled. A stateless server behind a plain load balancer therefore scans with run_ash_workspace_scan, over a .code-workspace file and projects inside the operator's grants, whose response carries each project's result, and reads results by path; run_ash_scan and source delivery need a stateful server or a platform that issues the session header.

With --trust-upstream-session-id, isolation between two callers is exactly as strong as the platform makes the header: ASH cannot tell a header the platform set from one a client set. The names ASH keeps under the workspace root for itself, __default__, __unidentified__ and .stdio-servers, are refused in any letter case, because a case-insensitive filesystem opens __DEFAULT__ as the same directory as __default__. The flag is refused with any transport other than streamable-http --stateless-http, where the server issues its own sessions.

docs.title: Config profiles
docs.text:
A profile is a named, pre-validated AshConfig registered at server startup via --profile NAME=path/yaml. Profiles are immutable for the lifetime of the process. Clients select a profile per session and may optionally patch it within the runtime-override allowlist (Track 10.3).

Discover the profiles a deployment offers with:

profiles = await mcp__ash__list_profiles()
# -> {"profiles": [{"name": "default", "path_sha256": "..."}], "count": 1}

path_sha256 is a SHA-256 of the profile file's absolute path, not of its contents, so it changes when the operator registers the name with a different file, and not when the file at the same path is edited. Either change takes a restart: the server reads each profile once, at startup. The paths and the profile contents themselves are never returned. An empty list means the operator registered no profiles, not that the call failed.

docs.title: Selecting a profile
docs.text:
mcp__ash__select_profile binds a registered profile to the calling session. Three modes:

  1. Static. select_profile(profile_name="default") — bind the profile as-is.
  2. Inherit-and-patch. select_profile(profile_name="default", patch_ops=[...]) — apply a JSON-Patch document, each op checked against the runtime-override allowlist first; a rejected op fails the whole call without mutating the session config. See Runtime config overrides.
  3. Full override. select_profile(profile_name="default", override_yaml="...") — replace the resolved config with a client-supplied YAML string, validated through AshConfig and held to the same runtime-override allowlist as patch_ops. See Overrides are patches.

patch_ops and override_yaml are mutually exclusive, and the parameter is profile_name — a profile must be named in every mode, including override.

Every later call in the session that does not name a config of its own runs under the bound one: run_ash_scan, resolve_ash_workspace and run_ash_workspace_scan. A config_path passed on the call still wins, because naming one is the more specific statement. In workspace mode the bound profile is the operator's config for every project: each field the profile sets is final, a project's own .ash.yaml fills only the fields it leaves unset, and a project with no .ash.yaml runs under the bound config alone. A copy the client patched is not layered over a project's own config. A session that bound no profile layers the server's ASH_CONFIG file the same way, unless that file is under the MCP workspace root. See Which config each project gets.

await mcp__ash__select_profile(profile_name="strict")
# -> {"success": True, "mode": "static", "config_path": ".../config/ash.yaml", ...}
await mcp__ash__run_ash_scan()  # runs under "strict"

The returned config_path names a file the server materialized inside your session's own workspace. That is how the binding reaches the scan: the scan entry point takes a config path rather than a config object, so the resolved config is written out and the path passed down. The file is inside the session sandbox, so this session may read it and another session may not. clear_source removes it along with the rest of the session workspace, after which calls fall back to ordinary config discovery.

Where the file is depends on the mode. The profile as registered is always written to the session's config/ash.yaml, holding only the fields the profile sets (so it can be layered over a workspace project's own config), and a static binding (or one with an empty patch_ops) returns that path. A binding with a non-empty patch_ops, or with override_yaml, returns client-config/ash.yaml, which holds the profile after your change and counts as your config, not the operator's; see A patched value is the client's. Binding again without a patch removes client-config/ash.yaml.

Sessions do not share a binding, and re-binding replaces the previous one for that session only.

docs.title: Before v3.4
docs.text:
select_profile was implemented but not registered, and no client could invoke it. Three things were missing rather than one: there was no --profile flag, so the registry was always empty and list_profiles always returned {"profiles": [], "count": 0}; the tool was never passed to @mcp.tool(); and nothing read the binding, because the scan entry point takes a config path and a bound AshConfig had nowhere to go. All three are closed. If you worked around this with config_path on every call, that keeps working unchanged.

ash mcp --profile NAME=path registers the profile: the ash mcp entry point declares every option of the command it delegates to, --profile included.

docs.title: Source delivery
docs.text:
A streamable-HTTP client typically does not share a filesystem with the server, so the source tree to scan must arrive over the protocol. ASH offers two paths (Track 10.2).

Both land the tree in the calling session's own workspace and record it as that session's source_dir. The session is the one the transport identifies (see Session identity), not a tool argument and not a header the server did not issue, so a client cannot choose a session it was not given. A session id is still a bearer value: anyone holding another session's id can act as that session, so keep ids out of logs and URLs others can read. On stdio there is a single client, so everything resolves to one default session.

Having delivered a tree, call run_ash_scan with no source_dir:

result = await mcp__ash__set_source_zip_finalize(upload_id=..., expected_sha256=...)
await mcp__ash__run_ash_scan()

An omitted source_dir means "the tree I just gave you" whenever the session has one. Passing a path explicitly still works and still has to satisfy the root policy. Naming a path you never delivered is how you scan a repository the operator mounted into the server, not one you uploaded.

The no-argument form depends on the session id being the same on both calls, which holds whenever the client's own connection keeps its session. When it does not hold, the call is refused rather than redirected:

Situation Result This session delivered a tree it is scanned stdio and nothing delivered the working directory is scanned, as it always has been A network caller with no session (see Session identity) refused, error_type: session_identity_required This session delivered nothing, another session did refused, error_type: session_source_mismatch This session delivered nothing, nor has any other refused, error_type: no_source_delivered

The two refusals exist because the alternative is worse than an error. Falling back to the server's working directory on a network transport scans a tree that holds none of the caller's code, completes normally, and reports no findings — a result a caller cannot distinguish from a clean repository. A scan that examined nothing and reads as clean is the failure mode this whole surface is meant to avoid, so the ambiguous cases say so instead. The mismatch error reports how many other sessions hold source, never which, so it diagnoses a rotating session id without disclosing one caller's session to another.

This matters most on Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, where it is not established that the id is stable: that platform mints its own session ids and, measured against live runtimes, returns a fresh one on nearly every response while honoring only the id from initialize. What the container sees per request could not be determined from outside. A stateless server identifies sessions there only when started with --trust-upstream-session-id, the declaration that the platform issues the header. On that target, capture the source_dir the delivery tool returns and pass it back to run_ash_scan(source_dir=...); see deploy/cdk/README.md for the detail and for a two-call probe that settles the question.

docs.title: Git ref
docs.text:
await mcp__ash__set_source_git(
    url="https://git.example.com/org/repo.git",
    ref="main",
    depth=1,
)

The client names the URL and the server runs git, so the operator decides what git may reach:

  • Only hosts listed in ASH_MCP_GIT_ALLOWED_HOSTS (comma- or whitespace-separated host names, matched exactly and case-insensitively against the URL's host, any port) are cloned. An ssh:// URL with %, ?, #, [ or ] between ssh:// and the path is refused with error_type: clone_url_not_permitted, so the host checked is the host git connects to. The list is empty by default, so every remote is refused until the operator names one: ASH_MCP_GIT_ALLOWED_HOSTS=github.com,git.example.com. A refusal has error_type: clone_host_not_permitted.
  • depth is a whole number of commits from 1 to 1000, a limit on how much history is fetched. A depth below 1 or above 1000 is refused with error_type: invalid_clone_depth before anything is created for the session. A value that is not a whole number is refused by the tool's argument validation before the tool runs.
  • A re-delivery needs room for both trees at once: the new clone is made beside the delivered source, which is deleted only after it. When the disk is short, call clear_source first. A first delivery has no source to free: a clone, fetch or checkout that runs out of space says only that the disk is full.
  • Each git command a delivery runs (the clone, and for a ref the fetch and the checkout) has 10 minutes. A command still running then is stopped together with the processes it started (ssh, git-remote-https), the partial tree is removed, and the call fails with error_type: clone_timed_out.
