  • Only https://, ssh:// and scp-like user@host:path URLs. http:// and git:// (no integrity protection), file:// and plain paths (the server's own filesystem) are always refused, as are URLs that begin with - or use the ext:: transport.
  • HTTP redirects are not followed; give the URL the host redirects to (for example with the .git suffix).
  • git never uses the server's credentials or configuration. It runs with an environment built from a short allowlist (no ssh agent socket, askpass helper, proxy or token variables), with system and global git config switched off, with an empty credential.helper, with GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, with GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1 (a checkout writes git-lfs pointer files and starts no transfer), with only the https and ssh protocols allowed, and without following http redirects. Every git command of a delivery (the clone, and for a ref the fetch and the checkout) passes -c core.fsmonitor=false -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null, so git starts no fsmonitor command and no hook, whatever a repository's config names, and -c gc.auto=0 -c maintenance.auto=false, so git starts no background maintenance in the directory it clones into. ssh runs with -F /dev/null, no identity file, no agent, batch mode and StrictHostKeyChecking=yes, so an ssh host's key must be in the system-wide known-hosts file (/etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts).
  • ssh_key_id must be omitted. The server registers no ssh keys, so any id is refused with error_type: ssh_key_not_registered. Raw private keys are never accepted over the wire.

Run the server as an account with no git or ssh credentials anyway: the rules above keep the server's credentials out of git, and a dedicated account keeps them off the host. An operator who needs git to go through a proxy cannot configure one here; deliver the tree as a zip instead.

depth=1 is the default; increase only when the scan needs older revisions. The cloned working tree lands under the per-session workspace and becomes the session's source_dir.

docs.title: Chunked zip upload
docs.text:
For agents that don't have git access to the source, upload the tree as a zip in ≤1 MiB chunks, then finalize:

import base64, hashlib

upload_id = "session-upload-1"
zip_bytes = open("repo.zip", "rb").read()
sha = hashlib.sha256(zip_bytes).hexdigest()

# Send in 1 MiB chunks
chunk_size = 1024 * 1024
chunks = [zip_bytes[i : i + chunk_size] for i in range(0, len(zip_bytes), chunk_size)]
for seq, chunk in enumerate(chunks):
    await mcp__ash__set_source_zip_chunk(
        upload_id=upload_id,
        sequence=seq,
        data_b64=base64.b64encode(chunk).decode(),
        last=(seq == len(chunks) - 1),
    )

await mcp__ash__set_source_zip_finalize(
    upload_id=upload_id,
    expected_sha256=sha,
)

Hard limits enforced server-side:

  • Max zip size on the wire: 100 MiB.
  • Max extracted size: 500 MiB.
  • Max files: 50000.

Any of these triggers an immediate failure. Out-of-order sequences, checksum mismatches, and zip entries with .., absolute paths, or symlinks pointing outside the session workspace are all rejected before extraction.

mcp__ash__clear_source wipes the session workspace and resets source_dir if you need to reload.

While a scan of the session runs, clear_source, set_source_git and set_source_zip_finalize are refused with error_type: source_delivery_busy: each would remove or replace the tree the scan is reading, and a scan whose tree changes under it can report clean for code it never examined. Call them again once get_scan_progress reports the scan finished. Uploading chunks is not refused, because chunks land beside the tree rather than in it. "Runs" starts when run_ash_scan returns the scan id, not when the scan begins reading, and a session that ends in that time keeps its tree until the scan returns. The other way round, run_ash_scan is refused with the same error_type while one of those calls is changing the session's tree. run_ash_workspace_scan by a session that has delivered a tree, or bound a profile, holds the session the same way until the scan's work is done, even when the call is cancelled first, and is refused the same way while the tree is changing. A session that has delivered nothing has nothing of its own for a workspace scan to hold, so its scan of a directory the operator granted takes no hold and creates nothing under the workspace root.

docs.title: Config files in delivered source
docs.text:
A delivered tree can carry its own .ash.yaml, and a client can name any file in its session workspace as run_ash_scan's config_path. Such a file was written by the client, not the operator. So was any other file a client names as config_path (or to get_config and validate_config), unless it is in a directory ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS names or is one of the profile files the server writes in the session's own config/ directory, ash.yaml and the per-call profiles, call-profile- followed by 16 lowercase hex digits and .yaml (or call-profile.yaml), directly in config/ (a path in another session's workspace is refused). Any other file in config/ is the client's, and neither config/ nor client-config/ may be a scan target or a workspace output_dir, so no scan writes there. A config in another checkout the server may scan is that checkout's, and the operator let the server scan it, not take its settings. A path is judged where it sits, at each symlink on the way, and by the file it reaches, so a link a client delivered is the client's wherever it points, and so is a file reached through a linked directory such as .ash, and every base such a file extends. A config named through a link in a delivered tree may extend only files in that tree. A refusal names the path the client used, not the file a link reaches, and a validation error for such a file names the file and where each problem is without quoting the values in it. A scan with no config_path reads the .ash.yaml it finds in the target only when the file it resolves to is in a directory the caller may read config from, the check get_config applies to a file it finds: one that links elsewhere is refused with error_type: config_input_not_permitted before it is read. The workspace tools check each project's .ash.yaml the same way, and every other config source in the project's directory, a pyproject.toml included, before discovery opens any of them; they refuse with exit code 4. The profile select_profile writes after a client's patch_ops or override_yaml, client-config/ash.yaml, is the client's too, and so are the workspace tools' config_overrides (see A patched value is the client's). Everything below applies to all of these.

First, it may not change a field the session's runtime-override policy denies. denied_paths and denied_value_patterns apply to every file of the config's chain that a client delivered, as resolution parsed it, matched as for patch_ops (either - or _, every spelling of a plugin's section, globs). They apply whether or not runtime overrides are enabled, since a config file is not an override. Only what the file changes counts: a value equal to the server's at the same key (an ash config init file writes the defaults) is accepted, while every op in the file's patch is checked as written. A denied_value_patterns entry also matches mapping keys, and refuses a matching key in a delivered file even where the server's config has the same key; only the session's patched profile, client-config/ash.yaml, which repeats the registered profile with the client's checked patch applied, is not refused for a key the server's config has.

  • The policy is the registered profile the session bound with select_profile, or else the one in ASH_CONFIG (the defaults when it sets none, or when ASH_CONFIG names a file under the MCP workspace root, which is a client's; ASH logs a warning then). It is never read from the session's copy of the profile, which a client's patch_ops produced, and /global_settings/mcp is a default denied_paths entry, so a client cannot change the policy.
  • Under the default denied_paths, sandbox and ash_plugin_modules are checked against the server's own settings instead (below), and a delivered tree's own global_settings.suppressions and global_settings.ignore_paths apply, as they do on the CLI. Each suppression and ignore path the operator did not supply is marked client_supplied: true in the results' config, and a SARIF suppression from one carries properties.clientSupplied. Scanners and converters skip only the operator's ignore paths, so the files under a client-supplied ignore path are still scanned, and each finding there is kept as a suppressed result marked the same way rather than dropped. The results show what the client's config hid.
  • What the marking looks like: in SARIF the suppression has a justification that starts with (ASH, client-supplied config) and names the entry, and properties.clientSupplied: true; its kind is inSource for a suppression entry and external for an ignore path or a scanner exclusion (below). See Suppressions an MCP client's config supplied. The flat-json and CSV reports show the finding with is_suppressed: true and that justification as suppression_justification, and the GitLab SAST report quotes it in the finding's solution. A suppressed finding does not count toward fail_on_findings, as with any suppression.
  • Exclusions in a scanner's own options are reported the same way rather than applied. An entry the delivered file adds to bandit's excluded_paths, checkov's skip_path, opengrep's or semgrep's exclude, syft's exclude or ferret-scan's exclude_patterns is removed from the option before the scanner runs, so the scanner sees those files, and each finding of that scanner the entry would have left out is suppressed and marked as above, naming the option (scanners.bandit.options.excluded_paths entry 'tests'). Each entry is matched as its scanner reads it: bandit's as the **/<path>/** glob ASH passes bandit, checkov's as checkov's own filter reads it (a regular expression found in, or a substring of, the path of the file or of a directory above it), and the others as globs matching the path or any directory in it. syft writes an SBOM, not findings, so each component a syft entry would have dropped is listed and carries an ash:clientSuppliedExclusion property instead. A scanners.trivy.options.ignore_file or scanners.trivy-repo.options.ignore_file from the delivered file is not passed to trivy. If it is a regular file inside the scanned tree, read without following a link, each unexpired ID in it (one per line, or the id and paths of a .trivyignore.yaml) suppresses and marks that scanner's findings with that rule ID; any other file, including a link to one, is not read, and the warning that says so quotes nothing from it. An entry the operator supplied (the scanner's default, the bound profile, or a file of the chain no client delivered) stays in the option and applies as before. Each moved entry is logged as a config warning and recorded in the results as a config_warning validation checkpoint.
  • A .semgrepignore in the delivered tree is not honored, as in any tree: ASH runs semgrep and opengrep with --x-ignore-semgrepignore-files and their default exclusions, so it leaves no files out. The results name the file as client-supplied in a config_warning validation checkpoint. To leave files out, list them in global_settings.ignore_paths, where they apply marked as above.
  • A profile's own denied_paths adds to the current default list: a list that is not one of ASH's defaults is denied together with every default entry, so listing one more field lifts nothing, and a list that holds some default entries but leaves others out still gets them, with a warning naming those it leaves out. sandbox, ash_plugin_modules, suppressions and ignore paths keep the handling above unless the profile's own list names them (the field itself, an entry above it, or one inside it, such as /global_settings/suppressions, /global_settings/** or /sandbox/mode); a field it names is decided by denied_paths like any other, as a whole, so a delivered file that sets it is refused. With replace_default_denied_paths: true the list is used as written instead, and each default entry it leaves out is named in a warning. denied_value_patterns apply everywhere. A list equal to any default ASH has shipped, as ash config init writes it, still counts as the default, and gets every entry of the current default list. Every denied_paths entry and denied_value_patterns key starts with /; one that does not would match nothing, so the config is refused as invalid.
  • global_settings.mcp in a delivered file has no effect, since the policy never comes from one, so it is not checked.
  • A file that changes a denied field is refused, not trimmed: run_ash_scan and get_config return error_type: config_field_denied with every such field named, validate_config lists each one as a denied_by_runtime_policy error (for content, only from a remote caller), and a workspace with such a project config fails to resolve. If the policy itself cannot be established (the bound profile is no longer registered, the server's default config cannot be loaded, or the profile has two sections that read as the same plugin), a config with a client-delivered file is refused with error_type: config_policy_unreadable; a scan that reads no such file is unaffected.

Its sandbox settings and plugin modules may restrict the server's but never widen them, wherever the scan target is. The server's settings are those of the profile this session bound with select_profile, or else ASH_CONFIG and the defaults (only the defaults when ASH_CONFIG names a file under the MCP workspace root). A file that asks for more is refused with error_type: config_field_denied, naming the setting; an equal or tighter value scans:

  • sandbox.network_scanners may list only scanners the server's settings give network. A shorter list takes network away from the scanners it leaves out.
  • sandbox.extra_read_paths may list only paths the server's settings grant.
  • sandbox.read_path_scanners and sandbox.env_scanners come from the server's settings. A server config file inside a git checkout grants nothing either, so ASH_CONFIG has to name a file outside every checkout for its grants to apply.
  • sandbox.mode can turn the sandbox on, but cannot turn it off or move it to another backend when the server's config sets a mode.
  • ash_plugin_modules may add only an installed module outside the scanned tree, and never automated_security_helper.plugin_modules.ash_aws_plugins or automated_security_helper.plugin_modules.ash_snyk_plugins (or a module inside either), which send findings or source off the host with the operator's credentials. A scanner or reporter from either package that another module the file adds lists or imports is not selected unless the server's own config loads it. A plugin class a module the file adds registered is not selected by a later scan in the server that does not load that module itself, and neither is one list_scanners loaded. The plugin registry is the server process's, but each scan uses only the plugin modules it names: a module that one session's profile names, or that list_scanners loaded, adds no classes or event handlers to another scan that does not name it.

Its reporter destinations and credentials, each scanner's own config file, and which version of a tool runs are default denied_paths entries, so a file that sets one is refused. A config file inside the scanned tree is scanned without the first two, and may still choose a tool's version within the limits in Settings a repository's config cannot choose. The options a reporter from a plugin module declares in destination_options are not, because the module is imported after the file is checked: a file that sets one is scanned with the server's value, and a warning names it. See Configs an MCP client delivered.

!ENV reads the server's environment, so for a remote caller no config file resolves it unless the operator set the file aside: a file under ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS, or the session's config/ash.yaml. That covers a file the client delivered or names, a file found in a directory it names (get_config's search_dir), a scan target's own .ash.yaml, including one in a repository under ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS, and every base such a file extends. A file that uses !ENV, tagged or as a plain value that starts with a ${VAR} or ${VAR:default} reference, is refused with a config error naming the file and the line or key. run_ash_scan and get_config return error_type: config_env_not_resolved, and run_ash_scan does not start the scan. validate_config lists the refusal as an error of type config_env_not_resolved, and refuses a remote caller's config_content that uses !ENV the same way. resolve_ash_workspace and run_ash_workspace_scan return error_type: config_env_not_resolved with exit code 3 for a project config that uses it. To use !ENV in a remote scan, put the setting in a registered profile or a file under ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS. The server's own config, the file ASH_CONFIG names and each registered profile, resolves !ENV for every caller, wherever it is outside the MCP workspace root.

On stdio, where the caller launched the server and holds its environment already, only a file under the MCP workspace root is refused; a repository config the local user names or scans keeps !ENV. A symlink in a delivered tree counts as delivered wherever it points. With raw, get_config shows a reference in a file that may use !ENV as it is written.

Everything else in the file applies as usual. The registered profile the server materializes for select_profile, the session's config/ash.yaml, is the operator's and keeps its grants, as does a file under ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS that is outside every git checkout and outside the scanned directory. A file under ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS also resolves !ENV as usual. A patched profile in client-config/ash.yaml is the client's, and config/ash.yaml is the trusted base it is held to.

get_config shows the sandbox section the same way, as a scan of the session's delivered source (or, with none delivered, the working directory) would apply it.

docs.title: Restricting scan targets
docs.text:
run_ash_scan also accepts a server-side path directly, and ASH writes its output tree inside whatever directory it is given. ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS bounds that: it holds a list of directories, separated by the platform path separator, and a scan target must resolve to one of them or to something beneath one.

ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS=/srv/repos

Targets are resolved before the comparison, so a symlink sitting inside an allowed root but pointing outside it is refused.

A session that has delivered source over the protocol also gets its own workspace directory, ASH_MCP_WORKSPACE_ROOT/<session_id>, so set_source_git and set_source_zip_finalize keep working regardless of what the variable names — you do not need to list ASH_MCP_WORKSPACE_ROOT yourself. Only the calling session's own directory is allowed, not the shared root, so one tenant cannot name another tenant's workspace as a scan target.

Because setting the variable replaces the default list, list every directory the server legitimately scans. In the container images that means including the source mount /src alongside any workspace path, or a no-argument run_ash_scan() — which defaults to the working directory — will be refused.

Set this on any deployment where clients are not fully trusted. Without it, ASH falls back to refusing a short fixed list of system directories (/boot, /dev, /etc, /proc, /root, /sys, the filesystem root, and the Windows equivalents), which is a safety net rather than a boundary: every other directory the server process can reach stays a valid target. Naming a directory in ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS replaces that list, which is also how you arrange a deliberate scan of a system path.

docs.title: Runtime config overrides
docs.text:
The runtime-override surface is the security boundary that lets clients tweak a profile without giving them the whole config (Track 10.4). It is gated by a Pydantic-declared allowlist on AshConfigGlobalSettingsSection.mcp.runtime_overrides.

The allowlist defines:

  • enabled: bool = False — the master switch. Defaults to off; runtime patches are denied unless the operator flips this on per profile.
  • allowed_paths: list[str] — JSON-Pointer prefixes the client may target. A trailing /* means "this whole subtree". Example: /scanners/*/options/severity_threshold.
  • denied_paths: list[str] — explicit blocks; always wins over allowed_paths. A profile's own list is added to the defaults below unless replace_default_denied_paths: bool = False is set to true, and every entry starts with /. The defaults are /fail_on_findings, /fail_on_incomplete_scanners, /content_db_staleness, /content_db_staleness_overrides, /honor_ignore_files, /content_db_staleness_offline_image_default, /sandbox and /sandbox/**, /ash_plugin_modules and /ash_plugin_modules/**, detect-secrets' scan_settings/filters_used and scan_settings/plugins_used (each with /**) and baseline_file under /scanners/detect-secrets/options (a client could otherwise turn on secret verification, which sends candidate secrets to their issuers, or make the scanner import a file), /global_settings/ignore_paths, /global_settings/suppressions, /global_settings/mcp and /global_settings/mcp/** (the policy itself), the scanner options that drop findings by rule ID, by a baseline or by category, such as /scanners/opengrep/options/exclude_rule, /scanners/checkov/options/skip_frameworks and /scanners/*/options/offline, each scanner's own config file and tool version, such as /scanners/bandit/options/config_file and /scanners/*/options/tool_version, the programs a scanner runs, the modules it loads, and whether it honors the ignore comments in the files it scans, such as /scanners/actionlint/options/shellcheck, /scanners/trivy-repo/options/module_dir and /scanners/gitleaks/options/honor_inline_ignores, /scanners/zizmor/options/online_audits (which lets the GitHub token reach zizmor), /reporters/bedrock-summary-reporter/options/aws_* and the Bedrock reporter's other destinations, such as /reporters/bedrock-summary-reporter/options/model_id, the whole section of each AWS reporter, /reporters/s3/**, /reporters/aws-security-hub/**, /reporters/cloudwatch-logs/** and /reporters/bedrock-summary-reporter/** (a client's enabled: false for one of the four AWS reporters is not refused under these entries, but it takes no effect: the profile's enabled applies, and a warning names the client's value. enabled of a reporter that writes only local files is not denied; all of them are listed in Configs an MCP client delivered), the whole section of each scanner that sends data off the host: /scanners/snyk-code/** (the source), /scanners/npm-audit/** (dependency lists), /scanners/detect-secrets/** (candidate secrets, when verifying), /scanners/semgrep/** and /scanners/opengrep/** (usage metrics), /scanners/trivy/** and /scanners/trivy-repo/** (usage data, when telemetry is on), and /scanners/zizmor/** (the GitHub token, with online audits), and the archive converter's four extraction limits, /converters/archive/options/max_members, max_member_bytes, max_total_bytes and max_compression_ratio, which also refuse a write at /converters/archive/options, /converters/archive or /converters. Those four, the /sandbox and /ash_plugin_modules entries, the detect-secrets settings and the entries for the reporters and scanners that send data off the host are kept in any denied_paths a profile sets, replace_default_denied_paths: true included: a profile can add denials but cannot let a client raise the extraction limits, turn those settings on, or turn on or reconfigure a plugin that sends data off the host through config overrides (a workspace scan's scanners and excluded_scanners arguments, which are not overrides, can still leave a scanner out of a run, but not add one), and a whole-config write at the root pointer is refused for the same reason. A profile whose list equals a default ASH shipped earlier, as ash config init wrote it, gets the current default list. A denied_paths entry, and a denied_value_patterns key, matches a path whatever mix of - and _ either one is spelled with, because ASH reads bedrock-summary-reporter and bedrock_summary_reporter as the same key. Under /scanners, /reporters and /converters, an entry naming a plugin's section also matches every other spelling ASH reads as that plugin's config: case, punctuation and the words Scanner, Reporter and Converter are ignored, so /reporters/BedrockSummary is refused by the bedrock-summary-reporter entry. A plugin segment that is a glob (*, ?, [) stands for the keys of known plugins it matches, so /scanners/trivy-*/options/ignore_file also refuses /scanners/TrivyRepo/options/ignore_file. Known plugins are those that ship with ASH and any plugin whose section the profile already configures. Another plugin, from ash_plugin_modules or an installed plugin package, is covered by a glob entry only under spellings the glob matches as written; configure its section in the profile, or name it literally, to cover every spelling.
  • denied_value_patterns: dict[str, str] — per-path regex denylist for dangerous values (e.g., scanner extra_args containing --no-verify or shell metacharacters).

Additional invariants enforced by apply_runtime_patch:

  • move and copy ops are rejected outright (they sidestep target-path checks).
  • A profile that names a key with a variable (${VAR}, or ${VAR:default} whether or not the variable is set) where ASH has built-in keys, such as a reporters, scanners or converters section, a built-in plugin's options or a list entry such as a suppression, is not patched at all: every op, override_yaml and workspace config_overrides against it is refused with one text, whatever the variable holds. A section named for a built-in merges with the built-in's, so any other answer would tell a client whether the variable names one. This is decided from the profile as written. Write the section's name as text to let clients patch the profile. Where ASH has no keys of its own, as in the options of a plugin ASH does not ship, an op may go through only a key the profile writes as text, and no test op may compare that mapping, what holds it, or anything in it.
  • No op may reach the reporters section of a reporter that isn't one of ASH's built-in reporters, whatever allowed_paths says. That covers the AWS reporters (s3, aws-security-hub, cloudwatch-logs, bedrock-summary-reporter, whose sections are also always-denied entries) and any reporter a plugin module brings. Such a reporter can send the findings off the host, to wherever its section says, with the server's credentials, so only the operator's own configuration sets that section.
  • Every spelling ASH reads as such a section counts, and so does every op type: a test would tell a client where the operator sends findings.
  • An add or replace of all of /reporters, or of the whole document, is refused when its value has such a section. A test or remove of /reporters, or a test of the whole document, is refused outright.
  • The one exception is a client's enabled: false of an AWS reporter, on its own (or adding its section with only enabled: false where the profile has none). It's accepted and takes no effect: the server logs a warning naming the op and keeps the operator's setting, for patch_ops, override_yaml and a workspace scan's config_overrides alike. enabled: false together with anything else in that section is refused.
  • A client can still change a built-in reporter's section, such as /reporters/markdown/enabled, where the allowlist permits it.
  • Patch documents larger than 64 KiB are rejected.
  • Any rejection raises RuntimePatchDeniedError with the offending op and the rule that fired; nothing is applied.

The full allowlist is exposed at runtime via the ash://schema/runtime-overrides resource so clients can introspect what is patchable before composing a patch.

docs.title: A patched value is the client's
docs.text:
The allowlist decides which keys a client may change. It does not make the value the client writes the operator's. So select_profile writes the profile after a non-empty patch_ops, or after override_yaml, to the session's client-config/ash.yaml, and the tools that use the session's bound config (run_ash_scan with no config_path, resolve_ash_workspace and run_ash_workspace_scan) resolve that file as a config the client delivered, as get_config and validate_config do when a client names it as config_path, with the rules in Config files in delivered source:

  • A suppression or ignore path the patch added is marked client_supplied, and a finding it hides is reported suppressed and marked.
  • An exclusion the patch added to a scanner's own options is reported, not applied. A scanners.trivy.options.ignore_file or scanners.trivy-repo.options.ignore_file it sets is not passed to trivy, and is read for marked suppressions only when it is inside the scanned tree, so a file in another checkout has no effect.
  • A scanner config file the patch names (config_file of bandit, grype or syft) is replaced by the registered profile's, and a tool path inside the scanned tree or in a delivered file is refused as for any config.
  • Its sandbox settings and plugin modules are restrict-only.

The trusted base is the profile as the operator registered it, written unpatched to the session's config/ash.yaml: the profile's own suppressions, sandbox grants and tool config files still apply, and only what the patch changed is the client's. The policy a patched profile is checked against is the registered profile's too, never the patched copy's.

The workspace tools' config_overrides get the same rules. An override the allowlist accepts changes each project's config, and what it sets is marked, reported or confined as a patched value is.

A profile a workspace tool is given for one call (profile) is the operator's, and is written to a file of its own per profile, config/call-profile-<digest>.yaml (the first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 of the profile name), so it leaves the session's own binding as it was.

docs.title: Overrides are patches
docs.text:
override_yaml is checked by the same rules, not by a second copy of them. The server validates the YAML as an AshConfig, diffs it against the profile, and sends the resulting add/remove/replace ops through apply_runtime_patch. An override is accepted exactly when that patch would be: never while enabled is false, and only if every field it changes is in allowed_paths, outside denied_paths, and clear of denied_value_patterns. A refusal returns success: false with an override denied: error naming the op and the rule.

Because an override replaces the profile wholesale, a field the YAML leaves out reverts to its default, and that counts as a change. Omitting sandbox from an override of a profile that sets sandbox.mode: bwrap is a replace at /sandbox/mode, refused by the /sandbox entry. To change one field with override_yaml, restate the profile and edit that field; patch_ops is usually the shorter way to say the same thing.

docs.title: Safe example
docs.text:
A profile that has mcp.runtime_overrides.enabled: true and allows /scanners/*/options/severity_threshold plus /global_settings/allowlist. The client raises bandit's threshold to HIGH and narrows the allowlist:

patch_ops = [
    {
        "op": "replace",
        "path": "/scanners/bandit/options/severity_threshold",
        "value": "HIGH",
    },
    {
        "op": "add",
        "path": "/global_settings/allowlist/allowed_paths",
        "value": ["src/", "lib/"],
    },
]

select_profile(profile_name="default", patch_ops=patch_ops)

docs.title: Unsafe example
docs.text:
The same profile receives a patch that targets a denied path:

patch_ops = [
    {
        "op": "replace",
        "path": "/global_settings/fail_on_findings",
        "value": False,
    },
]

select_profile(profile_name="default", patch_ops=patch_ops)
# raises RuntimePatchDeniedError:
# {
#   "rejected_op": {"op": "replace", "path": "/global_settings/fail_on_findings", ...},
#   "reason": "path '/global_settings/fail_on_findings' matches denied_paths rule",
#   "rule": "denied_paths"
# }

The session config is unchanged. The client may inspect ash://schema/runtime-overrides to see why the path is blocked and either pick an allowed alternative or ask the operator to add it to allowed_paths.

docs.title: Session lifecycle
docs.text:
Per-connection state is held in a process-local MCPSession keyed by FastMCP connection id. The object carries the session's workspace path and the locks and claims that keep a scan, a change to the delivered tree and the TTL sweep from running over one another:

MCPSession {
  id,
  workspace_root,   # ASH_MCP_WORKSPACE_ROOT/<session_id>
  created_at,
}

What a client bound to the session is not stored on that object. Both stores are keyed by the session id and are the source of truth: the delivered source directory is recorded by the source delivery module, and the selected profile, its resolved config and any JSON-Patch document by the profile registry.

Workspaces live under ASH_MCP_WORKSPACE_ROOT (defaults to $XDG_CACHE_HOME/ash-mcp/<session_id>/). A session's workspace (its delivered tree, uploads in progress and the config select_profile materialized), its bound profile and its delivered-source record are removed when the session ends:

Transport The session ends streamable-HTTP, stateful when the client's DELETE is answered (the removal is complete before the response is sent), when the MCP SDK answers 404 on the server's endpoint (--mount-path) for a session it discarded (after its 30-minute idle timeout, say) and a client asks about it again (a 404 for any other path, which has no route, ends nothing), and for every session the server issued when the server shuts down sse when the event stream closes stdio when the last stdio server sharing the workspace root exits (every stdio server of one user shares __default__, so one server's exit leaves it in place while another runs) streamable-HTTP, --stateless-http never visibly: see the sweep below

A session that ends while one of its scans runs keeps its tree until that scan returns.

The server cannot see every end: a stateless server has no session at all, and a stateful session the MCP SDK closes for being idle (after 30 minutes) sends nothing ASH observes unless a client uses its id again. So every HTTP server also sweeps the workspace root, before it answers its first request and then at most every five minutes, and removes the workspace of any session nobody used for longer than --session-workspace-ttl seconds (default 86400, 24 hours). Each request that names a session counts as a use. The sweep removes only directories ASH created as session workspaces, each of which carries a .ash-mcp-session marker file; it never removes anything else under the root, the stdio session's workspace (its own servers remove it), a symlink, or a workspace a running scan holds. A session whose scan is running, or whose tree is being changed, is skipped, not queued for removal when the scan returns, and its age is read again just before removal, so a session used meanwhile is kept. So is a session that a chunk of an upload or a profile selection is writing; one that arrives while the sweep removes its session is refused with error_type session_workspace_busy, and is sent again (an upload from its first chunk), since the session's state is gone once the removal is done. That hold is the server's own: a server sharing the workspace root does not see a write in progress on another server. Give ASH_MCP_WORKSPACE_ROOT a directory that belongs to ASH alone anyway: session workspaces created before the marker existed are never swept. Servers that share one ASH_MCP_WORKSPACE_ROOT sweep each other's idle workspaces by the same rule, and each running scan holds a locked entry under <root>/.ash-mcp-scans/<session id>/ so that no server's sweep removes a workspace another server is scanning. Those locks are file locks: a filesystem that does not share them between hosts does not carry that protection. The request that starts a sweep is answered once the sweep finishes; requests that arrive while it runs are not held for it.

Concurrency:

  • Scans within a single session are serialized; one client cannot launch parallel scans against itself.
  • Scans across sessions run in parallel under the existing scan_registry semantics — a noisy session can't block another tenant's scan.

Each session runs at most mcp-resource-management.max_concurrent_scans_per_session scans at once (default 2; 0 for no limit), set in the operator's config that ASH_CONFIG names and never in a scanned or delivered one. A run_ash_scan counts until its scan returns, and a run_ash_workspace_scan counts once, however many projects it has, until its work is done, even if the call is cancelled first. One more scan is refused with error_type: session_scan_limit until one finishes; other sessions go on scanning. Callers with no session share one count under the same limit. On a stateless server run without --trust-upstream-session-id that is every caller, so the limit there is for the whole server; run_ash_workspace_scan is the scan such a caller can start.

Scans are visible per session. list_active_scans, get_scan_progress and cancel_scan see and act on the calling session's own scans only, including the per-project scans run_ash_workspace_scan registers. Another session's scan id gets exactly the answer an id that was never issued gets, and a listing's stats count only the caller's scans. Two sessions cannot scan the same directory at once, because both would write its .ash/ash_output; the second is refused with "already has an active scan", and the refusal names the running scan's id only to the session that started it.

docs.title: Auth
docs.text:
The streamable-HTTP transport ships with one built-in gate: a static header check via --auth-header-name and the expected value. Connections without the configured header (or with the wrong value) are rejected before any tool dispatches.

The value can be given three ways, and only one at a time:

  • --auth-header-value-file PATH reads it from a file once at startup. The file must be a regular file, not a symlink, with no permissions for its group or other users (chmod 600; the mode isn't checked on Windows). One trailing newline is dropped.
  • --auth-header-value-fd N reads it from an inherited file descriptor, 3 or above, once at startup, and closes it. A file (a memfd, say) is read from its start, a pipe from where it is.
  • --auth-header-value VALUE puts the value on the server's command line, which every local user can read (/proc/<pid>/cmdline, ps), including from outside a container on its host. It still works, and the server prints a warning naming the two options above. On the command line the value must be visible ASCII (letters, digits and punctuation, with spaces or tabs between them), so it is checked in the bytes the header will carry; any other character is refused, because a terminal and an HTTP client can disagree about its bytes. A file or descriptor carries the bytes 0x80 to 0xFF exactly.

An empty value, one with a control character (a line break, NUL, any other byte below 0x20 except a tab, or DEL), or one longer than 16 KiB is refused, as is more than one form. Every refusal exits with the usage-error code before anything is served.

The server compares the header's bytes, which HTTP reads as latin-1. A value with a character outside latin-1 can't be a header value, so build_streamable_http_app and build_sse_app refuse an auth_header_value that has one, before they build anything.

HTTP drops a space or tab at either end of a header value, so a value that starts or ends with one could never be matched. The command line, a file and a descriptor all refuse such a value, with the same exit code; a space or tab between other characters is kept. build_streamable_http_app and build_sse_app refuse it too, and raise ASHValidationError for an auth_header_value with a control character, as they do for one with a character outside latin-1. They also refuse an auth_header_name given without an auth_header_value, and the reverse, as the command line does, rather than build an app without authentication.

This is sufficient for single-tenant deploys where one trusted client owns the server. For multi-tenant deployments:

  • Run ASH behind a reverse proxy (nginx, traefik, an API gateway) that terminates TLS and authenticates the caller.
  • Have the proxy inject the static header value so ASH only accepts traffic that has already been authenticated upstream.
  • Run one server per tenant if their configs must differ. Per-tenant config selection over the protocol is not available yet — see Selecting a profile is not available yet — so a single server cannot currently give two tenants two different configs.

The runtime-override allowlist (Track 10.4) plus per-session workspaces (Track 10.5) are the in-process isolation primitives. They are not a substitute for upstream tenant authentication.

docs.title: Docker example
docs.text:
Single-container invocation:

docker run \
  -p 8000:8000 \
  -v /etc/ash:/etc/ash:ro \
  -e ASH_MCP_WORKSPACE_ROOT=/var/cache/ash-mcp \
  -e ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS=/src:/var/cache/ash-mcp \
  ash mcp \
    --transport streamable-http \
    --host 0.0.0.0 \
    --port 8000 \
    --allowed-host localhost:8000 \
    --allowed-host 127.0.0.1:8000 \
    --profile default=/etc/ash/default.yaml \
    --profile strict=/etc/ash/strict.yaml \
    --auth-header-name x-ash-token \
    --auth-header-value-file /etc/ash/mcp-token

/etc/ash/mcp-token holds the value, with mode 600 and owned by the user the container runs ASH as.

docker-compose.yml snippet pairing ASH with an nginx TLS terminator:

services:
  ash-mcp:
    image: ash:latest
    command:
      - mcp
      - --transport=streamable-http
      - --host=0.0.0.0
      - --port=8000
      - --allowed-host=ash-mcp.example.com
      - --profile=default=/etc/ash/default.yaml
      - --profile=strict=/etc/ash/strict.yaml
      - --auth-header-name=x-ash-token
      - --auth-header-value-file=/etc/ash/mcp-token
    volumes:
      - /etc/ash:/etc/ash:ro
      - ash-workspace:/var/cache/ash-mcp
    environment:
      ASH_MCP_WORKSPACE_ROOT: /var/cache/ash-mcp
      ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS: /src:/var/cache/ash-mcp
    expose:
      - "8000"

  nginx:
    image: nginx:1.27
    ports:
      - "443:443"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx/conf.d:/etc/nginx/conf.d:ro
      - ./nginx/tls:/etc/nginx/tls:ro
    depends_on:
      - ash-mcp

volumes:
  ash-workspace:

The nginx config is responsible for TLS termination and for injecting x-ash-token: ${ASH_TOKEN} on every request that has already authenticated against the tenant's identity provider. It must forward the client's Host (proxy_set_header Host $host;), which is the --allowed-host value ASH checks.

docs.title: Security note
docs.text:
The streamable-HTTP transport puts the MCP server on the network. A few invariants to keep in mind:

  • The auth header is the only built-in gate. There is no per-tool RBAC, no per-tenant rate limiting, no audit log beyond standard logging. Anything more sophisticated belongs in a fronting proxy.
  • Set ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS. Scan targets are confined to the roots it names, plus the per-session workspace. The fallback when it is unset refuses only a short list of system directories and leaves the rest of the server's filesystem available as a scan target, so on a network-reachable deployment it is not a substitute for naming the roots yourself. See Restricting scan targets.
  • Always run behind TLS in production. ASH does not terminate TLS itself. Use nginx, traefik, an API gateway, or a service mesh sidecar.
  • The runtime-override allowlist defaults to disabled. A profile must explicitly set mcp.runtime_overrides.enabled: true and enumerate allowed_paths for any client patching to succeed, through patch_ops or override_yaml. Leaving it off is the safe default — clients can still pick profiles, just not modify them.
  • set_source_git clones only from hosts in ASH_MCP_GIT_ALLOWED_HOSTS, which is empty by default, and never with the server account's credentials or git configuration. See Git ref.
  • Source-upload limits are per-session, not per-tenant. A misbehaving tenant can still consume their session quota. Pair the transport with upstream rate limits if untrusted clients can connect.
  • Workspaces are removed when the session ends, or after --session-workspace-ttl unused. Don't rely on session-resident state to survive reconnects; persisted state across server restarts is explicitly out of scope (Track 10.8). See Session lifecycle.

docs.title: Cross-references
docs.text:
• Local single-user MCP setup: ASH MCP Server Guide
  • Performance tuning under concurrent sessions: MCP Server Performance and Scalability
  • Full tool inventory: MCP Tools Reference
  • Track 10 spec: tasks/todo.md, sections 10.1 through 10.9

docs.title: Workspace mode over MCP
docs.text:
Workspace mode resolves a VS Code .code-workspace file into N projects, scans each one with its own ASH config and its own severity threshold, and aggregates the results into a single workspace payload. It was CLI-only (ash --workspace foo.code-workspace). Two MCP tools now expose it:

  • resolve_ash_workspace — resolves the workspace and returns the plan. Scans nothing.
  • run_ash_workspace_scan — resolves, scans every project, and returns the per-project verdict.

Both are registered on the same server as the single-directory tools documented in the ASH MCP Server Guide, and both work over stdio and streamable-HTTP.

docs.title: When to use which
docs.text:
resolve_ash_workspace is the MCP equivalent of ash --workspace ... --dry-run. It reads the workspace definition and every project's own ASH config, then reports which directories became projects, what key each was given, which config file was found for it, which scanners that config enables, which threshold the project will be judged against, and which projects were dropped and why. Nothing is scanned, no output tree is written, and no registry slot is taken.

Call it first when a workspace is unfamiliar. Resolution is the cheap half; a workspace of eight repositories can take minutes to scan and milliseconds to resolve, and a definition problem — a folder nobody cloned, two entries naming one directory, a project config that will not parse — surfaces in the resolve call rather than after the scan has already run.

run_ash_workspace_scan then scans the same plan from the same inputs. Unlike run_ash_scan, it does not return early with a scan ID: it waits for the whole workspace and returns the verdict.

docs.title: resolve_ash_workspace
docs.text:
resolve_ash_workspace(
    workspace_file="/srv/repos/platform/dev.code-workspace",
    workspace_config="/etc/ash/workspace-policy.yaml",  # optional
    allow_missing_projects=False,  # optional
    config_overrides=["global_settings.severity_threshold=HIGH"],  # optional
)
Argument Meaning workspace_file Absolute path to the .code-workspace definition. workspace_config Path to a workspace policy file. Must exist when given; ASH does not fall back to searching for one, because that would apply different policy than the one you named. Omit it and the workspace root is searched, and having no policy is not an error. A policy file, named here or found beside the definition, is used only from a directory ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS names. One anywhere else, including any file an MCP client delivered, is refused: a policy sets suppressions and ignore paths for every project, so it has to be the operator's. A delivered policy that is a symlink is the client's wherever it points, and one that reaches a file outside the directories the session may read config from is refused before it is read, with error_type: config_input_not_permitted. A project's own .ash.yaml that links outside them is refused the same way. allow_missing_projects Mark project directories that are absent or unreadable as skipped instead of refusing the workspace. They stay in the plan, so the response still accounts for every folder the definition listed. config_overrides key=value overrides, applied to each project's config during resolution. Applied here and not only at scan time, so the threshold the plan reports is the threshold a scan will enforce. They come from the client, so they are checked against the session config's runtime_overrides allowlist first, as select_profile's patch_ops are; with runtime overrides off (the default), any override is refused. Each override is checked by the key it names (in either - or _ spelling) as well as by what it changes, so setting a key to the value the session config already holds still needs that key to be allowed. An accepted override is still the client's value: what it sets is marked, reported or confined as a config the client delivered is (see A patched value is the client's).

The response carries:

  • plan — the rendered plan, the same text ash --workspace ... --dry-run prints. Written for a human to read; its layout is not a contract.
  • projects — the same decisions as structured data. Read this if you need to branch on a threshold or a scanner list. Each entry's config_source is the project's own config file, or the session's profile for a project with none, and operator_config is the profile layered over a project's own config, or null. See Which config each project gets.
  • skipped_projects — one entry per dropped project, with a reason.
  • exit_code — 0 on success. See Exit codes.

docs.title: Which config each project gets
docs.text:
The session's profile (the one select_profile bound, or the one the call names with profile) is the operator's config, as --config is on the CLI (see The operator's config). Every field the profile sets is final for every project, and a project's own .ash.yaml fills only the fields the profile leaves unset. A project without a config of its own runs under the session's config alone.

What is layered over a project's own config is the profile as the operator registered it, not a copy the client patched with patch_ops or override_yaml. A value the client patched in is never final over a project's own config: it applies only to a project with no config of its own, and there it is limited as a config the client delivered is (see A patched value is the client's). If the session's copy of the registered profile is gone while the patched copy is not, the call is refused with exit code 3; bind the profile again with select_profile.

A session that bound no profile, and a call that names none, run under the server's own config, the file ASH_CONFIG names: it is layered over each project's own config the same way. Not when that file, or a base it extends, is under the MCP workspace root, which makes it a file a client delivered; then nothing is layered.

A profile a call names with profile is written to a file of its own per profile in the session's config/ directory, so two calls in one session that name different profiles do not change each other's plan.

docs.title: run_ash_workspace_scan
docs.text:
run_ash_workspace_scan(
    workspace_file="/srv/repos/platform/dev.code-workspace",
    workspace_config="/etc/ash/workspace-policy.yaml",  # optional
    allow_missing_projects=False,  # optional
    config_overrides=None,  # optional
    output_dir=None,  # optional
    scanners=None,  # optional
    excluded_scanners=None,  # optional
    offline=False,  # optional
    clean_output=True,  # optional
)

The first four arguments mean what they mean for resolve_ash_workspace. The rest:

Argument Meaning output_dir Where the workspace output tree goes. Defaults to <workspace root>/.ash/ash_output, with each project's own output under <output_dir>/projects/<project key>/. The default is beneath the workspace root and not beneath the server's working directory, which for a server launched by an editor or an agent is whatever that process happened to have. scanners Restrict every project to these scanner names. excluded_scanners Exclude these scanners from every project. Takes precedence over scanners. offline Run without network access. clean_output Remove each project's previous ash_aggregated_results.json before scanning. Runs after the confinement check, never before it.

A scanner that scanners or excluded_scanners leaves out is SKIPPED with a skipped_reason naming the parameter (not named by the scanners parameter, excluded from this run (the excluded_scanners parameter)), and a selection no project could run is refused naming both parameters; a CLI scan names --scanners and --exclude-scanners instead.

The response carries:

  • scan_ids — a map from project key to registry scan ID. One entry per project that will actually be scanned.
  • projects — each project's status, finding counts, threshold and whether it exceeded that threshold.
  • results_path — where the unified workspace results were written.
  • exit_code — the workspace verdict.

success reports whether the scan ran, not whether it passed. A scan that found actionable findings ran fine; the verdict is in exit_code.

docs.title: One registry entry per project
docs.text:
Every existing MCP scan is one directory and one registry entry, so "which scan is this" and "which directory is this" have always been the same question. A workspace scan is one tool call over N directories, so it registers N entries. Each project key in scan_ids maps to an ID you can hand to get_scan_progress and get_scan_results for that project alone.

A project skipped at resolution gets no entry and no ID. A registry entry is a claim that a scan is pending or running on a directory; making that claim for a directory nobody will scan would block a later legitimate scan of the same path and would make list_active_scans report work nobody is doing.

cancel_scan with one project's ID stops that project the way it stops a single scan. The other projects carry on, and the response reports the cancelled project as failed.

docs.title: Server limits
docs.text:
The server's max_concurrent_scans and scan_timeout_seconds (see Server limits) apply to a workspace scan as to a single one, with the workspace as the unit:

  • The workspace scan counts as one scan against max_concurrent_scans, however many projects it has. Counted per project, a workspace with more projects than the limit could never start. Beyond the limit it is refused before anything is written, with the same error a run_ash_scan gets.
  • Because the whole workspace is one scan, how many of its projects run at once is capped too: at most min(4, cpu_count), the bound a workspace gets when its config sets none. A scanned workspace's workspace.max_parallel_projects can lower it but not raise it over MCP. The CLI honors the configured value.
  • scan_timeout_seconds covers the whole workspace scan, counted from when it starts running. Past it, every project's entry is marked failed with an error_message naming the limit, a project that had already finished included (its files on disk are complete), every project still running is stopped, and the call returns success: false with error_category operation_timeout and the scan_ids. The unified results file and the workspace reports are not written, unless the limit is reached while they are being written.

docs.title: Progress reporting
docs.text:
Progress arrives as completed projects over total projects, with the project key in the message — payments-api complete (3/7 projects). report_progress carries three fields and none of them is a project, so the project has to travel in the message.

The denominator is projects and not scanners on purpose. ASH's per-scanner progress estimate only ever grows as more scanner result files appear, and each project's fraction is capped below 1.0, so summing per-project fractions produces a number that drifts and never arrives — a client watching it could not tell a stalled scan from a slow one. A project count terminates.

docs.title: Allowed roots govern the projects, not the workspace file
docs.text:
ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS is the setting that bounds what the MCP server may scan. It applies to a workspace project by project, for resolve_ash_workspace and run_ash_workspace_scan alike: every project directory the workspace resolves to is checked against it, before any project's own .ash.yaml is read.

That is a wider reach than the single-directory tools have, arrived at indirectly. run_ash_scan is handed one directory by the client. A workspace scan is handed one file and gets N directories out of it, none of which the client stated — so checking the workspace root alone would be worse than useless, since the resolver already guarantees every project sits below the root and one allowlisted root would then authorize the whole tree beneath it.

One project outside the permitted roots refuses the whole workspace. Nothing is scanned, and the error names the offending project keys. Scanning the projects that pass and reporting success is the failure workspace mode exists to prevent: a green result covering fewer projects than you asked for, with the passing projects supplying the reassurance. There is no --allow-missing-projects equivalent for this, because a confinement refusal is a fact about what the server is permitted to touch rather than a fact about this machine.

Two paths are deliberately not subject to the roots:

  • the .code-workspace file itself, and
  • the workspace_config policy file.

Both are config inputs. ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS answers "which directories may the server read source from and write an output tree into", and neither of these is that — each is read once, nothing is written near it, and they are supplied by the same caller who supplies config_path on run_ash_scan, which the roots also leave alone. Confining them would break the ordinary arrangement where workspace definitions sit beside a checkout rather than inside one, and where one policy file governs several checkouts. On a network transport they are checked instead against the directories the session may read config from, as config_path is: one outside them is refused with config_input_not_permitted and exit code 3 before it is read.

A policy file the workspace root holds, which ASH finds when workspace_config is omitted (.ash-workspace.yaml and the other names, at the root or in its .ash/), is checked as a project's own config is. On a network transport, an entry there that resolves outside the directories the session may read config from, a link to a missing file included, refuses the workspace with config_input_not_permitted before anything is read, and the refusal names neither the outside path nor anything in the file. A .ash that is itself a link outside those directories is refused the same way before any name in it is looked at, so the answer is the same whatever the directory it leads to holds. On Windows a junction counts as a link. A directory bind-mounted at .ash, which takes root to make, can't be told from one of the workspace's own and is looked in.

So a working configuration looks like this:

ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS=/srv/repos ash mcp

with the definition at /srv/repos/platform/dev.code-workspace, its projects at /srv/repos/platform/api and /srv/repos/platform/web, and a shared policy at /etc/ash/workspace-policy.yaml. One root entry covers every project beneath it at any depth; you do not enumerate projects, and you do not re-edit the variable when the workspace gains one.

docs.title: With ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS unset, only the minimal system-directory denylist applies
docs.text:
Say this plainly, because it is easy to assume otherwise: leaving the variable unset does not bound a workspace scan. It leaves the short fixed refusal list in force — on Linux and macOS /boot, /dev, /etc, /proc, /root, /sys and the filesystem root; on Windows the Windows directory, Program Files, ProgramData and a bare drive root. Everything else is accepted, including home directories, /usr and /var, because that is where code lives.

That list is a safety net, not a security boundary. It declines the handful of directories that hold host configuration and kernel interfaces rather than source code, and it says nothing about the rest of the filesystem. A .code-workspace file can list any folder below its own root, so on a server with the variable unset, a workspace definition is free to point the scanner at essentially any tree the server process can read. If you need the surface actually bounded, set ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS; nothing else here does that job. Setting it replaces the default list rather than adding to it, which is also how a deliberate scan of a system directory is arranged.

docs.title: Ordering: read the definition, confine, then read project configs and scan
docs.text:
The order is forced by what each step needs, and it shows up in the errors you get.

Confinement needs the project directories, which come from the workspace definition, so the definition is read and checked first. A workspace file that is both malformed and outside the permitted roots reports the malformation — a folder nobody cloned, say — rather than the confinement refusal. That is the right way round: the malformation is the part you can act on, and reporting the refusal would send you to edit an environment variable when the real problem is a line in the workspace file.

Confinement then runs before any project's own config is read. A project outside the permitted roots refuses the workspace, with exit code 4, without its .ash.yaml being opened, so neither tool reports anything from a config the server may not read: not its label, scanners or threshold in a plan, and not its parse errors.

Every filesystem write happens after the confinement check, including the clean_output deletion and the creation of each project's output directory. A refused workspace leaves nothing behind.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Both tools return an exit_code alongside the standard error keys, carrying the code the CLI would have exited with, plus exit_code_meaning with the documented description. The distinction matters because it routes to different people:

exit_code Meaning Who acts 0 Success. — 2 Actionable findings above a threshold. The scan ran. The owners of the projects listed with exceeds_threshold true. 3 Invalid project config. The workspace is fine and one project's own config is not. Also a workspace definition, policy file or project config outside the directories the session may read config from, whether you named it (workspace_file, workspace_config) or ASH found it (error_type config_input_not_permitted, the code run_ash_scan gives the same refusal), and a link in the output tree, refused before anything is written, as run_ash_scan refuses one. That project's owner, whoever sets the server's config roots, or for a link whoever controls the output directory. The message names the project, the file, or the component that is a link. 4 Workspace definition or policy refusal, or a project or output directory outside the allowed roots. Whoever owns the workspace file or the server's allowed roots. 5 Usage error: a scanners selection no project can run, or a file where the output directory or a project's projects/<key> directory goes (error_type output_dir_not_usable, Output directory is not a directory: <path>, as run_ash_scan refuses it), refused before any project is registered, or one of those directories that cannot be created (Output directory cannot be created: <path> (<reason>), the same error_type). The caller, or for a file whoever controls the output directory. 1 Internal error — an ASH bug, not your input. File an issue.

An unexpected failure is reported as 1 and not as 4 on purpose. Reporting an ASH bug as a workspace error would send you to inspect a workspace file that is correct.

docs.title: Why these tools never exit the process
docs.text:
The CLI's workspace path is built to exit: interactions/run_ash_scan.py calls sys.exit on a non-zero workspace code, and _run_workspace_mode calls sys.exit on all three of its failure paths. That is correct for a process whose only job is one scan.

It would be fatal for a server. SystemExit derives from BaseException rather than Exception, so the except Exception handlers that wrap the MCP tools would not catch it: one malformed .code-workspace file from one client would terminate the interpreter and take every other session's in-flight scan with it — and silently from the clients' point of view, because the connection simply drops.

So the MCP tools call resolve_workspace and execute_workspace directly. Both raise and neither exits, and every failure comes back as a response dictionary carrying the exit code.

docs.title: Container mode
docs.text:
Workspace mode over MCP always runs locally. The MCP tools do not accept a run mode, and the local workspace branch is the one gated at automated_security_helper/interactions/run_ash_scan.py:1085 on opts.mode != RunMode.container.

The CLI's ash --workspace --mode container works by running ash --workspace inside the container and reading the workspace payload back out. There is no MCP equivalent, and adding one would mean the server building or pulling an image and starting a container on behalf of a client — which is a materially different privilege from reading a directory. If you need workspace mode in a container, drive the CLI.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• The scan is synchronous. run_ash_workspace_scan returns when the whole workspace is done. It runs off the event loop so the server stays responsive to other sessions, and it emits progress notifications, but there is no early-return-with-a-handle form the way run_ash_scan has. For a large workspace, make sure your client's tool timeout accommodates the full run.
  • Two spellings of one directory are a refusal, not a de-duplication. A definition listing both proj and proj/ is refused. De-duplicating silently would change what you asked for, and an operator who wrote two entries meant something by it.
  • A failed project writes no results file, so it never counts as complete in the progress stream. Progress stops short rather than reaching the total. The verdict is in the return value, not in the progress notifications; progress is a liveness signal.

docs.title: Plugin Development Guide
docs.text: ASH v3 features a flexible plugin architecture that allows you to extend its functionality through custom plugins. This guide provides an overview of the plugin system and how to develop your own plugins.

docs.title: Built-in Plugins
docs.text:
ASH ships with a comprehensive set of built-in plugins that provide core functionality:

  • Built-in Plugins Overview: Complete guide to all built-in plugins
  • Security Scanners: 16 built-in security scanners (Bandit, Semgrep, Checkov, etc.)
  • Report Formats: 15 output formats (SARIF, HTML, CSV, etc.)
  • File Converters: Archive extraction and Jupyter notebook processing
  • Event Handlers: Scan lifecycle event handling

docs.title: Plugin Types
docs.text:
ASH supports three types of plugins:

  1. Scanners: Perform security scans on files and generate findings
  2. Reporters: Generate reports from scan results in various formats
  3. Converters: Transform files before scanning (e.g., convert Jupyter notebooks to Python)

docs.title: Plugin Architecture
docs.text:
ASH plugins are Python classes that inherit from base plugin classes and are registered using decorators. The plugin system is designed to be:

  • Modular: Each plugin has a specific responsibility
  • Configurable: Plugins can be configured via YAML configuration
  • Discoverable: Plugins are automatically discovered and loaded
  • Extensible: New plugin types can be added in the future

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
To create a custom plugin:

  1. Create a Python module with your plugin implementation
  2. Register your plugin using the appropriate decorator
  3. Add your plugin module to the ASH configuration

For detailed instructions and examples, see the specific plugin type documentation:

  • Scanner Plugins
  • Reporter Plugins
  • Converter Plugins
  • Plugin Best Practices

docs.title: Plugin Module Structure
docs.text:
A typical plugin module has the following structure:

my_ash_plugins/
├── __init__.py
├── converters.py
├── scanners.py
└── reporters.py

The __init__.py file should register your plugins for discovery:

# my_ash_plugins/__init__.py
from my_ash_plugins.scanners import MyCustomScanner
from my_ash_plugins.reporters import MyCustomReporter
from my_ash_plugins.converters import MyCustomConverter

# Make plugins discoverable
ASH_SCANNERS = [MyCustomScanner]
ASH_REPORTERS = [MyCustomReporter]
ASH_CONVERTERS = [MyCustomConverter]

docs.title: Using Custom Plugins
docs.text:
Add your custom plugin module to the ASH configuration:

# ASH config file (.ashrc.yaml in a new project)
ash_plugin_modules:
  - my_ash_plugins

A repository's .ash/.ash.yaml may name only modules installed outside the scanned tree, and not ASH's ash_aws_plugins and ash_snyk_plugins packages, which send findings or source off the host. A class from either package that your package lists or imports is selected only when the operator loads your package, or theirs, with --ash-plugin-modules or a config outside the tree. See Settings a repository's config cannot choose.

Or specify it on the command line:

ash --ash-plugin-modules my_ash_plugins

The module must be inside ASH's plugin namespace: under automated_security_helper. or ash_plugins, or a top-level package named ash_plugins or ending in _ash_plugins, as my_ash_plugins does, and must be a regular package or module: one with an __init__.py, not a namespace package. Any other name, and ASH's plugin root automated_security_helper.plugin_modules itself, refuses the scan with exit code 3 before anything is imported.

A scan uses ASH's built-in plugins (those defined in ash_builtin) plus the plugins and event handlers of the modules it names this way: those a named module defines, imports, or lists in its ASH_* declarations, but not those only a subpackage of it defines. When one process runs several scans (the MCP server, or a program calling run_ash_scan more than once), a module only another scan named takes no part.

docs.title: Real-World Examples
docs.text:
ASH includes several built-in plugins that you can use as examples:

  • Scanner Examples: Bandit, Semgrep, Checkov
  • Reporter Examples: Markdown, HTML, JSON, S3, BedrockSummary
  • Converter Examples: Jupyter, Archive

You can find these plugins in the ASH source code:

  • Scanners: automated_security_helper/plugins/scanners/
  • Reporters: automated_security_helper/plugins/reporters/
  • Converters: automated_security_helper/plugins/converters/

For more detailed diagrams specific to each plugin type, see: - Scanner Plugin Diagrams - Reporter Plugin Diagrams - Converter Plugin Diagrams - Event Subscriber Diagrams

docs.title: Plugin Lifecycle
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the lifecycle of plugins during an ASH scan:

sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant ASH as ASH Core
    participant PM as Plugin Manager
    participant CP as Converter Plugins
    participant SP as Scanner Plugins
    participant ES as Event Subscribers
    participant RP as Reporter Plugins

    User->>ASH: Start Scan
    ASH->>PM: Load Plugins
    PM->>CP: Initialize
    PM->>SP: Initialize
    PM->>ES: Initialize
    PM->>RP: Initialize

    ASH->>ES: Emit ScanStarted Event
    ES-->>ASH: Handle Event

    ASH->>CP: Convert Files
    CP-->>ASH: Converted Files

    ASH->>ES: Emit ConversionCompleted Event
    ES-->>ASH: Handle Event

    ASH->>SP: Scan Files
    SP-->>ASH: Scan Results

    ASH->>ES: Emit ScanCompleted Event
    ES-->>ASH: Handle Event

    ASH->>RP: Generate Reports
    RP-->>ASH: Reports

    ASH->>ES: Emit ReportingCompleted Event
    ES-->>ASH: Handle Event

    ASH-->>User: Scan Complete

docs.title: Converter Plugin Class Hierarchy
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the class hierarchy for converter plugins:

classDiagram
    class PluginBase {
        +context: PluginContext
        +config: Any
        +validate_plugin_dependencies() bool
        +model_post_init(context)
        #_plugin_log(message, level, target_type, append_to_stream)
        #_run_subprocess(cmd, stdout_preference, stderr_preference)
    }

    class ConverterPluginBase {
        +convert() List[Path]
        +results_dir: Path
    }

    class ConverterPluginConfigBase {
        +name: str
        +enabled: bool
        +options: ConverterOptionsBase
    }

    class ConverterOptionsBase

    class CustomConverter {
        +convert() List[Path]
    }

    PluginBase <|-- ConverterPluginBase
    ConverterPluginBase <|-- CustomConverter
    ConverterPluginConfigBase -- CustomConverter : configures
    ConverterOptionsBase -- ConverterPluginConfigBase : contains

docs.text:
The following diagram shows how configuration flows through a converter plugin:

flowchart TD
    A[ASH config file] --> B[Configuration Parser]
