  • Reporter Details: Complete guide to output formats
  • Configuration Guide: Advanced configuration options
  • Plugin Development: Create custom plugins

docs.title: actionlint
docs.text: actionlint checks GitHub Actions workflow files: workflow syntax, ${{ }} expression types, script injection from untrusted event data, hard-coded container credentials, if: conditions that are always true, undefined needs: jobs, unknown runner labels, and more. It is a single Go binary, MIT licensed. zizmor, also a builtin scanner, flags template injection too; ASH does not deduplicate across scanners, so with both enabled such a step is reported by each, under its own rule id.

docs.title: Enabling it
docs.text: actionlint is a builtin scanner, enabled by default: a default scan runs it. scanners.actionlint.enabled: false in the ASH config turns it off, and --scanners and --exclude-scanners select it as they select any scanner. If the tool is not installed, the scanner is reported MISSING and the scan exits 1 (the incomplete-scan gate), as for every builtin scanner; ash dependencies install and the container image provide it.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
Where How Container image Installed (pinned v1.7.12) Local / pip install ash dependencies install --tool actionlint downloads the pinned release asset and checks its SHA256 Nix pkgs.actionlint is in the flake's scanner set

The pinned version and digests are in automated_security_helper/utils/tool_downloads.py, transcribed from the release's actionlint_<version>_checksums.txt.

docs.title: What is scanned
docs.text:
ASH passes actionlint every *.yml / *.yaml file whose parent directory is .github/workflows, at any depth, taken from the scan set. That includes a source directory that is itself .github (its workflows/*.yml) or .github/workflows. Files excluded by .gitignore, .ignore (while honor_ignore_files is on, the default) or global_settings.ignore_paths, anything under ASH's output directory, and files under directories named node_modules, .venv or venv are not passed; zizmor skips the same workflows. A workflow that is a symlink pointing outside the scan root, or a broken symlink (its target is missing, or links loop), is skipped with a warning; actionlint would fail the whole run on a file it cannot open. Other YAML is never linted.

A uses: ./... in a workflow makes actionlint read the action metadata or reusable workflow it names, from the repository root, and its findings then quote what it read (the action's name and its input names). A workflow with such a reference that resolves outside the scanned repository, through .. or a symlink, is skipped with a warning, so actionlint never reads that file. References that stay inside the repository are checked as usual.

If the scan root has no workflow files, actionlint does not run and the scanner reports SKIPPED (it evaluated nothing). A scan that selects only actionlint (--scanners actionlint) on such a tree therefore exits 1 with "Scan ran no scanners".

actionlint is a native binary, so --python-only does not run it.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
scanners:
  actionlint:
    enabled: true           # the default; false turns it off
    options:
      config_file: null     # actionlint config; a relative path is taken from where it is set
      shellcheck: null      # "shellcheck" to enable it; null disables the integration
      pyflakes: null        # "pyflakes" to enable it; null disables the integration
      severity_threshold: null
      scan_timeout: 1800

docs.title: config_file
docs.text:
ASH always passes actionlint -config-file with a config of its choosing, and it is never the scanned repository's own:

  1. options.config_file, when the operator set it: from --config-overrides, or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory (one that is not repository-written). A relative path is taken from the directory of the ASH config file that sets it, or from the working directory for --config-overrides, not from the source directory (see Relative paths in the operator's settings), and an absolute one is used as given; the file the operator names may be inside the scanned tree. A path that does not exist fails the scan with ERROR, and so does a path inside the tree that leads out of it through a symbolic link, without running actionlint: the scanned repository decides what is at that path, actionlint quotes the start of a value it cannot parse, and ASH logs a config's ignore patterns.
  2. Otherwise an empty config ASH writes outside the scanned tree, in a directory of the scanner run's own that is removed when the run ends.

A .github/actionlint.yaml or .github/actionlint.yml in the scanned repository is not read (ASH notes it at INFO), and config_file set by an ASH config inside any git checkout or the scanned directory, or by an MCP client, is ignored with a warning. A config's paths.<glob>.ignore patterns make actionlint drop findings before ASH sees them, so they would be neither reported nor counted as suppressed. Tune findings with ASH suppressions, which are both. If the operator's config has ignore patterns, ASH logs a warning naming them. ASH reads the config with YAML aliases refused, as it reads every YAML config; actionlint accepts aliases, so for a config that uses one ASH cannot list the patterns, and its warning says that actionlint may still drop findings the config ignores.

docs.title: shellcheck and pyflakes
docs.text:
actionlint runs shellcheck on run: scripts and pyflakes on shell: python steps when they are on PATH, and skips them silently when they are not. Results would then depend on what a host happens to have installed, so ASH disables both by default (actionlint -shellcheck= -pyflakes=).

To use them, set the option to shellcheck or pyflakes, which is looked up in the absolute directories on PATH and in ASH's bin directory, and handed to actionlint as an absolute path. If the configured tool cannot be found or is not executable, the scanner reports MISSING rather than running without it. shellcheck and pyflakes findings are LOW severity. Neither is installed in the ASH container image.

Each option names the program actionlint pipes every run: script to, started from the root of the scanned tree. Set to a shell or an interpreter, that program would run each run: script instead of checking it. ASH's config usually comes from the repository being scanned (.ash/.ash.yaml), so from a config file inside any git checkout or the scanned directory each option accepts only its own name. Another program, or any path, is honored only from --config-overrides or a config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory:

ash scan --config-overrides 'scanners.actionlint.options.shellcheck=/opt/shellcheck/bin/shellcheck'

Whoever sets it, a program that resolves inside the scanned tree is refused. An operator's relative path is resolved against the source directory and must land outside the tree, and a path inside the tree that a symbolic link there leads out of it is refused too, whether you wrote it or a name was found at it through an absolute PATH entry inside the tree, because the link, not you, chose the program. A refused value is logged as a warning and actionlint runs with that integration off.

A relative PATH entry, such as . or bin, is never searched, for actionlint itself or for these programs. actionlint runs from the scanned directory, where such an entry could name a program the repository committed, so ASH starts actionlint, and passes it shellcheck and pyflakes, by absolute path only. A tool reachable only through a relative entry is MISSING.

docs.title: Severity mapping
docs.text:
actionlint has no severity of its own; its upstream SARIF template marks everything error. ASH maps each finding by its rule kind (the SARIF ruleId):

Severity SARIF level Findings HIGH error expression findings whose message says the value is "potentially untrusted" (script injection), and credentials (a password written into container: or services:) MEDIUM warning if-cond (an if: that is always true), permissions, and deprecated-commands for set-env / add-path LOW note everything else: syntax-check, other expression errors, action, runner-label, job-needs, glob, matrix, events, id, env-var, shell-name, workflow-call, set-output / save-state deprecations, shellcheck, pyflakes

A kind not in this table (a newer actionlint) is LOW and logged once. A binary whose version differs from the pin runs with a warning, since the mapping keys on kinds and message text of the pinned release. The snippet of a credentials finding (the password itself) is not copied into the report. With the default MEDIUM threshold, lint-only findings do not fail a scan and script injection does.

docs.title: Suppressions
docs.text:
Rule, path and line suppressions work as for any scanner. The rule id is the actionlint kind:

global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - rule_id: runner-label
      path: .github/workflows/self-hosted.yml
      reason: Custom self-hosted runner labels
    - rule_id: expression
      path: .github/workflows/triage.yml
      line_start: 20
      line_end: 20
      reason: Title is only echoed into the job log

Script injection is reported under expression, the same kind as expression type errors, so suppressing expression by rule alone also suppresses injection findings. Use a line-scoped suppression for those.

Package- and symbol-scoped suppressions do not apply: a workflow file has no package identity and no function or class symbols.

docs.title: Offline
docs.text: actionlint makes no network calls (its action metadata is compiled in), so it works unchanged with ASH_OFFLINE=true and on air-gapped hosts. A run that exceeds scan_timeout is killed and reported as ERROR with a timeout message.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: actionlint exits 0 when clean, 1 when it found problems, 2 for a bad command line and 3 for a fatal error such as an unreadable file or an invalid config. ASH treats 0 and 1 as success and everything else as ERROR, as it does output that is not the expected JSON and an exit code that contradicts the findings. The source tree and the converted files are separate runs, each judged by its own exit code. The raw output is kept at scanners/actionlint/<target>/actionlint.json (with credentials snippets removed) and the SARIF ASH built from it at actionlint.sarif.

docs.title: Relation to zizmor
docs.text: zizmor also audits GitHub Actions workflows, including template injection. If ASH's zizmor scanner is enabled as well, the two run independently: they share no configuration or results, and an injection is reported once by each.

docs.title: cfn-lint and cfn-guard
docs.text: cfn-lint and cfn-guard are two builtin CloudFormation scanners. Both read the same templates cfn-nag reads, and neither needs network access to scan.

docs.title: Enabling it
docs.text:
cfn-lint and cfn-guard are builtin scanners, enabled by default: a default scan runs them. scanners.cfn-lint.enabled: false in the ASH config turns one off, and --scanners and --exclude-scanners select them as they select any scanner. If cfn-guard is not installed, the scanner is reported MISSING and the scan exits 1 (the incomplete-scan gate), as for every builtin scanner. cfn-lint is installed on first use when ASH is online, and is MISSING only when that install fails and none is on PATH. ash dependencies install and the container image provide both.

--python-only runs cfn-lint, a Python package ASH runs through uv, and does not run cfn-guard, a native binary.

docs.title: cfn-lint
docs.text: cfn-lint validates AWS CloudFormation templates against the CloudFormation resource schemas and its own rule set: misspelled or invalid properties, values a service rejects, end-of-life Lambda runtimes, unused parameters and similar problems. It checks that a template is correct, not that it is secure, which is why its severities sit below the security scanners' (see the mapping below).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
cfn-lint is a Python package (MIT-0). ASH installs it with uv tool install 'cfn-lint[sarif]>=1.43.3,<2.0.0', either on first use or ahead of time:

ash dependencies install --tool cfn-lint

The sarif extra is required; it provides the SARIF output format ASH reads. An existing cfn-lint on PATH is used when it satisfies that requirement; without uv, any cfn-lint on PATH is used as it is. The ASH container image ships cfn-lint, and the Nix flake supplies nixpkgs' cfn-lint with the sarif extra.

docs.title: Which files it scans
docs.text: The same files cfn-nag scans: every .json, .yaml and .yml file in the scan set (after ASH's ignore paths, and the .gitignore and .ignore files while honor_ignore_files is on, the default) that parses as YAML or JSON and has a top-level Resources mapping. A file with a Resources mapping that ASH cannot model as CloudFormation is reported as a target the scanner could not evaluate, so it counts toward partial coverage instead of disappearing. Templates in the converted target (archives ASH extracted) are scanned too. A template that is a symlink, sits under a symlinked directory, or has more than one hard link is skipped with a warning, because cfn-lint would read it where it points. In the source directory, a link whose target is outside the scanned tree does not get that far: the scan set leaves it out, with the warning Not scanning '<path>': link leaves the scanned tree, and lists it among the inputs not scanned (see Ignore files and the scan set).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
scanners:
  cfn-lint:
    enabled: true
    options:
      # A .cfnlintrc to use, outside the scanned tree. When unset, ASH gives
      # cfn-lint an empty configuration (see "Configuration files" below).
      config_file: /etc/ash/cfnlintrc
      # Regions to validate against, or [ALL_REGIONS]. When unset, us-east-1 (see
      # "Regions" below).
      regions: [us-east-1, eu-west-1]
      # Rule ids or prefixes to skip everywhere, or to enable (e.g. "I" for
      # informational rules, which cfn-lint does not run by default).
      ignore_checks: [W3005]
      include_checks: [I]
      # Let a template's own Metadata ignore_checks and configure_rules apply
      # (see "Suppressions").
      honor_inline_ignores: false
      # Version constraint for the installed tool.
      tool_version: ">=1.43.3,<2.0.0"
      # Seconds allowed for the uv install of cfn-lint.
      install_timeout: 300
      # Seconds each cfn-lint invocation may run before it is killed (the default;
      # null means no limit).
      scan_timeout: 1800

Region names, rule ids and prefixes are validated when the config is loaded, so a value cannot be passed through to cfn-lint as an option of its own.

docs.title: Regions
docs.text: Some of cfn-lint's checks depend on the region, for example whether a resource type exists there (rule E3006). regions names the regions to check against. When it is unset, cfn-lint uses the regions a template names in its own Metadata: cfn-lint: config: regions, then those in the config_file you named, and otherwise us-east-1. On its own, cfn-lint would read AWS_REGION and AWS_DEFAULT_REGION before falling back to us-east-1. ASH does not let it, so a template gives the same findings on every host: an empty AWS_REGION, which a CI job gets from an unset variable, would otherwise make cfn-lint fail on every template.

docs.title: Configuration files
docs.text:
Left to itself, cfn-lint reads a .cfnlintrc from the directory it runs in (the scanned repository) and from your home directory. ASH does not let it: unless config_file names a file, ASH passes cfn-lint an empty configuration of its own, which it writes outside the scanned tree and removes when the scan ends, and which stops both lookups. A .cfnlintrc is not passive settings. Its append_rules key names Python files that cfn-lint loads as rules, so a .cfnlintrc in the scanned repository would make cfn-lint import and run a rule module from the scanned tree. Its other keys, such as ignore_checks, would change what cfn-lint reports without appearing in the ASH config, which is where ASH takes ignore_checks, include_checks and regions from instead.

For the same reason config_file is honored only when the operator sets it, through --config-overrides or a config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory (one that is not repository-written), and only for a file outside the scanned tree. A relative config_file is taken from the directory of the ASH config file that sets it, or from the working directory for --config-overrides, not from the source directory (see Relative paths in the operator's settings). A config_file from the repository's own .ash/.ash.yaml or from an ASH config in any other git checkout, or one naming a file inside the tree, is ignored with a warning and cfn-lint gets ASH's empty configuration, and so is a path inside the tree that leads out of it through a symbolic link there. A config an MCP client delivered that sets config_file is refused, since it is a default denied_paths entry. A file you name this way is used with append_rules included, and one that does not exist fails the scan. cfn-lint resolves the relative paths in it, such as append_rules and custom_rules entries, against its working directory rather than the file's directory. ASH runs cfn-lint in a new, empty directory outside the scanned tree that only your user can enter and that is removed after the scan, so a relative path names nothing: neither a file in the scanned repository nor one in a shared directory such as /tmp. Write those paths as absolute paths: a relative one makes cfn-lint fail on every template. Under --sandbox, a file outside the tree is not mounted unless it is listed in sandbox.extra_read_paths.

tool_version is appended to the package name when ASH installs cfn-lint, so it must be a version constraint such as >=1.43.3,<2.0.0. Anything else, including a direct reference such as @ file:///..., is ignored with a warning and the default constraint is used.

ignore_checks and tool_version are honored only when you set them as the operator, with --config-overrides or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory. ignore_checks drops findings before ASH sees them, so they are neither reported nor counted as suppressed, and tool_version chooses the cfn-lint release that is installed. Set by an ASH config inside a git checkout or the scanned directory, each is ignored with a warning and its default is used; a config an MCP client delivered that sets either is refused, since both are default denied_paths entries. To silence a finding in a repository, use an ASH suppression.

docs.title: Severity mapping
docs.text:
cfn-lint classifies every rule by the first letter of its id. ASH maps that letter to an ASH severity and sets the SARIF level to match, so every report agrees:

cfn-lint rule Meaning ASH severity SARIF level E.... The template is invalid or will fail to deploy MEDIUM warning W.... Best-practice or hygiene problem LOW note I.... Informational (only with include_checks: [I]) INFO none

These sit below the severities of security scanners on purpose. At ASH's default threshold (MEDIUM) an invalid template fails the scan and a warning does not. Raise or lower that per scanner with scanners.cfn-lint.options.severity_threshold. cfn-lint's own class is never lost: it is the first character of the rule id.

E0003 is not reported as a finding. cfn-lint uses it for its own configuration errors, including a template path it could not open, so ASH counts the affected templates as not evaluated.

docs.title: Suppressions
docs.text:
ASH suppressions apply to cfn-lint findings by rule_id, path, and line_start/line_end:

global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - rule_id: E2533
      path: templates/legacy.yaml
      line_start: 14
      line_end: 14
      reason: The function is pinned to this runtime until it is retired.

Package-scoped suppressions do not apply (cfn-lint reports on templates, not packages), and neither do symbol-scoped ones, which target functions and classes in source code. A template's own ignores, Metadata: cfn-lint: config: ignore_checks on the template or on a resource, do not apply by default, and neither do the rule settings a template gives in Metadata: cfn-lint: config: configure_rules, such as E3031 exceptions or E1029 custom_excludes. cfn-lint would drop what they hide before ASH sees it, so those findings would appear neither as findings nor in ASH's suppressed counts and unused-suppressions report. ASH passes cfn-lint every rule outside your own ignore_checks (and the ignore_checks of the config_file you named) as mandatory, which cfn-lint applies whatever the template says. To let templates ignore or configure away their own findings, set honor_inline_ignores: true as the operator, with --config-overrides or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory; set by an ASH config inside one it is ignored with a warning.

A template's ignore_checks can also reach the template cfn-lint reads after it in the same run. cfn-lint keeps the last template's settings while it reads the next one, and when that one cannot be parsed (duplicate keys, for example) it drops the parse errors (E0000) if the kept ignore_checks cover them, mandatory or not. A list given on the command line replaces a template's, so ASH always passes cfn-lint --ignore-checks: your own ignores, or W0000 when there are none. No rule has that id, and every rule is mandatory then, which cfn-lint ranks above an ignore, so it ignores nothing. With honor_inline_ignores: true ASH passes no placeholder, because it would replace the template-level ignore_checks you let in. It runs cfn-lint once per template instead, so a template's ignores apply to that template only. That costs one cfn-lint start-up per template: with cfn-lint 1.57.2, the 8 CloudFormation templates in ASH's own test data took 3.4 s in one run and 12.0 s in eight.

Rule settings need one more step. cfn-lint takes configure_rules whole from the first place that sets any: the command line, then the template, then the config file. So ASH passes the configure_rules of the config_file you named on the command line, one cfn-lint --configure-rule=RULE:key=value per setting, and when there are none it passes E3012:strict=false, which is E3012's default and changes no finding. Two limits follow from cfn-lint's command-line format. A setting it cannot carry, a list of more than one item or a value containing a comma, a colon or an equals sign, is left out with a warning, and that rule runs with its default; for the built-in rules the default reports at least as much. A config_file that sets merge_configs fails the scan, because cfn-lint would then merge a template's settings into the command line's. So does a config_file that uses a YAML alias: ASH reads the file with aliases refused, as it reads every YAML config, and cfn-lint would read it in full, so ASH could not check what it sets. With honor_inline_ignores: true, ASH passes neither, and cfn-lint reads your config_file as written, a template's configure_rules taking precedence over it.

docs.title: Offline use
docs.text: cfn-lint needs no network to scan. Its resource schemas ship inside the package, and it only downloads updates when asked to (cfn-lint --update-specs and similar), which ASH never does. A scan inside a network namespace with no interfaces produced the same results as one with network access. Installing cfn-lint needs network once; in offline mode (ASH_OFFLINE=true) a cfn-lint that is not already installed is reported as MISSING with the reason.

docs.title: How ASH runs it
docs.text:
cfn-lint --format sarif --output-file=<results> [options] -- <template> ...

in a new, empty directory outside the scanned tree, with every path absolute; ASH reports each location relative to the source directory. Template paths are escaped before they are passed, because cfn-lint expands each filename argument as a glob pattern: a template named a[1].yaml would otherwise not be linted at all. Long template lists are split across several invocations to stay within command-line length limits. With honor_inline_ignores: true each template has an invocation of its own (see "Suppressions").

cfn-lint's exit status is a bitmask of the levels it reported (2 error, 4 warning, 8 informational); any combination of those is a completed run. Other exit statuses, a timeout, missing output, or an E0003 result mark every template in that invocation as not evaluated, so one such template costs the findings of the others in its batch; with honor_inline_ignores: true it costs only its own. The scan then reports partial coverage and exits 1 by default, so nothing is lost silently. The source tree and the converted files are separate targets, and each records the worst exit status of its own invocations.

docs.title: License
docs.text: cfn-lint is MIT-0 (MIT No Attribution). It is installed as a separate tool and is not bundled into ASH's Python package.

docs.title: cfn-guard
docs.text: AWS CloudFormation Guard (cfn-guard) evaluates CloudFormation templates against policy-as-code rules written in the Guard DSL. cfn-guard ships no rules of its own, so ASH pins a rule source, the AWS Guard Rules Registry, and lets you add or substitute your own rules.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
ash dependencies install --tool cfn-guard

installs two pinned artifacts, each verified against a SHA256 recorded in ASH's source (automated_security_helper/utils/tool_downloads.py):

  • the cfn-guard 3.2.1 release binary for your platform (Linux, macOS and Windows, amd64 and arm64), into ASH_BIN_PATH;
  • the AWS Guard Rules Registry release 1.0.2 rules archive. Its output/*.guard files are extracted into aws-guard-rules-registry-1.0.2/ under $ASH_CFN_GUARD_RULES_DIR, or under <ASH_BIN_PATH>/../share/cfn-guard-rules when that is unset. ASH's source also pins what the archive extracts to: one SHA256 over the names and digests of all 50 rule files. The extracted files are checked against it before they are moved into place. A .ash-rules-manifest.json beside them records what was installed; no check relies on it.

A download whose bytes do not match the pinned digest is refused. The ASH container image ships both, installed read-only for the scan user: the rules are in /usr/share/ash/cfn-guard-rules, which the image checks at build time is owned by root, as is every directory above it. nixpkgs has no cfn-guard package, so the nix flake packages the same pinned release binary (nix/cfn-guard.nix), and the nix shell installs the rules bundle into ASH_CFN_GUARD_RULES_DIR on first entry, and again on any entry where the bundle there is not the pinned one: after an ASH upgrade that changes the pin, or when the rule files there no longer match the pinned contents.

ash dependencies install keeps a bundle that is already in place only when its rule files match the pinned contents; otherwise it downloads and installs the pinned archive again. Without network access that download fails, and the install stops with a message that names the directory, says its rules do not match the pinned contents, and says that network access, or the ASH container image, is needed. The rules already there are left as they were.

Before every scan ASH checks the installed rule files against the pinned contents in the same way. A rule file that was edited, removed, renamed or added, or is not a regular file, makes the scanner MISSING with the reinstall command rather than scanning with it. Files in that directory without the .guard suffix are not part of the bundle and are not read.

docs.title: Rule sets
docs.text:
The registry release contains 50 rule-set files: one per compliance framework (CIS AWS Benchmark, NIST 800-53, PCI DSS, HIPAA and others), a Well-Architected Security Pillar set, a Well-Architected Reliability Pillar set, and guard-rules-registry-all-rules.

The default is wa-Security-Pillar, the registry's mapping of the AWS Well-Architected Security Pillar (45 rules: public access, encryption, logging, TLS, IAM and similar). guard-rules-registry-all-rules (67 rules) was considered and not chosen: it adds 22 reliability and operations rules, such as backup plans, Multi-AZ, deletion protection, S3 replication and object lock, and Lambda concurrency, which are not security findings and would fail templates for reasons a security scan should not. The compliance-framework sets are a choice for your own context rather than a default.

scanners:
  cfn-guard:
    enabled: true
    options:
      # Bundled registry rule sets, by file name without ".guard".
      rule_sets:
        - wa-Security-Pillar
        - cis-aws-benchmark-level-1
      # Your own .guard files or directories. A relative path is taken from the
      # directory of this config file (from the working directory for
      # --config-overrides). Evaluated in addition to rule_sets; set
      # rule_sets: [] to use only these.
      rules_paths:
        - policy/guard
      # Seconds each per-template cfn-guard run may take.
      scan_timeout: 1800

A rule-set name with a .guard extension or characters outside letters, digits, ., _ and - fails config validation. A well-formed name that is not in the bundle makes the scanner MISSING, with the list of available names.

rule_sets is honored only when you set it as the operator, with --config-overrides or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory. A narrower set drops findings before ASH sees them: wa-Reliability-Pillar alone turns the 24 findings on ASH's test template into 9, losing every public-access, encryption and logging finding. Set by an ASH config inside a git checkout or the scanned directory, or by an MCP client, it is ignored with a warning and wa-Security-Pillar is evaluated.

rules_paths is honored only when you set it as the operator, with --config-overrides or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory; a path the operator names may be inside the scanned tree. A relative entry is taken from the directory of the ASH config file that sets it, or from the working directory for --config-overrides (rules_paths=[...] or rules_paths+=<path>), not from the source directory (see Relative paths in the operator's settings). The scanned repository decides what is at such a path, so one that leads out of the tree through a symbolic link in it, to a file or a directory, makes the scanner MISSING and is not read. Set by an ASH config inside a git checkout or the scanned directory, or by an MCP client, it is ignored with a warning, and if rule_sets is empty as well, cfn-guard evaluates the default wa-Security-Pillar set instead of nothing. cfn-guard prints a rules file it cannot parse, all of it, in its error, so a path the scanned repository chose could otherwise put any file the scan can read into the report.

For a directory, ASH collects the files cfn-guard would read from it: .guard and .ruleset files at any depth, case-sensitively, not entering symlinked subdirectories. cfn-guard follows a symlinked rules file, so one that resolves outside the directory you named is refused with a warning; a link that stays inside it is read. ASH reads each file itself and gives cfn-guard a copy, written in a directory of that scanner run's own outside the scanned tree, made with mode 0700 and removed when the run ends, which is also why rules_paths needs no sandbox grant: under --sandbox, cfn-guard can read that directory and cannot write to it. A directory with no rules files selects nothing, and when nothing else is selected the scanner is MISSING ("no cfn-guard rules are selected"): cfn-guard given such a directory would report a clean run. A rules_paths entry that does not exist, a named file that is not a regular file, or a subdirectory that cannot be listed also makes the scanner MISSING.

docs.title: Why the rules are not age-checked
docs.text: ASH holds downloaded content databases (grype's and trivy's vulnerability databases, the offline semgrep and opengrep rulesets) to a maximum age, because those are fetched at build or scan time and can go stale silently. The Guard rules are not declared there. They are a fixed release archive pinned by digest, like the policies inside the pinned checkov package: they change only when ASH changes the pin, and an age bound would measure how recently the same bytes were copied rather than how current the rules are. Release 1.0.2 is the newest the registry has published.

docs.title: Which files it scans
docs.text: The same files cfn-nag and cfn-lint scan: every .json, .yaml and .yml file in the scan set that parses as YAML or JSON and has a top-level Resources mapping. A file with a Resources mapping that ASH cannot model as CloudFormation is counted as not evaluated.

docs.title: Severity mapping
docs.text:
Every failed cfn-guard rule is reported as HIGH with SARIF level error.

cfn-guard marks every failure error and the registry's rules carry no severity of their own, so there is nothing per rule to map from. Every finding is HIGH because a template that violates a rule of the compliance set you chose has failed that control; the default set checks security configuration (public access blocks, encryption, logging, TLS). That includes rules that are less severe in isolation, such as a missing access log: to keep those out, choose a narrower rule set with options.rule_sets, or suppress the rule by id. ASH sets issue_severity on each result as well as the SARIF level, so the summary, the exit-code gate and every reporter all read HIGH. Adjust what fails the scan with scanners.cfn-guard.options.severity_threshold. cfn-guard reports one result per failing clause, so one rule can appear more than once for the same resource. Many rules are in more than one of the registry's rule sets, and cfn-guard reports such a rule's results once for each selected set that holds it; ASH reports each identical result once.

docs.title: Suppressions
docs.text:
ASH suppressions apply by rule_id, path, and line_start/line_end. Each result is located at the line cfn-guard reports, usually the resource's Properties, so a line-scoped suppression names that line:

global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - rule_id: S3_BUCKET_LOGGING_ENABLED
      path: templates/logging-bucket.yaml
      reason: This bucket is the access-log destination.

Package-scoped and symbol-scoped suppressions do not apply to templates. The registry's rules also honor cfn-guard's own in-template suppression, which never reaches ASH:

Resources:
  LogBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Metadata:
      guard:
        SuppressedRules:
          - S3_BUCKET_LOGGING_ENABLED

docs.title: Offline use
docs.text: cfn-guard needs no network to scan: the binary is static and the rules are local files. A scan inside a network namespace with no interfaces produced the same results. If the binary or the rules are missing in an air-gapped environment, the scanner is MISSING with the reason; nothing is fetched at scan time.

docs.title: How ASH runs it
docs.text:
Once per template:

cfn-guard validate --rules=<rules file>... --data=<template> \
  --output-format=sarif --structured --show-summary=none

One template at a time because one unparseable data file makes cfn-guard exit 255 with no output for the whole invocation, and because cfn-guard writes result locations as absolute paths, which ASH replaces with the repository-relative path of the template it ran. Exit 0 means every rule passed or was skipped and 19 means at least one failed; any other status, a timeout, or a 19 with no results marks that template as not evaluated. As for cfn-lint, the source tree and the converted files each record the worst exit status of their own runs.

docs.title: Licenses
docs.text: cfn-guard and the AWS Guard Rules Registry are both Apache-2.0. Neither is bundled into ASH's Python package; both are downloaded by ash dependencies install or shipped in the container image as separate artifacts.

docs.title: Built-in Converter Diagrams
docs.text: This document provides visual diagrams of the ASH built-in converter architecture and workflows using Mermaid.

docs.title: Converter Architecture Overview
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the high-level architecture of the ASH built-in converters:

flowchart TD
    A[ASH Core] --> B[Plugin Manager]
    B --> C[Converter Registry]

    C --> D[Built-in Converters]

    D --> E[Archive Converter]
    D --> F[Jupyter Converter]

    G[Source Files] --> D

    E --> H[Extracted Files]
    F --> I[Python Files]

    H --> J[Scanner Plugins]
    I --> J

docs.title: Converter Execution Flow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the execution flow of the built-in converters:

sequenceDiagram
    participant ASH as ASH Core
    participant PM as Plugin Manager
    participant CR as Converter Registry
    participant CV as Converter
    participant FS as File System
    participant ES as Event System

    ASH->>PM: Load Converters
    PM->>CR: Get Registered Converters
    CR-->>PM: Return Converter List

    ASH->>ES: Emit ConversionStarted Event

    loop For Each Converter
        ASH->>CV: Validate Converter
        CV-->>ASH: Return Validation Status

        alt Converter Valid
            ASH->>CV: convert()
            CV->>FS: Read Source Files
            FS-->>CV: Return File Contents

            CV->>CV: Process Files
            Note over CV: Transform File Content

            CV->>FS: Write Converted Files
            FS-->>CV: Files Written

            CV-->>ASH: Return Converted Paths
        else Converter Invalid
            ASH->>ES: Emit ConverterError Event
        end
    end

    ASH->>ES: Emit ConversionCompleted Event

docs.title: Archive Converter Workflow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the workflow of the Archive Converter:

flowchart TD
    A[Source Archive] --> B[Archive Converter]

    B --> C{Archive Type?}

    C -->|ZIP| D[Read the member list]
    C -->|TAR, TAR.GZ| E[Read headers one at a time]

    D --> F{Over an extraction limit?}
    E --> F

    F -->|Yes| G[Refuse the whole archive: nothing written, recorded with the limit]
    F -->|No| H{Member is an archive?}

    G --> N[Scan exits 1 when fail_on_incomplete_scanners is on]

    H -->|Yes| I[Recorded as not scanned, not extracted]
    H -->|No| J[Extract scannable regular files, at most their declared size]

    J --> M[Scanner Plugins]

Extraction is one level deep: an archive inside an archive is never extracted, and is reported as not scanned. The limits are max_members, max_member_bytes, max_total_bytes and max_compression_ratio; see Archive Converter.

docs.title: Jupyter Converter Workflow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the workflow of the Jupyter Converter:

flowchart TD
    A[Jupyter Notebook] --> B[Jupyter Converter]

    B --> C[Parse Notebook JSON]

    C --> D[Extract Cells]

    D --> E{Cell Type?}

    E -->|Code| F[Extract Code]
    E -->|Markdown| G{Extract Markdown?}

    G -->|Yes| H[Convert to Comments]
    G -->|No| I[Skip Cell]

    F --> J[Combine Code]
    H --> J

    J --> K[Add Cell Markers]

    K --> L[Write Python File]

    L --> M[Scanner Plugins]

docs.title: Converter Configuration Flow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows how configuration flows through the built-in converters:

flowchart TD
    A[ASH config file] --> B[Configuration Parser]
    C[CLI Arguments] --> B
    B --> D[ASH Configuration]
    D --> E[Converter Configuration]

    E --> F[Global Converter Settings]
    E --> G[Converter-Specific Settings]

    F --> H[Converted Directory]
    F --> I[Enabled Converters]

    G --> J[Archive Converter Config]
    G --> K[Jupyter Converter Config]

    J --> L[Archive Converter]

docs.title: Built-in Converters
docs.text:
ASH includes 2 built-in converters that preprocess files to make them suitable for security scanning. Converters handle file format transformations and archive extraction automatically.

For detailed visual diagrams of the built-in converter architecture and workflows, see Built-in Converter Diagrams.

docs.title: Converter Overview
docs.text: Converter Purpose Input Formats Output Archive Converter Extract compressed archives zip, tar, tar.gz Extracted files of known scannable extensions Jupyter Converter Process Jupyter notebooks .ipynb Python source code

docs.title: Archive Converter
docs.text:
Purpose: Automatically extracts compressed archives to enable scanning of contained files.

Supported Formats: - ZIP files (.zip) - TAR archives (.tar, .tar.gz). A file is selected by its last suffix only, in any case and after any trailing dots and spaces (which Windows drops from a name, so app.zip. is a zip), so a .tgz is not extracted. A file in the tree named as any other archive or compressed format in the list below (.tgz, .tar.bz2, .7z, .jar, .whl and the rest) is recorded as a refused input that was not extracted, so the summaries show that its contents were not scanned. It does not fail the scan.

Configuration: 

converters:
  archive:
    enabled: true
    options:
      max_members: 100000             # members, directories included
      max_member_bytes: 268435456     # 256 MiB, one member's declared size
      max_total_bytes: 1073741824     # 1 GiB, all members' declared sizes added up
      max_compression_ratio: 100      # that total over the archive's size, above 512 KiB

Key Features: - One level of extraction. A member that is itself an archive or compressed file is not extracted; it is recorded as not scanned. That is a last suffix, in any case and after any trailing dots, of .zip, .tar, .gz, .tgz, .bz2, .tbz, .tbz2, .xz, .txz, .zst, .tzst, .lzma, .lz, .tlz, .lz4, .Z, .tz, .7z, .rar, .cpio, .jar, .war, .ear, .aar, .apk, .whl, .egg, .nupkg, .deb or .rpm. - Extraction limits, described below - Only members with a scannable extension are written, as regular files - Each archive is extracted into a directory of its own, named from its path. Two archives whose names fold to the same directory name (a b.zip and a-b.zip) get two directories, the second with -2 appended, so neither overwrites the other's members and removing one archive's output never touches the other's - Automatic cleanup after scanning

docs.title: Extraction limits
docs.text:
Before anything is written, every member of an archive is checked against four limits. Each is an inclusive maximum on what the archive declares:

Option Default Bounds max_members 100000 the number of members, directories included max_member_bytes 268435456 (256 MiB) the size one member declares max_total_bytes 1073741824 (1 GiB) the sizes all members declare, added up max_compression_ratio 100 that total divided by the archive's size on disk, once the total is over 512 KiB

Every member counts, including members that would not be extracted, because reading a compressed tar means decompressing every member to reach the next header, and each member counts as at least 512 bytes (a tar header) toward max_total_bytes, so an archive of empty members is not free.

All the archives one scan extracts (one project, in workspace mode) also share a budget of four times max_members members and four times max_total_bytes bytes: 400,000 members and 4 GiB with the defaults, four archives at the per-archive limits, and under the 5 GB GitHub strongly recommends a whole repository stays below. The archive that would take the scan over it is refused, naming max_members or max_total_bytes as the limit to raise, and does not use up the budget, so a later archive that still fits is extracted. Raising the per-archive limit raises the shared budget with it. An archive over any limit is refused whole: nothing from it is written or scanned, and it is recorded once, with the limit named, under converter_results.archive.refused_inputs (see below). Such a refusal counts as incomplete conversion, so with fail_on_incomplete_scanners on (the default) the scan exits 1 and names the archive and the limit. The refusal is also listed in the console summary, ash.summary.txt, ash.summary.md, ash.flat.json (converter_refusals) and ash.sarif (an execution notification at level error). Names come from the archive, so they are shown as inert text: in ash.summary.md each refusal is a code span, so a name such as @someone or a URL is not a mention or a link, and in ash.summary.txt, on the console and in the log every control or bidirectional-formatting character in a name is written as an escape (\x1b, \u202e).

Reading a tar's headers is bounded as well, because tarfile reads an extended (pax) header, a GNU long name or a sparse map into memory while it parses the header, before any of the limits above can be checked. The decompressor is chosen from the archive's leading bytes (gzip, bzip2, xz, and zstd on Python 3.14), a single read of more than 1 MiB while parsing headers is refused, and the header pass may read 4 MiB plus 2 KiB per member in all. An archive over either is a failed input, as an archive that cannot be read is (see below). Real headers are a few hundred bytes; GNU tar's pax format, which writes an extended header for every member, reads about 1.5 KiB per member.

A zip's entries are counted against max_members before zipfile opens it, because zipfile builds a record for every entry of the central directory as it opens an archive. The directory is found with zipfile's own end-record reader, so it is the one zipfile would read, and the count is taken both from what the end record declares and by walking the entries' fixed headers. A zip with more entries than the limit is refused before zipfile reads them.

While copying, no member is written past the size it declares. For a sparse tar member, whose map tarfile writes before it truncates the file to its declared size, a map that places data past that size, or whose entries overlap or are out of order, refuses the member.

The defaults let ordinary source archives through. GitHub refuses files larger than 100 MiB in a repository, and an AWS Lambda deployment package may hold up to 250 MB unzipped, so a member of 256 MiB and a total of 1 GiB leave room above both. Source code compresses by a few times (2 MiB of ASH's own Python sources: 3.1 times as a zip, 3.7 as a tar.gz), while a file of zeros compresses by about 1000. Apache POI refuses a zip part that compresses better than 1%, a ratio of 100, by default; the ratio here is taken over the whole archive, so one very compressible member among ordinary ones does not reach it. The ratio is not checked until the members declare more than 512 KiB in all: below that an archive can write no more than 512 KiB whatever it compresses to, and a small fixture archive of indented JSON can compress 140 times. POI likewise skips its ratio check for an entry of 100 KiB or less; the floor here is higher because it applies to a whole archive rather than one entry.

Who can raise a limit: an operator, with --config-overrides (for example --config-overrides converters.archive.options.max_total_bytes=4294967296) or a config file outside the scanned tree, such as ASH_CONFIG's or one passed with --config. A config file the scanned repository wrote (.ash/.ash.yaml in the tree, or a workspace project's own config) and a config an MCP client supplied can lower a limit but not raise it: a higher value is replaced by the trusted one, with a warning naming the option. A repository's own config file replaces ASH_CONFIG as any selected config file does, so a limit it leaves out is the default. MCP runtime overrides of the four options, or of a section holding them, are refused by the default global_settings.mcp.runtime_overrides.denied_paths, and still refused when a profile sets its own denied_paths list.

Use Cases: - Scanning packaged applications - Analyzing deployment artifacts - Processing downloaded dependencies - Auditing compressed source code

docs.title: Jupyter Converter
docs.text:
Purpose: Extracts Python code from Jupyter notebooks for security analysis.

Configuration: 

converters:
  jupyter:
    enabled: true
    options:
      tool_version: null      # Version constraint for the conversion tool
      install_timeout: 300    # Seconds allowed for tool installation

How conversion runs: nbconvert is given a copy of the notebook in a directory that holds nothing else, and runs there rather than in the scanned tree, so neither a module nor a template directory in the tree is used. The copy is named notebook.ipynb, whatever the notebook is called, because nbconvert reads its notebook argument as a glob pattern; the converted file is named after the original. ASH picks the exporter: python for a Python notebook or one that names no language, script otherwise. The copy has metadata.language_info.nbconvert_exporter removed, so the notebook does not choose the exporter class, and keeps metadata.language_info.file_extension only when it is a plain extension such as .r.

nbconvert is run with uv tool run. When uv cannot start, or reports that it could not run nbconvert (offline with nbconvert not in its cache, for one), ASH runs an installed jupyter-nbconvert by the absolute path it found on PATH or in ASH's own bin directories ($ASH_BIN_PATH, by default ~/.ash/bin, and off Windows /usr/local/bin). It does not look for one in the working directory or through a relative PATH entry, and one inside the scanned tree, such as in an activated .venv/bin in the repository, is not run unless you allow it; see Tools inside the scanned directory.

Under --sandbox: nbconvert, its version probe and its dependency check run in the scanner sandbox, and nbconvert is never installed (install_timeout does not apply); install it first with ash dependencies install. nbconvert may read its copy of the notebook and its tools, not the source tree or the output directory (under Landlock and firejail, a tree inside a directory those backends show stays readable). When no sandbox backend can be used, no notebook is converted and each is listed in refused_inputs; such a notebook, and one nbconvert fails on inside the sandbox, is listed in the row's failed_inputs and fails the scan while fail_on_incomplete_scanners is on. See Converters in the sandbox page.

Key Features: - Code cell extraction - Cell number preservation for accurate line mapping - Markdown cell processing (optional) - Python syntax validation

Use Cases: - Data science project security - ML model code analysis - Educational content scanning - Research code auditing

When nbconvert is needed: only when the scan set holds a notebook. With none, the converter neither looks nbconvert up nor installs it, and asks uv nothing; with one, it uses an installed nbconvert or installs it with uv, within install_timeout.

docs.title: Inputs a converter does not read
docs.text:
A converter reads a file only if it is a regular file inside the scanned tree. It skips, with one warning naming the file:

  • a symlink, wherever it points, and any file under a symlinked directory;
  • a path outside the scanned tree;
  • a directory, FIFO, socket or device;
  • a file with more than one hard link.

Inside an archive, the archive converter also skips members that are symlinks, hard links or special files, members whose names are absolute or contain .., sparse members whose map reaches past their declared size, and members that are themselves archives, which are not extracted. An archive over an extraction limit is skipped whole.

Each skipped input is recorded in ash_aggregated_results.json under converter_results.<converter>.refused_inputs, with its path relative to the scanned tree, the archive member's name where there is one, and the reason:

"refused_inputs": [
  {"path": "notebooks/report.ipynb", "member": null, "reason": "it is a symbolic link"},
  {"path": "dist/app.tar", "member": "../setup.py", "reason": "its path contains a '..' component"},
  {"path": "dist/app.zip", "member": "vendor/lib.tar.gz", "reason": "it is named as an archive or compressed file (such as .zip, .tar.gz, .jar or .7z), and an archive inside an archive is not extracted, so its contents are not scanned"},
  {"path": "data/dump.zip", "member": null, "reason": "its members declare more than 1073741824 bytes, the max_total_bytes extraction limit", "limit": "max_total_bytes"}
]

Within one archive, the first 20 members refused for each reason are listed one by one, with a warning each. The rest are one record, with member null and unlisted_members set to how many more there were, and one warning, so an archive of thousands of links or nested archives does not produce thousands of records.

limit is present only for an archive refused for an extraction limit, which is the one kind of refusal that leaves a whole archive unscanned: the completeness gate counts it. The others are reported in the summaries and reports as well, and do not change the exit code.

A .gz that is one gzip-compressed file rather than a tarball, such as data.json.gz, is decompressed to the name without .gz (data.json) and that file is scanned, within the extraction limits and the scan's budget like an archive with one member. Its size is known only by reading it, so at most the limit is written before it is refused. A name ending .tar.gz says the content is a tarball, and a .tar.gz that holds no tar is a failed input.

A Git LFS pointer named like an archive, which is what a checkout without its LFS objects holds in place of each LFS-tracked .zip or .tar.gz, is recorded as a refused input naming the file, with the remedy: fetch the LFS objects (git lfs pull, or lfs: true on the CI checkout step) before the scan. It does not fail the completeness gate, because the archive is not in the tree to scan. Only a whole file in the pointer format counts: under 1024 bytes, a version line first that git-lfs reads (version https://git-lfs.github.com/spec/v1, or one of the older https://hawser.github.com/spec/v1 and http://git-media.io/v/2), key value lines of printable ASCII, and an oid sha256: and a size line. No zip, tar or gzip file the converter can extract meets that, so a readable archive is always extracted.

To have a skipped file converted, replace the link with the file itself. To have a nested archive's contents scanned, extract it into the tree before the scan.

docs.title: Inputs a converter could not convert
docs.text:
An archive that zipfile and tarfile cannot read is not extracted at all: a bad CRC, a truncated or damaged stream (a damaged single-file gzip included), an empty file, a .tar.gz that holds no tar, headers over the read limits above, or members that cannot all be written, such as a file member named like a directory another member made. A tar's members must end at an end-of-archive block (512 zero bytes, which every common tar writer puts after the last member): tarfile stops reading members without an error at a damaged header or where the archive is cut off, so a tar that stops anywhere else is truncated or damaged, and is not extracted either. Such an archive, and a notebook nbconvert could not convert (it exited non-zero, timed out, or wrote no output), are recorded under converter_results.<converter>.failed_inputs, with the reason:

"failed_inputs": [
  {"path": "notebooks/report.ipynb", "reason": "nbconvert exited with code 1"},
  {"path": "dist/old.tar", "reason": "ReadError: unexpected end of data"}
]

Other errors are recorded the same way, as <Type>: <message>. The progress line and the convert-complete event say how many files could not be converted.

An archive that cannot be read is not extracted at all: a bad CRC, a truncated or damaged stream (a damaged single-file gzip included), an empty file, a .tar.gz that holds no tar, or headers over the read limits above. Anything already written from it is removed, so the scanners never read a partial extraction as the archive.

The scanners never saw those files in converted form, so with fail_on_incomplete_scanners on (the default) the scan exits 1 and names the converter and the files, as it does for a converter whose tool is missing while it had inputs. ash merge combines every shard's failed inputs, and workspace mode reports them per project in incomplete_converters. The summaries, the flat JSON report (converter_refusals, with scan_incomplete true) and ash.sarif (an execution notification at level error) list them with the refusals. Exclude such a file with global_settings.ignore_paths if its contents need not be scanned.

docs.title: Integration with Scanners
docs.text:
Converters automatically prepare files for scanner consumption:

# Archives are extracted, then contents scanned
ash project.zip --scanners bandit,semgrep

# Jupyter notebooks converted to Python, then scanned
ash analysis.ipynb --scanners bandit,detect-secrets

docs.title: Archive Issues
docs.text:
Extraction failures: 

converters:
  archive:
    enabled: true                # An archive that cannot be read is a failed input and fails the completeness gate

Large archives: an archive over an extraction limit is refused and the scan exits 1, naming the archive and the limit. Raise the limit as an operator: 

ash scan --config-overrides 'converters.archive.options.max_total_bytes=4294967296'
or exclude the archive with global_settings.ignore_paths if its contents need not be scanned.

docs.title: Jupyter Issues
docs.text:
Malformed notebooks: 

converters:
  jupyter:
    enabled: true                # A notebook that will not parse is a failed input

docs.text:
The following diagram shows the high-level architecture of the ASH event system:

flowchart TD
    A[ASH Core] --> B[Event Emitter]

    B --> C[Event Registry]

    C --> D[Built-in Event Handlers]

docs.title: Event Flow Sequence
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the sequence of events during an ASH scan:

sequenceDiagram
    participant ASH as ASH Core
    participant EM as Event Manager
    participant SCL as Scan Completion Logger
    participant SEC as Suppression Expiration Checker
    participant SP as Scanner Plugins
    participant CP as Converter Plugins
    participant RP as Reporter Plugins

    ASH->>EM: Emit EXECUTION_START
    EM->>SEC: Notify EXECUTION_START
    SEC->>SEC: Check Suppression Expirations
    SEC-->>ASH: Log Expiration Warnings

    ASH->>EM: Emit CONVERSION_START
    EM->>CP: Notify CONVERSION_START

    CP->>CP: Convert Files
    CP-->>ASH: Return Converted Files

    ASH->>EM: Emit CONVERSION_COMPLETE

    ASH->>EM: Emit SCAN_START

        SP-->>ASH: Return Results

        SCL->>SCL: Process Completion

    RP->>RP: Generate Reports
    RP-->>ASH: Return Reports

    ASH->>EM: Emit REPORTING_COMPLETE

docs.title: Built-in Event Handlers
docs.text:
ASH includes built-in event handlers that respond to scan lifecycle events.

For detailed visual diagrams of the built-in event handler architecture and workflows, see Built-in Event Handler Diagrams.

docs.title: Event Handler Overview
docs.text: Handler Purpose Events Key Features Scan Completion Logger Enhanced scan progress logging SCAN_COMPLETE Remaining scanner tracking Suppression Expiration Checker Check for expiring suppressions and ignore paths EXECUTION_START Proactive expiration warnings

docs.title: Scan Completion Logger
docs.text:
Purpose: Provides enhanced logging when scanners complete, showing remaining scanner information.

Events: SCAN_COMPLETE

Module: automated_security_helper.plugin_modules.ash_builtin.event_handlers.scan_completion_logger

Example Output: 

INFO: Remaining scanners (2): semgrep, checkov
INFO: All scanners completed!

docs.title: Suppression Expiration Checker
docs.text:
Purpose: Checks for suppressions and ignore paths that are approaching their expiration date and warns users at the start of execution.

Events: EXECUTION_START

Module: automated_security_helper.plugin_modules.ash_builtin.event_handlers.suppression_expiration_checker

Key Features: - Warns about suppressions and ignore paths expiring within the next 30 days, including the entries of bandit excluded_paths, checkov skip_path and syft exclude - Lists, in one warning, the suppressions and ignore paths that have already expired (including any whose expiration date is today), since they no longer apply - Provides helpful guidance on updating suppressions - Skips the suppression check under --ignore-suppressions; ignore paths are still checked, because that flag turns off suppressions only and ignore paths still apply - Detailed logging with rule ID, file path, expiration date, and reason

Example Output: 

The following ignore paths and suppressions have expired and no longer apply:
  - Ignore path 'build/generated/**' expired on 2024-06-30. Reason: Generated until the build moves
Remove them, or move their expiration dates, in your ASH configuration file.
The following ignore paths will expire within 30 days:
  - Ignore path 'vendor/**' expires on 2024-07-20. Reason: Vendored until the upgrade
To update ignore path expiration dates, modify your ASH configuration file
The following suppressions will expire within 30 days:
  - Rule 'B101' for 'src/test.py' expires on 2024-07-15. Reason: Test file with intentional assert
To update suppression expiration dates, modify your ASH configuration file

docs.title: Enhanced Offline Mode Logging
docs.text:
The offline mode validation system has been enhanced with emoji-prefixed logging:

  • Semgrep offline mode: Found 150 rule files in cache
  • Semgrep is running in offline mode but no rule cache was found. Set $SEMGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR to a directory containing .yaml/.yml rule files.
  • Grype offline mode: Cache directory validated with 5 files
  • Grype offline mode: Database is 45 days old, past the 120h bound grype enforces online; consider updating

There is no fallback to the online p/ci ruleset when the cache is missing. An offline run that silently fetched the registry ruleset would be a different scan than the one that was requested, reported as the one that was requested. The scanner declines instead: it records the reason above, ash reports it as MISSING, and the run fails the completeness gate when --fail-on-incomplete-scanners is in effect.

docs.title: Custom Event Handlers
docs.text:
You can create custom event handlers:

from automated_security_helper.plugins.events import AshEventType
from automated_security_helper.plugins import ash_plugin_manager


def my_custom_callback(**kwargs):
    scanner = kwargs.get("scanner", "unknown")
    print(f"Scanner {scanner} completed!")
    return True


ash_plugin_manager.subscribe(AshEventType.SCAN_COMPLETE, my_custom_callback)

Where the handler is defined decides which scans notify it. A handler defined in your own program, outside ASH's plugin namespace, is notified in every scan that program runs. A handler defined in a plugin package is notified only in scans whose ash_plugin_modules name that package, and only when the package defines, imports or lists it (see Using Custom Plugin Packages).

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
1. Better Observability - Comprehensive visibility into scan execution
  2. Integration Capabilities - Easy integration with external systems
  3. Custom Automation - Trigger custom actions based on scan events
  4. Improved Debugging - Detailed event logging for troubleshooting

docs.title: Gitleaks scanner
docs.text:
gitleaks finds credentials (API keys, tokens, private keys) by matching its rule set against file contents. ASH runs it as gitleaks dir over the files in the scan target. It does not scan git history.

detect-secrets stays on by default and is unaffected; the two can run side by side. ASH does not deduplicate across scanners, so a secret both of them find is reported twice, once under each scanner's name and rule id; suppress it for each scanner, or enable only one.

docs.title: Enabling it
docs.text:
Gitleaks is a builtin scanner, enabled by default: a default scan runs it. scanners.gitleaks.enabled: false in the ASH config turns it off, and --scanners and --exclude-scanners select it as they select any scanner. If the tool is not installed, the scanner is reported MISSING and the scan exits 1 (the incomplete-scan gate), as for every builtin scanner; ash dependencies install and the container image provide it.

gitleaks is a native binary, so --python-only does not run it.

docs.title: Installing gitleaks
docs.text:
• Container image: included. The image installs the pinned release (currently v8.30.1) whether or not you enable the scanner.
  • Local mode: ash dependencies install downloads the pinned release asset from GitHub and checks it against the SHA256 recorded in automated_security_helper/utils/tool_downloads.py before installing it. A download that does not match is refused.
  • Nix mode: the flake supplies nixpkgs' gitleaks.
  • A gitleaks already on PATH is used as is. ASH is tested against the pinned version.

gitleaks makes no network calls while scanning, so it works offline and in air-gapped environments with no extra setup.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
scanners:
  gitleaks:
    enabled: true
    options:
      # A gitleaks TOML config; a relative path is taken from where it is set.
      config_file: null
      # A gitleaks JSON report whose findings gitleaks ignores (--baseline-path).
      baseline_path: null
      # Honor gitleaks:allow comments in the scanned tree. Off by default.
      honor_inline_ignores: false
      # Skip files larger than this many megabytes. Operator-only.
      max_target_megabytes: null
      # Seconds before the gitleaks process is killed. Inherited by every scanner.
      scan_timeout: 1800
      # This scanner's override of the global severity threshold. Every gitleaks
      # finding is CRITICAL, so any threshold still fails on them.
      severity_threshold: null

docs.title: Which gitleaks config is used
docs.text:
The scanned repository's own gitleaks configuration is not used. A .gitleaks.toml can replace gitleaks' rules or allowlist every path, and a .gitleaksignore drops findings by fingerprint, before ASH sees the report: what they hide is neither reported nor counted as suppressed. Tune findings with ASH suppressions, which are both.

  1. options.config_file, when the operator set it: from --config-overrides, or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory (one that is not repository-written). A path that does not exist fails the scan rather than falling back to gitleaks' default rules.
  2. Otherwise, if GITLEAKS_CONFIG or GITLEAKS_CONFIG_TOML is set in the environment, gitleaks resolves the config from it. Under --sandbox those variables are not passed in, and step 3 applies.
  3. Otherwise gitleaks' default rules, through a config ASH writes that extends them and adds nothing. It is passed as gitleaks --config, so gitleaks does not fall back to a .gitleaks.toml in the scanned tree. ASH writes it outside the scanned tree, with the empty directory it passes as gitleaks --gitleaks-ignore-path, and removes both when the scan ends.

config_file, baseline_path, max_target_megabytes or honor_inline_ignores set by an ASH config inside any git checkout or the scanned directory (such as .ash/.ash.yaml), or by an MCP client, is ignored with a warning, and a .gitleaks.toml or .ash/.gitleaks.toml in the tree is noted at INFO. The operator's files may be absolute paths or point outside the source directory. A relative config_file or baseline_path is taken from the directory of the ASH config file that sets it, or from the working directory for --config-overrides, not from the source directory (see Relative paths in the operator's settings). A file the operator names may also be inside the scanned tree, unless that path leads out of the tree through a symlink: the scanned repository decides what is there, so such a path stops the scanner with an error and gitleaks is not run.

gitleaks always reads .gitleaksignore at the root of the path it scans, whatever gitleaks --gitleaks-ignore-path says, and has no flag to turn that off. When the scan root has one, ASH copies the files it names into a directory of its own, at the same paths, runs gitleaks once more over the copies (there is no .gitleaksignore there), and reports the findings the first run dropped. That directory is outside the scanned tree, in a directory of the scanner run's own made with mode 0700, and under --sandbox gitleaks can read it and cannot write to it. ASH reads .gitleaksignore the way gitleaks does (a line ends at a newline only, surrounding whitespace is trimmed as Go trims it, and a backslash in a path is a slash), so it re-scans the files gitleaks matched. Files the first run does not read are not copied: files under .git or another directory gitleaks' allowlists skip, files reached through a symlink, and anything that is not a regular file. A failed re-run fails the scan, and the copies are deleted when it ends. The re-run copies at most 10,000 files and runs within one scan_timeout; when the file names more, the rest are not re-scanned, a warning gives their number, and the scan exits 1 as incomplete, because a finding the file hides in them would not be reported.

A .gitleaksignore at the scan root that is a symlink, a FIFO or another file that is not a regular file, or one with a second hard link, stops the scanner with an error before gitleaks runs: gitleaks would open whatever the name points to and copy lines of it into its log.

gitleaks' options are described by the JSON schema (automated_security_helper/schemas/AshConfig.json) and listed above.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text: gitleaks reports no severity of its own. ASH rates every gitleaks finding CRITICAL, in the summaries and in every report: the SARIF result has level: error and the finding carries CRITICAL as its own severity, which ash.flat.json and the CSV report read. A detect-secrets finding carries only level: error, so the summaries rate it CRITICAL too, while ash.flat.json and the CSV report read HIGH for it; the same credential found by both scanners can therefore read differently in those two reports. gitleaks has no per-rule confidence to grade on: each rule says "a credential of this kind is present".

docs.title: Secret values never reach ASH's output
docs.text:
ASH always runs gitleaks --redact=100, so gitleaks writes REDACTED in place of each secret in its report and its log. ASH also overwrites any report snippet that is not REDACTED before the result is stored, so the value cannot appear in ash_aggregated_results.json, the SARIF, or any other report.

gitleaks is a secrets scanner (tool type SECRETS), so a gitleaks finding is a secret finding: in ASH's reports the line it reports reads [masked: a secret finding reports this line] in every snippet, its own included (see "Secret values in reports" in the output formats page), and the Bedrock summary reporter counts gitleaks findings rather than sending them to the model. gitleaks' own report under scanners/gitleaks/ keeps its REDACTED.

gitleaks' log repeats each line of a .gitleaksignore it cannot parse. ASH cuts those lines short in the log it keeps (GitleaksScanner.stderr.log), and does not quote gitleaks' log in error messages; an error names the log file instead.

docs.title: Suppressing findings
docs.text:
Use ASH suppressions: they are recorded in the reports and counted. gitleaks' own mechanisms drop findings before ASH sees the report, so only these still apply:

  • A gitleaks:allow comment on the line with the secret, only when the operator sets options.honor_inline_ignores: true with --config-overrides or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory. By default ASH runs gitleaks --ignore-gitleaks-allow, so the comment hides nothing; set from a config inside a git checkout or the scanned directory, the option is ignored with a warning.
  • [[allowlists]] in an operator's config_file (paths, regexes, stopwords, per-rule).
  • An operator's baseline_path: a previous gitleaks JSON report whose findings are ignored.

The scanned repository's .gitleaks.toml and .gitleaksignore do not apply (see above).

ASH suppressions use the gitleaks rule id (for example github-pat, aws-access-token) and the path relative to the source directory:

global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - rule_id: github-pat
      path: tests/fixtures/settings.py
      line_start: 12
      line_end: 12
      reason: Fabricated token used by the test suite

Rule, path and line suppressions apply. A symbol suppression (the enclosing function or class) applies to a finding in a source language ASH can parse. Package-scoped suppressions do not apply: a gitleaks finding is about a file, not a dependency. global_settings.ignore_paths removes gitleaks findings under those paths, and findings inside ASH's own output directory are removed, except in the files ASH extracted from archives and notebooks, and in files the repository committed there. In a git checkout, a file git tracks in that directory is the repository's and keeps its findings; outside a checkout nothing tells the repository's files from ASH's, and every finding there is removed.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: ASH runs gitleaks --exit-code=2, because gitleaks otherwise exits 1 both when it finds leaks and when it fails. 0 (nothing found) and 2 (leaks found) are success; any other code, including 1 for an unreadable config or path, makes the scanner report an error and the scan exit 1.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Working tree only. Secrets that were committed and later removed are not reported; run gitleaks git separately if you need history.
  • gitleaks reads ASH's output directory when it sits inside the source tree (the default .ash/ash_output), because it has no option to skip a directory. ASH discards the findings there, except those in files the repository committed to that directory, but the files are still read. That directory holds the files ASH extracts from archives and notebooks; gitleaks scans those copies separately, so a secret in an archive is reported once, at its extracted path.
  • The SARIF semanticVersion that gitleaks 8.30.1 writes is wrong (v8.0.0), so ASH removes it; the real version comes from gitleaks --version.

sequenceDiagram

docs.text:
Purpose: Exports findings in comma-separated values format for spreadsheet analysis.

Configuration: 

reporters:

    enabled: true
    # The CSV reporter exposes no options. Suppressed findings are filtered by
    # global_settings.suppressions, not per reporter.

docs.text:

docs.title: Flat JSON Reporter
docs.text:
Purpose: Simplified JSON format with flattened structure for easy processing.

Configuration: 

reporters:
  flat-json:              # Note the hyphen; 'flatjson' is not a reporter name
    enabled: true
    options:
      include_metadata: true
      include_scanner_metrics: true
      include_summary_metrics: true

Output Structure: 

{
  "findings": [
    {
      "scanner": "bandit",
      "file": "src/app.py",
      "line": 42,
      "severity": "HIGH",
      "rule_id": "B602",
      "message": "subprocess call with shell=True",
      "suppressed": false
    }
  ]
}

The report also carries converter_refusals, always present: every input a converter did not read, as {"converter", "path", "member", "reason", "limit", "scan_incomplete", "unlisted_members"}; unlisted_members is set on the one record that counts an archive's member refusals past the first 20 of a reason. The list also holds every input a converter could not convert (its failed_inputs). scan_incomplete is true for those and for an archive refused for an extraction limit, which fail the completeness gate; see Inputs a converter does not read.

Use Cases: - Simple data processing scripts - Custom integrations - Lightweight parsing

docs.title: GitLab SAST Reporter
docs.text:
Purpose: Generates reports in GitLab Security Dashboard format for seamless CI/CD integration.

Configuration: 

reporters:
  gitlab-sast:            # Note the hyphen; 'gitlab_sast' is read the same, but the linter flags it
    enabled: true
    options:
      exclude_suppressed: false

Output Structure: - GitLab SAST report format - Vulnerability details with locations - Severity mapping to GitLab standards - Scanner metadata and timestamps

Use Cases: - GitLab CI/CD pipeline integration - GitLab Security Dashboard visualization - Compliance with GitLab security workflows

Integration Example: 

# .gitlab-ci.yml
security_scan:
  stage: test
  script:
    - ash . --reporters gitlab-sast
  artifacts:
    reports:
      sast: output/gl-sast-report.json

docs.title: GitHub GHAS Reporter
docs.text:
Purpose: Produces a streamlined SARIF report optimized for GitHub Advanced Security (Code Scanning).

The standard SARIF reporter outputs a faithful representation of scanner results, but GitHub Code Scanning requires specific fields to display severity correctly. Without properties["security-severity"] on rules, GitHub falls back to showing raw SARIF levels ("Error"/"Warning"/"Note") instead of security severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low).

This reporter solves that by:

  1. Ensuring every rule has properties["security-severity"]: the scanner's own value when it provides one, else the most severe of the rule's results that the file contains, graded the way the summary and the exit code grade them (properties.issue_severity first, else the SARIF level), else the rule's defaultConfiguration.level, else 6.0 (Medium). A suppressed finding left out of the file does not raise its rule's score; a rule whose findings are all left out stays in the list with that default score. A rule that a result in the file names (as ruleId or rule.id) but the scanner did not declare gets an entry too, scored from its results
  2. Flattening rules from tool.extensions[] into tool.driver.rules for reliable rule resolution
  3. Stripping verbose fields to significantly reduce file size (~80% smaller than the standard SARIF)
  4. Excluding suppressed findings by default (GitHub has its own dismissal workflow)

Configuration: 

reporters:
  github-ghas:
    enabled: true
    options:
      exclude_suppressed: true  # Exclude ASH-suppressed findings (default: true)

Output File: reports/ash.ghas.sarif

Severity Mapping (when security-severity is not provided by the scanner), from the finding's ASH severity: issue_severity when the scanner declares one, else the SARIF level (error CRITICAL, warning MEDIUM, note LOW, none INFO; a missing level is warning):

ASH severity security-severity GitHub displays as CRITICAL 9.5 Critical HIGH 8.0 High MEDIUM 6.0 Medium LOW 3.0 Low INFO 1.0 Low

When a scanner already provides security-severity (e.g., Grype with CVSS scores), that value is preserved as-is.

Use Cases: - GitHub Advanced Security Code Scanning - GitHub Security tab integration - Pull request security annotations - Repository security overview

Integration Example: 

# .github/workflows/ash-security-scan.yml
name: ASH Security Scan

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]

permissions:
  contents: read
  security-events: write

jobs:
  scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'
      - name: Install ASH
        run: pip install git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git
      - name: Run ASH scan
        run: ash --mode local --no-fail-on-findings
      - name: Upload GHAS SARIF
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        if: always()
        with:
          sarif_file: .ash/ash_output/reports/ash.ghas.sarif
          category: ash-security-scan
