  sarif:
    enabled: true
    # The SARIF reporter exposes no options.

Key Features: - One run with ASH as tool.driver and each scanner as a tool.extensions[] entry with its own name, version and rules; each result's rule.toolComponent and rule.index point at its rule there (see Output formats) - IDE integration (VS Code, IntelliJ) - GitHub Security tab integration - Rich metadata and locations - Tool interoperability - Converter inputs that were not scanned, as an extra invocation per converter whose toolExecutionNotifications carry descriptor id ASH-CONVERTER-INPUT-NOT-SCANNED, located at the input: level error for an archive refused for an extraction limit, warning for every other refusal

Use Cases: - IDE security annotations - GitHub Advanced Security - Security tool chains - Compliance reporting

docs.title: SPDX Reporter
docs.text:
Purpose: Software Package Data Exchange format for license compliance.

Configuration: 

reporters:
  spdx:
    enabled: true
    # The SPDX reporter exposes no options.

Key Features: - SPDX 2.3 JSON, built from the same CycloneDX SBOM as the cyclonedx reporter - Declared licenses, when the SBOM gives an SPDX license ID or expression - Package versions and purl external references - DESCRIBES and CONTAINS relationships from the scanned project to each package

Package-level only: there are no file entries, and download location, concluded license and copyright text are NOASSERTION.

Use Cases: - License compliance - Open source governance - Legal review processes - Supply chain transparency

docs.title: Text Reporter
docs.text:
Purpose: Simple plain text output for console display and logging.

Configuration: 

reporters:
  text:
    enabled: true
    options:
      include_summary: true
      include_findings_table: true
      include_detailed_findings: true
      max_detailed_findings: 50
      top_hotspots_limit: 10

Key Features: - Console-friendly output - Color-coded severity levels - Compact summary format - Configurable verbosity

Use Cases: - Command-line usage - Log file output - Simple CI/CD notifications - Quick security overviews

docs.title: YAML Reporter
docs.text:
Purpose: Structured YAML output for configuration-style data representation.

Configuration: 

reporters:
  yaml:
    enabled: true
    # The YAML reporter exposes no options.

Key Features: - Human-readable structure - Configuration file compatibility - Hierarchical data organization - Comment support

Use Cases: - Configuration-based workflows - Infrastructure as Code integration - Human-readable data exchange - Custom processing pipelines

docs.title: GitLab CycloneDX Reporter
docs.text:
Purpose: Emits the CycloneDX SBOM in the artifact shape GitLab's dependency scanning consumes.

Distinct from the plain CycloneDX Reporter: the payload is the same SBOM, but the file is named for GitLab's dependency_scanning report artifact so a pipeline can hand it straight to GitLab.

Configuration: 

reporters:
  gitlab-cyclonedx:       # Note the hyphens
    enabled: true

Output file: reports/ash.gl-dependency-scanning-report.cdx.json

Use Cases: - GitLab dependency scanning - GitLab Security Dashboard dependency view

Integration Example: 

# .gitlab-ci.yml
security_scan:
  stage: test
  script:
    - ash . --reporters gitlab-cyclonedx
  artifacts:
    reports:
      dependency_scanning: .ash/ash_output/reports/ash.gl-dependency-scanning-report.cdx.json

docs.title: Unused Suppressions Reporter
docs.text:
Purpose: Lists the suppression rules in your configuration that matched no finding during the scan.

A suppression that stops matching is invisible without this report: the finding it used to hide may have been fixed, or the rule may have been written against a path or rule ID that no longer exists. Either way the rule is now dead configuration, and a dead suppression is a rule nobody is reviewing.

This reporter is enabled by default, so every scan writes it.

Configuration: 

reporters:
  unused-suppressions:    # Note the hyphen
    enabled: true

Output file: reports/ash.unused-suppressions.json

Use Cases: - Suppression hygiene reviews - Pruning suppressions after a fix lands - Catching suppressions written against a stale rule ID or path

docs.title: Common Combinations
docs.text:
# Development workflow
ash --reporters text,html,sarif

# CI/CD pipeline
ash --reporters sarif,junitxml,gitlab-sast

# Compliance reporting
ash --reporters spdx,cyclonedx,ocsf

# Executive reporting
ash --reporters html,markdown,csv

docs.title: Configuration Example
docs.text:
reporters:
  # Quick feedback
  text:
    enabled: true
    options:
      include_summary: true
      include_detailed_findings: false

  # Detailed analysis
  html:
    enabled: true

  # CI/CD integration
  sarif:
    enabled: true

  # Data processing
  csv:
    enabled: true

docs.title: Reporter Selection
docs.text:
Choose reporters based on your audience and use case:

# For developers
reporters: [text, sarif, html]

# For security teams
reporters: [html, csv, ocsf]

# For compliance
reporters: [spdx, cyclonedx, markdown]

# For CI/CD
reporters: [sarif, junitxml, gitlab-sast]

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
# Optimize for speed. The HTML and CSV reporters expose no options, so the lever
# is which reporters run at all rather than how each one behaves.
reporters:
  html:
    enabled: false          # Skip the largest artifact

  csv:
    enabled: true

docs.title: Output Organization
docs.text:
# Organize outputs by type
ash --output-dir results/ \
  --reporters sarif,html,csv \
  --output-format "{reporter}/{timestamp}"

docs.title: GitHub Actions
docs.text:
- name: Security Scan
  run: ash --reporters sarif,text

- name: Upload SARIF to GitHub Advanced Security
  uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
  if: always()
  with:
    sarif_file: .ash/ash_output/reports/ash.ghas.sarif
    category: ash-security-scan

docs.title: GitLab CI
docs.text:
security_scan:
  script:
    - ash --reporters gitlab-sast,text
  artifacts:
    reports:
      sast: results/gitlab-sast/results.json

docs.title: Jenkins

pipeline {
  stages {
    stage('Security Scan') {
      steps {
        sh 'ash --reporters junitxml,html'
        publishTestResults testResultsPattern: 'results/junitxml/*.xml'

docs.title: Scanner Execution Flow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the execution flow of the built-in scanners:

sequenceDiagram
    participant ASH as ASH Core
    participant PM as Plugin Manager
    participant SR as Scanner Registry
    participant SC as Scanner
    participant FS as File System
    participant ES as Event System

    ASH->>PM: Load Scanners
    PM->>SR: Get Registered Scanners
    SR-->>PM: Return Scanner List

    loop For Each Scanner
        ASH->>ES: Emit ScannerStarted Event
        ASH->>SC: Validate Scanner
        SC-->>ASH: Return Validation Status

        alt Scanner Valid
            ASH->>SC: scan(target, target_type)
            SC->>FS: Read Target Files
            FS-->>SC: Return File Contents

            SC->>SC: Process Files
            Note over SC: Run Security Analysis

            SC->>FS: Write SARIF Report
            SC-->>ASH: Return ScanResultsContainer

            ASH->>ES: Emit ScannerCompleted Event
        else Scanner Invalid
            ASH->>ES: Emit ScannerError Event
        end
    end

    ASH->>ES: Emit ScanCompleted Event

docs.title: Built-in Security Scanners
docs.text:
ASH includes 16 built-in security scanners that analyze different aspects of your code and infrastructure. Each scanner specializes in specific security domains and file types.

For detailed visual diagrams of the built-in scanner architecture and workflows, see Built-in Scanner Diagrams.

docs.title: Scanner Overview
docs.text: Scanner Purpose Languages/Formats Key Features Bandit Python security linter Python AST-based analysis, security-focused rules CDK-Nag AWS CDK security checker TypeScript, Python, Java CDK-specific security rules CFN-Nag CloudFormation security YAML, JSON AWS resource security validation Checkov Infrastructure-as-Code scanner Terraform, CF, K8s, Docker Policy-as-code framework Detect-Secrets Secret detection All text files Entropy-based secret detection Grype Container vulnerability scanner Container images, SBOMs CVE database matching NPM Audit Node.js dependency scanner package.json, package-lock.json NPM vulnerability database Opengrep Code pattern matching Multiple languages Custom rule engine Semgrep Static analysis scanner 30+ languages Community and custom rules Syft SBOM generator Container images, filesystems Software inventory generation actionlint GitHub Actions linter Workflow files Script injection, expression types cfn-lint CloudFormation validation YAML, JSON Resource schema checks cfn-guard CloudFormation policy YAML, JSON AWS Guard Rules Registry rules Gitleaks Secret detection All text files Rule-based secret detection, redacted Trivy Dependency vulnerabilities Manifests and lockfiles trivy fs, vulnerability scanner only zizmor GitHub Actions static analysis Workflows, composite actions Template injection, credential exposure

docs.title: Bandit
docs.text:
Purpose: Identifies common security issues in Python code through AST analysis.

Configuration: 

scanners:
  bandit:
    enabled: true
    options:
      severity_threshold: "MEDIUM"   # ALL, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL -- uppercase
      confidence_level: "high"       # all, low, medium, high -- lowercase
      ignore_nosec: false
      config_file: ".bandit"         # Selects individual tests; see below

Individual bandit test IDs are selected in a bandit configuration file, not through ASH options. severity_threshold belongs under options, alongside the rest.

ASH passes bandit an --exclude list for each scan. Besides excluded_paths and the virtual-environment and node_modules directories, it holds ASH's output directory when that is inside the scanned directory, so bandit does not read the converters' output twice, and a bandit glob for each of the scan's ignore_paths that is a file path (src/app.py), of the form dir/, dir/** or **/dir/**, or like src/*.py. Such a glob makes bandit skip only files the ignore path covers, though it can skip fewer: bandit matches case-sensitively and ASH does not. A pattern with a character class ([...]) is never passed to bandit: ASH lower-cases the pattern and the path before matching, so src/[!A-Z].py does not cover src/b.py, and bandit would skip it. bandit also skips any file whose path contains an entry as plain text, so an entry is not passed when a file path under the scanned directory contains it, which takes a *, ? or [ in a file or directory name (docs/*.md/app.py for the entry of docs/*.md). bandit also turns an entry that names an existing directory into <entry>/*, so an entry is not passed when it names one (an empty directory, or a symlink, literally named docs/*.md). Every ignore path is still applied when the results are processed, as for every scanner, so the findings it covers are dropped either way.

An excluded_paths entry is applied by bandit alone, and names a path anywhere below the scanned directory: app.py skips every file named app.py, vendor the files of every vendor directory (and a file named vendor), tests/* what the glob matches, and vendor/ or **/vendor/** only the files of vendor directories. bandit matches these case-sensitively. An entry with a ,, or with a . or empty path component, has no bandit form; the scanner logs a warning and skips nothing for it.

Key Checks: - SQL injection vulnerabilities - Hardcoded passwords and secrets - Use of insecure functions - Shell injection risks - Cryptographic weaknesses

Dependencies: bandit Python package

docs.title: CDK-Nag
docs.text:
Purpose: Validates AWS CDK constructs against security best practices.

Configuration: 

scanners:
  cdk_nag:
    enabled: true
    options:
      nag_packs:                       # Which cdk-nag packs to apply
        AwsSolutionsChecks: true
        HIPAASecurityChecks: false
      include_compliant_checks: false  # Also report compliant resources (INFO)

To skip a cdk-nag rule, suppress it like any other finding (rule_id: AwsSolutions-S1 under global_settings.suppressions).

Key Checks: - S3 bucket security configurations - IAM policy validation - VPC and networking security - Encryption requirements - Logging and monitoring setup

Dependencies: the aws-cdk-lib, cdk-nag and constructs Python packages in ASH's environment (ash dependencies install --tool cdk-nag adds them), and Node.js with node on PATH, which ASH does not install. The AWS CDK CLI is not needed. When either is missing the scanner is MISSING, and the reason it records says which: the unavailable packages, or "Node.js not found on PATH".

docs.title: CFN-Nag
docs.text:
Purpose: Scans CloudFormation templates for security anti-patterns.

Configuration: 

scanners:
  cfn_nag:
    enabled: true
    options:
      severity_threshold: "MEDIUM"

cfn-nag has no options of its own beyond those every scanner takes; suppress a rule with global_settings.suppressions.

Key Checks: - IAM policies with excessive permissions - Security groups with open access - Unencrypted resources - Missing logging configurations - Insecure resource configurations

Dependencies: cfn-nag Ruby gem

Template copy: cfn-nag is given a copy of each template, staged in its results directory as template.json, template.yaml or template.yml by the template's extension, and as template.yaml for any other extension. The cfn_nag_scan command line is therefore the same whatever the template is called, including on Windows, where cfn_nag_scan is a batch file. Findings name the original template.

docs.title: Checkov
docs.text:
Purpose: Comprehensive infrastructure-as-code security scanner with policy-as-code framework.

Configuration: 

scanners:
  checkov:
    enabled: true
    options:
      frameworks: ["terraform", "cloudformation", "kubernetes"]
      skip_frameworks: ["secrets"]
      skip_path:                         # Regular expressions, each with a reason
        - path: "tests/fixtures/.*"
          reason: "Vulnerable-by-design fixtures"
      config_file: ".checkov.yaml"       # Selects individual checks; see below
      additional_formats: ["cyclonedx_json"]

Individual check IDs and custom check directories are configured in a checkov configuration file, which config_file points at.

ASH adds a --skip-path for each of its own output directories inside the scanned directory, unless that directory's path holds a parenthesis, which checkov's terraform module finder cannot take, or ASH runs on Windows; then checkov reads the directory, ASH logs a warning naming it, and the findings checkov reports there are dropped.

Key Checks: - Cloud resource misconfigurations - Kubernetes security policies - Docker security best practices - Terraform module validation - Custom policy enforcement

Dependencies: Managed via uv tool run (automatically downloaded when needed)

docs.title: Detect-Secrets
docs.text:
Purpose: Prevents secrets from being committed to version control through entropy-based detection.

Configuration: 

scanners:
  detect_secrets:
    enabled: true
    options:
      baseline_file: ".secrets.baseline"  # detect-secrets baseline, relative to the source
      skip_generated_lockfiles: true      # Skip package-lock.json, yarn.lock and similar
      max_worker_output_mib: 256          # Most of the scan's findings output read back, in MiB

A finding is about 300 bytes of output, so the default of 256 MiB holds about 900,000 findings. Reading the output back costs about three times its size in memory. A scan whose output is larger fails, records no findings, and names max_worker_output_mib in its error.

max_worker_output_mib is at most 4096, and only the operator sets it: from --config-overrides or a config file outside the scanned tree. Whatever a config file inside the tree writes for it, a value past 4096 included, is ignored, with a warning, because the repository being scanned wrote that file. When such a file is part of the configuration, the limit is the operator's whether or not that file names it: an override's, the value a config file outside the tree gives it, or else the operator's base configuration's (the file ASH_CONFIG names, a workspace's default config, or 256), so a lower limit the operator set holds for a repository that says nothing about it.

Which detectors run, and which files and lines they skip, are set in the detect-secrets baseline (baseline_file) or in scan_settings, in detect-secrets' own format.

Key Checks: - High entropy strings (potential secrets) - AWS access keys and secret keys - Private keys and certificates - Database connection strings - API keys and tokens

Baseline: ASH reads a detect-secrets baseline for the plugins, filters and accepted findings to use. It takes baseline_file when set, else .ash/.secrets.baseline, else .secrets.baseline, each relative to the source directory, so the same tree gives the same result whichever directory ASH runs from. See Detect-Secrets in the configuration guide.

Secret verification: detect-secrets can send a candidate secret to the service that issued it. ASH does that only when the operator's own configuration turns it on, never from a baseline or config file the scanned repository holds, and never offline. See Secret verification.

Dependencies: detect-secrets Python package

docs.title: Grype
docs.text:
Purpose: Vulnerability scanner for container images and filesystems using CVE databases.

Configuration: 

scanners:
  grype:
    enabled: true
    options:
      severity_threshold: "MEDIUM"   # ALL, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL
      offline: false                 # Skip database updates
      config_file: null              # Explicit grype config, relative to the config file that sets it

Key Checks: - Known CVEs in installed packages - Operating system vulnerabilities - Language-specific package vulnerabilities - Container base image issues

Dependencies: grype binary

docs.title: NPM Audit
docs.text:
Purpose: Identifies known vulnerabilities in Node.js dependencies.

Configuration: 

scanners:
  npm_audit:
    enabled: true
    options:
      severity_threshold: "HIGH"  # ALL, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL

npm-audit has no options of its own beyond those every scanner takes.

Key Checks: - Known vulnerabilities in npm packages - Dependency tree analysis - Severity-based filtering - Fix recommendations

In offline mode npm-audit runs no audit, since npm, pnpm and yarn audit only against the registry's advisory service. Each lockfile is listed as not scanned in the results and the summaries, and with a lockfile to audit npm-audit is MISSING, so the scan fails under the default completeness gate. --exclude-scanners npm-audit leaves it out of an offline scan. See What offline mode turns off.

npm-audit runs npm, pnpm and yarn without the scanned repository's settings files: its .npmrc, the settings in pnpm-workspace.yaml, .yarnrc and .yarnrc.yml, including a yarn-path or yarnPath, which would run a file from the repository. Your own settings still apply: ~/.npmrc, the global npmrc, ~/.yarnrc and ~/.yarnrc.yml, so a private registry and its credentials work as before. npm and pnpm run from a private copy of each package's package.json and lockfile; yarn runs from a copy, outside the scanned tree, of its lockfile and every package.json below it, with YARN_IGNORE_PATH=1. Under --sandbox the tool's home is private, so only environment variables reach it, and yarn runs in the package directory reading no settings file (--no-default-rc, or YARN_RC_FILENAME for yarn 2 and later).

A pnpm.auditConfig in the repository's package.json (ignoreCves, ignoreGhsas) hides those advisories, as a suppression in the repository's ASH configuration would; --ignore-suppressions removes it from the copy pnpm audits.

npm, pnpm and yarn follow links. So every file npm-audit hands one of them (the package's package.json, the lockfiles it reads, npm-shrinkwrap.json included, and for yarn every workspace package.json below the package) has to resolve inside the scanned tree and be a regular file. A package with a file that is a link out of the tree, or that sits in a linked directory pointing out of it, is not audited: the file is listed as not scanned, with the reason "link leaves the scanned tree", and the scan fails, as for any lockfile left unaudited. A link to a file elsewhere in the scanned tree (another project of the workspace, in workspace mode) is followed.

Dependencies: Node.js, npm

docs.title: Opengrep
docs.text:
Purpose: Open source fork of Semgrep. Static analysis with extensive rule library covering security, correctness, and performance.

Configuration: 

scanners:
  opengrep:
    enabled: true
    options:
      config: "p/ci"        # Ruleset, directory of YAML rules, or URL
      exclude_rule: []      # Rule IDs to skip
      severity: []          # Report only rules of these severities
      scan_timeout: 1800    # Seconds before the invocation is killed
      version: "v1.30.2"    # OpenGrep version to use
      sha256: {}            # Required for any other version: digest per platform

ASH pins OpenGrep v1.30.2 and verifies its SHA256 before installing it. To use another version, supply the release asset's digest for each platform you install on, for example sha256: {"linux/amd64": "<64 hex characters>"}. GitHub lists a digest for every release asset, or run sha256sum on the downloaded asset. A platform with no digest is refused rather than installed unverified.

Key Checks: - Custom security patterns - Code quality issues - Best practice violations - Language-specific anti-patterns

Dependencies: opengrep binary

docs.title: Semgrep
docs.text:
Purpose: Static analysis with extensive rule library covering security, correctness, and performance.

Configuration: 

scanners:
  semgrep:
    enabled: true
    options:
      config: "p/ci"        # p/ci, p/security, p/owasp-top-10, a directory, or a URL
      scan_timeout: 1800    # Seconds before the invocation is killed
      exclude: ["test/", "*.min.js"]
      exclude_rule: []      # Rule IDs to skip

Key Checks: - OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities - Language-specific security issues - Code quality and maintainability - Custom organizational rules

Dependencies: Managed via uv tool run (automatically downloaded when needed)

docs.title: Syft
docs.text:
Purpose: Generates Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for dependency tracking and compliance.

Configuration: 

scanners:
  syft:
    enabled: true
    options:
      additional_outputs: ["syft-table"]   # Extra output formats beyond CycloneDX
      exclude: []                          # Paths to skip, as globs starting ./, */ or **/
      offline: false                       # Skip update checks

syft runs from outside the scanned tree and is not given a .syft.yaml or config_file from it, online or offline, because such a file can turn on remote license and package lookups. A config_file outside the tree is still used.

Key Features: - Package discovery across multiple ecosystems - SBOM generation in standard formats - Container and filesystem analysis - License identification

Dependencies: syft binary

docs.title: actionlint
docs.text:
Purpose: Lints GitHub Actions workflow files (.github/workflows): script injection from untrusted event data, expression types, hard-coded container credentials, always-true if: conditions.

Dependencies: actionlint binary (pinned; ash dependencies install and the container image provide it). See actionlint.

docs.title: cfn-lint and cfn-guard
docs.text:
Purpose: cfn-lint validates CloudFormation templates against the resource schemas; cfn-guard evaluates them against the AWS Guard Rules Registry (default rule set wa-Security-Pillar, every violation HIGH). Both read the templates cfn-nag reads.

Dependencies: cfn-lint (uv tool) and the cfn-guard binary with the Guard Rules Registry bundle (pinned). See cfn-lint and cfn-guard.

docs.title: Gitleaks
docs.text:
Purpose: Finds credentials in the working tree's files with gitleaks dir (no git history), beside detect-secrets. Findings are CRITICAL and values are redacted.

Dependencies: gitleaks binary (pinned). See Gitleaks.

docs.title: Trivy
docs.text:
Purpose: trivy fs over each target, the vulnerability scanner only by default, held to the trivy database's 24h bound. It reads no trivy configuration from the scanned repository unless configured.

Dependencies: trivy binary (pinned) and its vulnerability database (downloaded online; offline it must already be in the cache). See Trivy filesystem scanner.

docs.title: zizmor
docs.text:
Purpose: Static analysis of GitHub Actions workflows and composite actions, run with --offline; GitHub tokens are withheld unless the operator sets options.online_audits (--config-overrides or a config outside every git checkout and the scanned directory).

Dependencies: zizmor (uv tool). See zizmor.

docs.title: Scanner Selection
docs.text:
Choose scanners based on your technology stack:

# Python projects
ash --scanners bandit,detect-secrets,semgrep

# Infrastructure projects
ash --scanners checkov,cfn-nag,cdk-nag

# Container projects
ash --scanners grype,syft,checkov

# Node.js projects
ash --scanners npm-audit,detect-secrets,semgrep

docs.title: Performance Optimization
docs.text:
# Optimize for speed
scanners:
  semgrep:
    options:
      scan_timeout: 60      # Give up quickly rather than waiting the 1800s default
      config: "p/ci"        # A narrower ruleset than a full audit pack

  grype:
    options:
      offline: true         # Skip the database update round trip

docs.title: CI/CD Integration
docs.text:
# Different thresholds for different environments
scanners:
  bandit:
    options:
      severity_threshold: "LOW"    # Strict for production

  checkov:
    options:
      severity_threshold: "MEDIUM" # Balanced for staging

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
Scanner not found: 

# Check dependencies
ash dependencies --check --scanner bandit

# Install missing tools
pip install bandit semgrep detect-secrets

Performance issues: 

# Run with fewer concurrent scanners
ash --max-workers 2

# Exclude resource-intensive scanners
ash --exclude-scanners grype,syft

False positives: 

# Suppress specific findings
global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - rule_id: "B101"
      path: "tests/**"
      reason: "assert_used is expected in tests"

ASH suppresses findings through global_settings.suppressions, which applies to every scanner uniformly. Skipping a bandit test ID instead requires a bandit configuration file referenced by options.config_file; there is no skips option.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Reporter Configuration: Configure output formats
  • Suppressions Guide: Manage false positives
  • Custom Rules: Create organization-specific rules

docs.title: Trivy filesystem scanner (trivy)
docs.text: trivy matches the packages in your dependency manifests and lockfiles against its vulnerability database. ASH runs it as trivy fs over each scan target.

docs.title: Enabling it
docs.text:
The trivy scanner is a builtin scanner, enabled by default: a default scan runs it. scanners.trivy.enabled: false in the ASH config turns it off, and --scanners and --exclude-scanners select it as they select any scanner. If the tool is not installed, the scanner is reported MISSING and the scan exits 1 (the incomplete-scan gate), as for every builtin scanner; ash dependencies install and the container image provide it.

trivy is a native binary, so --python-only does not run it.

docs.title: Installing trivy
docs.text:
• Container image: included. The image installs the pinned release (currently v0.75.0).
  • Local mode: ash dependencies install downloads the pinned release asset from GitHub and checks it against the SHA256 recorded in automated_security_helper/utils/tool_downloads.py before installing it. trivy publishes no Windows arm64 asset, so there it has to be installed another way.
  • Nix mode: the flake supplies nixpkgs' trivy, and the nix shell keeps its vulnerability database in TRIVY_CACHE_DIR (default ~/.cache/ash/trivy), updating it on every entry; trivy returns at once when the database is current. Nix mode scans offline, so when the shell had no network and nothing is cached, trivy is reported MISSING with the reason; see Offline and air-gapped use.
  • A trivy already on PATH is used as is. ASH is tested against the pinned version.

docs.title: What it scans by default, and why
docs.text:
trivy has four scanners. This scanner runs one of them unless you, as the operator, ask for more:

trivy scanner By default Why vuln on Known vulnerabilities in dependencies, from trivy's own database. grype answers the same question from a different database; a second database is the reason to enable trivy. ASH does not deduplicate across scanners, so a vulnerability both find is reported by each, trivy usually under the CVE id and grype under the GHSA id, and one suppression by rule_id does not cover both. secret off detect-secrets runs by default. Both would report the same credential under different rule ids, and a suppression for one does not cover the other. misconfig off checkov, cfn-nag and cdk-nag cover IaC by default. license off License findings are a compliance question and depend on a license policy ASH does not hold. 
scanners:
  trivy:
    enabled: true
    options:
      # Any of vuln, secret, misconfig, license. At least one. Honored only from
      # the operator (--config-overrides or a config file outside every git
      # checkout and the scanned directory); set by a config inside one, it is
      # ignored with a warning.
      scanners: ["vuln"]
      # Report only vulnerabilities with a fixed version. Off: an unfixed
      # vulnerability is still a vulnerability. ASH logs a warning when it is on.
      ignore_unfixed: false
      # Look for licenses in source headers too. Only used with `license`.
      license_full: false
      # Only the operator sets it to false (--config-overrides or a config file
      # outside every git checkout and the scanned directory); any config may set
      # it to true. Offline, trivy sends nothing whatever this says.
      disable_telemetry: true
      # A trivy.yaml (from the operator), a .trivyignore and a trivy-secret.yaml,
      # each outside the scanned tree. Unset, the ones in the scanned repository
      # are NOT read; see below.
      config_file: null
      ignore_file: null
      secret_config_file: null
      # false follows ASH (--offline / ASH_OFFLINE); true forces trivy offline.
      offline: false
      # Gates the verdict, as for every scanner. Findings below it are still
      # reported. ASH does not pass it as trivy --severity.
      severity_threshold: null
      # Seconds before the trivy process is killed; also passed as trivy --timeout.
      # null leaves both unbounded: ASH passes trivy --timeout=2562047h (about 292
      # years), since it reads 0s as a deadline already passed. Its default is 5m.
      scan_timeout: 1800

docs.title: trivy configuration in the scanned repository
docs.text:
trivy reads trivy.yaml, .trivyignore and, for the secret scanner, trivy-secret.yaml from its working directory, which is the repository being scanned. Any of them can remove findings without the report saying so: a severity: [CRITICAL] or scan.skip-files entry in trivy.yaml removes every lower-rated or skipped finding, an ignore-policy it names (a Rego file) drops whatever the policy matches, each .trivyignore line removes an advisory, and trivy-secret.yaml can disable secret rules. A trivy.yaml can also point trivy at a directory of WASM modules (module.dir) and enable them, which runs them during the scan, and turn on a VEX repository download or client/server mode, which reach the network. So the builtin scanner passes trivy --config, trivy --ignorefile and trivy --secret-config pointing at files that set nothing (the empty config ASH ships, and an empty ignore file and secret config ASH writes outside the scanned tree), and a repository's own files are not read. It also passes trivy --module-dir naming an empty directory ASH makes outside the scanned tree for each run, so trivy loads no WASM module, from ~/.trivy/modules or a config's module.dir; unlike trivy-repo, the builtin scanner has no module_dir option. trivy reads no other file from a default location: trivy --ignore-policy has no default.

To use your own:

  • config_file: set it as the operator, through --config-overrides or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory (one that is not repository-written), for a file outside the scanned tree. Set by an ASH config inside a git checkout or the scanned directory, or naming a file inside the tree, it is ignored with a warning, and an MCP client cannot set it at all: /scanners/trivy/** is denied to every client, as for each scanner that can send data off the host. So is a path inside the tree that leads out of it through a symbolic link there: the link chose the file, not the operator. A relative path is taken from the directory of the ASH config file that sets it, or from the working directory for --config-overrides, not from the source directory (see Relative paths in the operator's settings). Unset or ignored, trivy gets TRIVY_CONFIG from the environment, for a file outside the scanned tree (a relative path in it is taken from the working directory ASH runs in, not from the source directory), and otherwise ASH's empty config.
  • ignore_file and secret_config_file: under the same rule as config_file, a relative path included. Otherwise TRIVY_IGNOREFILE and TRIVY_SECRET_CONFIG from the environment, for a file outside the scanned tree; a relative path in either is taken from the working directory ASH runs in. A file inside the tree is ignored with a warning, and trivy gets ASH's empty one, which ASH writes outside the scanned tree and removes when the scan ends. trivy-repo takes all three the same way.
ash scan --config-overrides 'scanners.trivy.options.ignore_file=/etc/ash/trivyignore'

A configured file that does not exist fails the scan rather than running without it.

ASH always passes trivy --exit-code=0, which outranks TRIVY_EXIT_CODE and an exit-code set in your config_file. trivy then exits nonzero only when it fails, and its report is read whatever it found. trivy-repo gets the same flag.

To accept a finding, prefer an ASH suppression, which is recorded in the reports and counted. The community trivy-repo plugin passes its own config file, modules directory, ignore file and secret config the same way; see its config_file, module_dir, ignore_file and secret_config_file options.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Each finding is reported at trivy's own severity for it (CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW), not at a band of its CVSS score, so a finding trivy rates HIGH is reported HIGH whatever its score. A finding trivy rates UNKNOWN falls back to ASH's usual SARIF mapping: the rule's CVSS score (security-severity), then the SARIF level.

severity_threshold works as for every other scanner: ASH applies it after the scan, to that severity, so a finding below it is still reported and does not fail the scan. ASH does not pass it as trivy --severity, which would drop those findings before ASH saw them.

The severity is read per finding, from the Severity: line trivy writes in each result's message, not from the result's SARIF rule. trivy writes one rule per advisory, and one advisory can be rated differently for two packages in the same scan (Debian, for example, rates some binutils advisories CRITICAL for binutils and LOW for gdb); the rule carries only one of those ratings.

docs.title: Suppressions
docs.text:
ASH suppressions apply as for any scanner:

  • rule_id is the advisory id (CVE-2021-23337, GHSA-...), or the check id (DS-0002) for misconfiguration findings.
  • path and line_start/line_end match the manifest and the line trivy reports for the package.
  • package_name, package_version and package_path match one package copy. For npm lockfiles, a result covering two installed copies of the same version is split into one result per copy, so a suppression can cover one copy and not the other.

Symbol-scoped suppressions (function or class) do not apply: a dependency finding points at a manifest entry, not at code.

docs.title: Vulnerability database and staleness
docs.text:
The database is declared as trivy-db in automated_security_helper/utils/content_databases.py, with a 24h bound measured from its UpdatedAt, which is trivy's own rule for its published database. After the scan, ASH reads UpdatedAt from trivy version --format json and fails the scan when the database is older than that (content_db_staleness: warn or --allow-stale-content-db turns the failure into a warning carried in every report). This is the same check grype's database gets. In an image built with OFFLINE=YES the stale database warns instead of failing; see Offline and air-gapped use.

  • Online, ASH updates the database once per scan before trivy and trivy-repo run (trivy image --download-db-only, outside the scanner sandbox and under a lock in trivy's cache, so the two never write it at the same time), and fails the scan if it cannot download one. The update runs from a directory outside the scanned tree with an explicit trivy --config: your config file when the scan uses one (config_file, or TRIVY_CONFIG), so a database mirror it names applies, and otherwise the empty one ASH ships. Both scanners then run with trivy --skip-db-update --skip-java-db-update, trivy --skip-check-update when misconfig is on, and trivy --cache-dir naming the cache the update wrote, so the scan only reads the cache. fs and repository scans never read the Java database.
  • If you turn trivy's own update off, with TRIVY_SKIP_DB_UPDATE=true or db.skip-update: true in your config file, ASH does not run its update either: trivy refuses to download a database under that setting, and you set it to keep trivy off the database registry, for example in CI that restores a cached database. ASH logs a warning naming the setting, and trivy and trivy-repo read the database already in the cache. The post-scan check still holds it to the 24h bound, so a cache you do not keep current fails the scan (or warns, under content_db_staleness: warn).
  • Offline, ASH passes trivy --skip-db-update --skip-java-db-update --skip-check-update, so trivy uses whatever database is in its cache (named with trivy --cache-dir, as below), and the post-scan check holds it to the bound.
  • Online or offline, trivy scans never contact package registries: ASH passes trivy --offline-scan on every scan, and the database refresh is the separate step above. trivy then resolves Maven dependencies from the pom.xml files in the scanned tree and the local Maven repository (~/.m2/repository), not from the repositories a pom.xml declares or Maven Central. trivy does not check for new versions or announcements either: online every scan gets trivy --skip-version-check, and offline TRIVY_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=true in trivy's environment turns the same check off (see What offline mode turns off), since a trivy too old to know the flag refuses the command over it and ignores the variable. trivy-repo gets the same.
  • Where the database is kept: where trivy itself keeps it on the host. That is TRIVY_CACHE_DIR when it is set, else $XDG_CACHE_HOME/trivy on Linux when that is set, else ~/.cache/trivy (~/Library/Caches/trivy on macOS, %LocalAppData%\trivy on Windows). ASH names that directory to the update, to every scan (trivy --cache-dir), online and offline, and to the post-scan check, so all three read one database, sandboxed or not: the sandbox does not pass XDG_CACHE_HOME, and trivy left to its own default there would read another cache. A cache.dir in a trivy.yaml does not move it; set TRIVY_CACHE_DIR instead.

The database is only read by the vuln scanner; with vuln off nothing is measured.

docs.title: Offline and air-gapped use
docs.text:
trivy needs a database in its cache to scan offline. With none, ASH reports trivy MISSING with the reason and the scan exits 1; trivy is not run. To provide one, on a machine with network access:

TRIVY_CACHE_DIR=/path/to/cache trivy image --download-db-only

and point the offline scan at the same TRIVY_CACHE_DIR.

With misconfig added to scanners, trivy's Terraform checks do not run offline: trivy downloads the source of every module block a .tf file names (from the Terraform registry, with the host's git, or over HTTPS) whatever offline flags it is given. ASH passes trivy --misconfig-scanners with the installed trivy's own default list minus terraform, read from trivy fs --help, and logs a warning; when that list cannot be read, misconfig is left out of the offline scan. checkov still checks Terraform. trivy-repo does the same. In nix mode, export TRIVY_CACHE_DIR before running ash scan --mode nix; the variable is passed through to the scan. The container image built with --offline ships a trivy database (in /deps/.trivy, its TRIVY_CACHE_DIR), downloaded at build time; the build fails if that download fails or leaves the cache empty. Once that database is older than the 24h bound, scans in that image still pass: the image holds trivy-db to warn rather than fail, so every report records the stale database and its age. Its findings still lack advisories published since the build, so refresh it anyway: rebuild the image, or mount a fresher cache as TRIVY_CACHE_DIR. To make the stale database fail the scan instead, set content_db_staleness_offline_image_default: false (see Stale content databases). This default follows ASH_OFFLINE_AT_BUILD_TIME=YES, which the offline image sets; without it, a stale database in a TRIVY_CACHE_DIR you provide is held to content_db_staleness.

docs.title: Running it alongside the trivy-repo community plugin
docs.text:
The community trivy-repo plugin (enabled through ash_plugin_modules) keeps its name and its defaults (all four trivy scanners, unfixed vulnerabilities dropped, license_full: true), and has a module_dir option trivy does not. It names its own config file and modules directory, so a trivy.yaml in the scanned repository is not loaded, and settings that file made no longer apply. The two share their implementation (the database update, the cache and the treatment of trivy's input files) but are separate scanners. trivy-repo keeps its own scan path: it gets no trivy --timeout (trivy's 5-minute default applies), no trivy --skip-dirs for ASH's output directory, no offline check for a missing database, and its findings are rated by ASH's usual SARIF mapping rather than at trivy's own severity (see Severity), so one finding can carry different ASH severities in the two scanners.

trivy is on by default, so listing the Trivy plugin for trivy-repo runs trivy twice, and each finding is reported once per scanner, under that scanner's name. Both read the same database, which is measured once for each: a stale database is reported, and fails the scan, under each scanner's name. The rule ids are the same, so one suppression by rule_id and path covers both. To avoid the duplicate, keep one: set scanners.trivy.enabled: false, or stop listing the plugin.

docs.title: zizmor (GitHub Actions)
docs.text:
zizmor is a static analyzer for GitHub Actions. ASH runs it over a repository's workflows and composite actions and reports template injection, dangerous triggers, credential persistence, unpinned actions, excessive permissions and the rest of zizmor's audits.

actionlint, also a builtin scanner, flags template injection from untrusted event data too. ASH does not deduplicate across scanners, so with both enabled such a step is reported by each, under its own rule id.

docs.title: Enabling it
docs.text: zizmor is a builtin scanner, enabled by default: a default scan runs it. scanners.zizmor.enabled: false in the ASH config turns it off, and --scanners and --exclude-scanners select it as they select any scanner. If no zizmor satisfying tool_version is found, ASH installs one with uv tool install (online only). If that fails, the scanner is reported MISSING and the scan exits 1 (the incomplete-scan gate), as for every builtin scanner; ash dependencies install and the container image provide it.

docs.title: What gets scanned
docs.text:
ASH passes zizmor two kinds of file, taken from its scan set so .gitignore, .ignore and global_settings.ignore_paths apply (the ignore files only while honor_ignore_files is on, the default):

  • workflows: *.yml and *.yaml directly inside a .github/workflows directory (the only place GitHub runs a workflow from; subdirectories are not scanned), including when the source directory is itself .github or .github/workflows;
  • composite actions: every action.yml and action.yaml.

Files under directories named node_modules, .venv or venv are skipped, and so is a file that is a symlink resolving outside the scan root, with a warning: zizmor would read it where it points. In the source directory, such a link is left out by the scan set before zizmor's check sees it, with the warning Not scanning '<path>': link leaves the scanned tree, and is listed among the inputs not scanned (see Ignore files and the scan set). A broken symlink (its target is missing, or links loop) is skipped with a warning too, since zizmor would fail the whole run on it. A repository with neither kind of file does not start zizmor; the scanner reports SKIPPED with zero findings, the same as cfn-nag on a repository with no templates.

zizmor is a Python package ASH runs through uv, so --python-only runs it.

A file named action.yml that is not a GitHub Actions definition is not counted. A workflow or action that zizmor cannot load (a YAML syntax error, or a file in .github/workflows that is not a valid workflow) is counted as a target that failed, which --fail-on-incomplete-scanners reports.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
scanners:
  zizmor:
    enabled: true
    options:
      persona: regular        # regular, pedantic or auditor
      config_file: null       # zizmor config; relative to where it is set, or absolute
      online_audits: false    # see "Network access and tokens"
      honor_inline_ignores: false  # see "Suppressions"
      tool_version: ">=1.29.0,<2.0.0"
      install_timeout: 300
      scan_timeout: 1800
      severity_threshold: null
  • persona: zizmor's persona. regular has the fewest false positives, pedantic adds code-smell findings, and auditor reports everything.
  • config_file: passed as zizmor --config, when the operator set it: from --config-overrides, or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory (one that is not repository-written). A relative path is taken from the directory of the ASH config file that sets it, or from the working directory for --config-overrides, not from the source directory (see Relative paths in the operator's settings); an absolute path is used as given. Without it, ASH runs zizmor --no-config, so a zizmor.yml or .github/zizmor.yml in the scanned repository is not read: a config there can disable audits or ignore findings, which zizmor then never reports, so they would be neither in ASH's results nor counted as suppressed. config_file set by an ASH config inside a git checkout or the scanned directory is ignored with a warning, and an MCP client cannot set it at all (see online_audits below). A configured file that does not exist fails the scan rather than being ignored. The file may be inside the scanned tree, but the scanned repository decides what is at such a path, so one there that leads out of the tree through a symbolic link fails the scan with ERROR and zizmor is not run. zizmor quotes the offending text of a config it cannot parse in its error, and that error reaches ASH's log and the scanner's stderr log, so do not point this at a file holding anything else.
  • honor_inline_ignores: when true, zizmor applies its own # zizmor: ignore[...] comments and the ignore rules of an operator's config_file. Off by default; see "Suppressions". Honored only when the operator sets it.
  • tool_version: the pip-style constraint for installing zizmor. A value that is not a valid constraint is ignored with a warning and the default is used. It decides which zizmor is installed and which one on PATH is accepted, so a value other than the default is honored only when the operator sets it (--config-overrides, or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory); set by an ASH config inside one, it is ignored with a warning.
  • install_timeout: seconds allowed for uv tool install of zizmor.
  • scan_timeout: seconds zizmor may run; past it zizmor is killed and the scanner reports ERROR.
  • severity_threshold: this scanner's override of the global severity threshold.

docs.title: Network access and tokens
docs.text:
ASH always runs zizmor --offline unless online_audits: true. Offline is the default because zizmor reads a GitHub token from GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN or ZIZMOR_GITHUB_TOKEN by itself, and a token that happens to be in a CI job's environment is not permission to use it. While offline, ASH removes those three variables from zizmor's environment.

online_audits: true drops zizmor --offline and lets those variables reach zizmor unchanged, which enables the audits that query the GitHub API (for example known-vulnerable actions and impostor commits). It is honored only when the operator sets it, with --config-overrides or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory; set by a config inside one, it is ignored with a warning and zizmor runs offline without the tokens. An MCP client cannot configure zizmor at all: its whole section, /scanners/zizmor/**, is denied to a client whatever a profile's denied_paths says, as for every scanner that can send data off the host. ASH never reads, copies or logs the token and never puts it on zizmor's command line. ASH's own offline mode (ASH_OFFLINE=true or ash scan --offline) overrides online_audits. Under --sandbox, zizmor never gets the token: the sandbox passes no GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN or ZIZMOR_GITHUB_TOKEN, so online audits cannot authenticate. It gets a network only when the operator lists zizmor in sandbox.network_scanners, and never when the scan is offline.

ZIZMOR_CONFIG, ZIZMOR_OFFLINE and ZIZMOR_NO_ONLINE_AUDITS are always removed from zizmor's environment, so a scan's result depends on the repository and the ASH config rather than on the shell it ran in. Use config_file instead of ZIZMOR_CONFIG.

docs.title: Severity mapping
docs.text:
zizmor rates each finding with a severity and a confidence. ASH combines them:

zizmor severity confidence Medium or High confidence Low High HIGH MEDIUM Medium MEDIUM LOW Low LOW INFO Informational INFO INFO

zizmor's scale stops at High, so no zizmor finding is CRITICAL. A low-confidence finding is one zizmor expects to be wrong some of the time, so it is reported one band lower. The SARIF level is set to match (HIGH error, MEDIUM warning, LOW note, INFO none), and zizmor's own values stay on the result as properties["zizmor/severity"] and properties["zizmor/confidence"]. A finding missing either value keeps zizmor's own level.

With the default MEDIUM threshold, the low-confidence artipacked finding (Medium, Low) is reported LOW and does not fail the scan on its own.

docs.title: Suppressions
docs.text:
Rule IDs are zizmor's audit names with a zizmor/ prefix, for example zizmor/template-injection. ASH suppressions by rule, path and line all apply:

global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - rule_id: zizmor/dangerous-triggers
      path: .github/workflows/release.yml
      line_start: 3
      reason: "Runs only on tags pushed by maintainers"

zizmor's own ignore comments (# zizmor: ignore[template-injection]) are not honored by default. Such a comment makes zizmor drop the finding before ASH sees it, so it would be neither reported nor counted as suppressed; ASH runs zizmor --no-ignores, which also turns off the ignore rules of an operator's config_file (its other settings still apply). To honor both, the operator sets honor_inline_ignores: true with --config-overrides or in an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory; set by an ASH config inside one, it is ignored with a warning. A zizmor.yml in the scanned repository is never read. Package-scoped and symbol-scoped suppressions do not apply: zizmor reports no packages, and a workflow has no functions or classes.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
ash dependencies install installs zizmor with uv tool install, the newest release within tool_version, and the ASH container image ships zizmor 1.30.1. ASH also uses any zizmor already on PATH whose zizmor --version satisfies tool_version, which covers the nix flake (nixpkgs supplies zizmor), Homebrew, and cargo install. Offline, ASH does not try to install zizmor; install it first.

zizmor is MIT licensed.

docs.title: Community Plugins
docs.text: This section is dedicated to community-developed plugins for ASH. Community plugins extend ASH's functionality with additional scanners, reporters, converters, and event handlers developed by the community.

docs.title: Security Scanners
docs.text:
• Ferret Scan Plugin - Integrates Ferret Scan for comprehensive sensitive data detection (credit cards, passports, SSNs, API keys, secrets, and more)
  • Snyk Code Plugin - Integrates Snyk Code for static application security testing (SAST) of source code vulnerabilities
  • Trivy Plugin - Integrates Aquasec's Trivy for vulnerability, misconfiguration, secret, and license scanning

These three ship inside ASH. Each takes part in a scan only when that scan names its plugin module in ash_plugin_modules or --ash-plugin-modules, as its page shows. The MCP list_scanners tool reports them either way; listing one does not add it to any scan.

docs.title: Contributing a Community Plugin
docs.text:
We encourage the community to develop and share plugins that extend ASH's capabilities.

To contribute a community plugin:

  1. Develop your plugin following the Plugin Development Guide
  2. Host your plugin in a public repository
  3. Open a pull request to add your plugin to this documentation
  4. Include the following information in your PR:
  5. Plugin name and description
  6. Link to the repository
  7. Installation instructions
  8. Configuration options
  9. Example usage

docs.title: Plugin Submission Guidelines
docs.text:
To ensure quality and security, community plugins should:

  • Be open source with a compatible license
  • Include comprehensive documentation
  • Follow ASH's plugin development best practices
  • Include tests and examples
  • Be actively maintained

docs.title: Plugin Review Process
docs.text:
When you submit a PR to add your plugin to this documentation, the ASH team will:

  1. Review the plugin code for security and quality
  2. Test the plugin functionality
  3. Provide feedback on any necessary changes
  4. Merge the documentation PR once the plugin meets the guidelines

docs.text:
